TRAGIC SMASH ‘Loving’ dad, 44, killed after being hit by six vehicles including cop car on major A-road is pictured as tributes paid

TRIBUTES have been paid for a “loving” dad who was killed in a six vehicle horror crash on a major A-road.

Gerard Trojanowski, 44, tragically died after being hit by multiple vehicles, including a marked police car, on the A40 in Wales.



Cops scrambled to the scene in Carmarthen at around 9.50pm on July 28 after reports of a pedestrian on the carriageway.

According to police, as they rushed to the busy road, five vehicles and one cop car hit the dad.



Gerard was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.

His family said: “Gerard was a loving husband and father. A wonderful and generous person with a good heart.

“He will always be in our memories. As a family we ask for privacy during this difficult time.”

After the tragedy, which saw the busy road shut for a day, Dyfed-Powys Police made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office of Police Conduct.

Cops also issued a wider appeal for any information regarding the incident.

News.title: Putin unleashes deadly ballistic missile bombardment as child among three dead just hours after Ukraine stadium blitzed
News.content:
A CHILD is among at least three people who have been killed after Vladimir Putin unleashed another deadly missile barrage near Kyiv.

It came just hours after the dictator blitzed one of Ukraine‘s largest sports stadiums on the eve of a top-flight match.



Moscow has ramped up attacks on Kyiv in recent months, but has been on the receiving end of some long-range Ukrainian drone attacks.

Russian forces pummelled the Ukrainian capital on Tuesday night, launching 28 missiles in a 20-minute nightmare that became one of the deadliest onslaughts this year.



At least 21 people died and dozens of homes were blown up.

Early this morning, a quick-fire salvo of ballistic missiles struck just east of the city in the Brovary district.

A child and two adults were killed in the village of Pukhivka, while at least three others were wounded.

Houses and cars were damaged by falling debris and a non-residential building was set ablaze, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration.



Shocking pictures from the heart of the action show firefighters tackling infernos cropping up across the city.

Witnesses reported hearing dozens of explosions and several air raid alerts amid the onslaught.

Ukraine’s state emergency service DSNS shared pictures of devastated buildings and garages, adding: “The number of victims is being clarified.”



Russia claimed to have blitzed a key factory that manufactures Ukrainian warheads.

Kyiv has been desperate to rebuild its stock of missile interceptors.

The Ukrainian Air Force was not able to destroy a single incoming Iskander-M ballistic missile overnight.

President Volodymyr Zelensky has meanwhile landed in the Serbian capital Belgrade to try to forge greater economic and security ties with President Aleksandar Vučić.

Despite the Ukrainian leader pushing to build wider support for Ukraine, Vučić has refused to apply sanctions to Russia.



Earlier this week, Zelensky mourned the “horrific casualties and destruction” caused by Putin’s last barrage.

He added that having stronger interceptor capability “could have saved lives”.

Ukraine’s supply of interceptors from allies has been “significantly reduced” this year, but Zelensky will be hopeful of getting a Patriot production license from the US.

Kyiv launched its own strikes overnight, hitting two oil depots deep inside Russia as well as Moscow-linked shadow ships in the Black Sea.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Zelensky has ruthlessly targeted Russian oil refineries this year, plunging the country into a fuel crisis.



Attempts to reach a peace deal have stalled of late, leading to an escalation in attacks.

News.title: The mystery of Mexico’s vast ‘Zone of Silence’ with no radio signal plagued by ‘alien’ sightings & mutated plants
News.content:
RADIO SILENCE The mystery of Mexico’s vast ‘Zone of Silence’ with no radio signal plagued by ‘alien’ sightings & mutated plants

SECONDS after a dazzling ball of light illuminates the sky above the vast expanse of desert, the object darts away at a “dizzying” speed and vanishes from view.

The extraordinary sight is just one of many reports of unexplained glowing objects in the sky in a remote corner of northern Mexico known as the Zone of Silence.



The 31-mile wide area deep in the Chihuahuan Desert has inspired many legends over the decades – drawing comparisons to the Bermuda Triangle and Area 51.

Phones stop working, radio signals fail and compasses spin out of control in this desolate part of the Mapimí Biosphere Reserve, according to those who have visited the area.



Many believe the phenomena are explained by a mystery electromagnetic phenomenon caused by the metals in the desert soil.

The area’s supernatural reputation first took off in 1970 when a US Air Force rocket went wildly off target and crash-landed in the desert.

At the time, some believed it was due to the area’s magnetic anomalies.

The area is known to be a hotspot for celestial activity, with meteorites reported to frequently come crashing down to earth in the desert.



But some claim the Zone of Silence attracts more than just asteroids, with numerous reports of UFO and extraterrestrial sightings.

Benjamín Marcelo Palacios Perches has lived his entire life on the edge of the zone and was born in nearby Escalón, Chihuahua.

He owns a ranch that he has named “Zona del Silencio” after the famous landmark, and offers accommodation, traditional sweatlodge ceremonies, stargazing and tours into the zone for visitors.

The 71-year-old frequently visits the zone and has had many mystifying experiences that he believes have no earthly explanation.

He told The Sun: “I and many other visitors have observed disc-shaped objects, triangular objects, cylindrical craft, and also balls of light and fireballs that make erratic movements.



“Movements that no human-made craft could perform, let alone dart away at the dizzying speeds we have witnessed.

“I have had the opportunity to observe all those objects, lights and fireballs.”



Benjamin said he experienced first-hand the electromagnetic anomalies associated with the zone that mean compasses and phones don’t work.

He believes the area acts as a “powerful magnet attracting celestial bodies”.

“I am absolutely convinced that these strange electromagnetic powers exist in the Zone of Silence – I have experienced them myself, but I am not the only one,” he said.

“When I was very young, I used to hear my grandfather and his generation speak of these strange occurrences.



“Now, I hear newer and newer generations – successive waves of people -continuing to speak of the same phenomena.”

The Zone of Silence is widely reported to have first been coined in 1966 when Augusto Harry de la Peña, the leader of an expedition for oil company Pemex, experienced problems with his radio.

Since then, thousands have visited the zone and come up with their own theories – which sceptics have dismissed as inventions to attract tourists.

Some of the claims include sightings of mutant animals and plants.

Among the more fantastical stories swirling around the zone are tales of encounters with tall, fair-haired beings who speak perfect Spanish and ask for water before they disappear without a trace.



Experts say the real reason for the stunted signals in the area is actually due to subterranean deposits of magnetite messing with receptors.

The extremely remote and mountainous region is also responsible for the poor reception much like many isolated areas and deserts.

Signal can actually be found in the Zone of Silence but only in certain areas.



The supernatural claims have also been widely debunked as urban legends passed down through generations.

Dr Fernando Ortega Gutierrez, a researcher at the Institute of Geology in Mexico City, said he had visited the zone and believed the electromagnetic phenomena could be explained by the soil’s composition.

“Our compass did not work, giving chaotic orientations of the needle,” he said.

“On examining the ground we were working at, we explained that fact, blaming itono the abundance of detrital grains of magnetite in the soils.

“The mountains around the area may be rich in magnetite-rich granites or iron ores.”



Travellers continue to come from around the world to witness these strange phenomena, including US digital nomad Hannah Pinkerton, who lives in Mexico teaching Spanish.

She visited the Zone of Silence last year and camped the night in the desert with a tour group, in an experience she documented on her travel website Destined for Adventure.

“It’s really beautiful, the sunset was really beautiful, and it was a nice camping experience – there is not a lot out there,” she said.

“It’s very quiet and peaceful, there’s not a lot of trees, there’s not a lot of mountains, there’s just a lot of sand and open land.”

Hannah said the Zone of Silence is not well known outside the Spanish-speaking world, but it is very well known in Mexico with friends telling her before she left that she might “see a spaceship”.



She said she is “open minded and curious” about the paranormal but did not see anything out of the ordinary.

“It’s a vast desert and it’s very quiet and peaceful, the radios and cell phones and things don’t work, so there is not a lot of distraction to take you away from the quietness,” she said.

Benjamin agreed the remoteness and beauty of the zone – as well as its strange phenomena – is what has “captivated” him for decades.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It is a remarkable place; one feels a very special energy that recharges the body, making one feel dynamic and highly active – as if infused with a surge of energy,” he said.

“That is the sensation one experiences in the Zone of Silence.”

News.title: Horrifying moment fast food staff scramble for cover as mass shooter fires into store window during deadly rampage
News.content:
THIS is the horrifying moment desperate workers clamber over each other after a gunman shoots into a drive-thru window amid a sick murder spree.

Terrifying footage captures the moment In-n-Out workers scramble for cover in the Idaho mass shooting which left three dead on August 1.



Shocking CCTV from inside the restaurant shows at least nine employees chaotically falling over each other as they try to evacuate the area.

The gunman, 24-year-old Chad Williams, acted alone before dying of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, officials said.



His motive remains unclear.

Now harrowing video, released by the Twin Falls Police Department, shows the moment the carnage began when Williams opened fire at the drive-thru window.

read more world news GUN HORROR At least three dead after 'gunman opens fire' outside burger restaurant

Employee Ashley Garibay, 23, was the first to be shot and later died from her injuries.

Williams then fatally shoots his second victim, 59-year-old Christopher Claunch, who was inside another car.



At that moment, former Twin Falls and Idaho State Police Officer Austin “AJ” Scott who happened to be there at the time starts running toward the gunman.

Williams takes aim and strikes the ex-cop.

Scott’s father later wrote on Facebook that his son was “critically injured” as a result and is facing a “long road of surgeries, rehab and recovery”.



After calmly parking his car, Williams then peers back into the restaurant’s payment window and fires another shot at employees who were inside rendering aid to Garibay.

His handgun jams and he walks back to his car to retrieve a rifle, offering staff a moment to escape

At this moment another hero off-duty cop jumps the counter inside the restaurant and can be seen instructing the workers to run for cover as he aims his gun at the window and later the door.

Now armed with a rifle, Williams fires at people in their cars at the drive-thru before he returns to the payment window to be met with the unidentified trooper.

They both exchange fire.



Williams then retreats from the window momentarily before returning and firing another shot inside.

He strikes a “Good Samaritan” who is attempting to assist the off-duty trooper and render aid to the victim inside, according to the video.

Williams then shoots at multiple vehicles stopped at a nearby red light, striking three victims, before running to a nearby Tesla charging station.

He fires at the first Tesla he sees before fatally shooting Dale Schultz, 66, and hitting the man’s now gravely injured wife, Reinette, inside their car – all while a third armed good Samaritan is firing at him.

Still holding his gun he then moved inside the nearby Twin Falls Visitor’s Center with the video showing two people cowering in the corner as he sulks around the location.



Finally then makes his way to a hiking trail, where a brave bystander tried to halt him to give others time to run away.

In a climactic moment, a officer’s bodycam footage captures the moment he spots Williams on a nearby river bank.

He shouts: “Hey, show me your hands.”

At that very moment, Williams “dies of a self-inflicted gunshot wound and falls into the canyon.”

A statement at the end of the video said: “The Twin Falls Police Department is certain that additional acts of heroism and rendering aid to those in need contributed to the saving of lives,” the statement reads.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“At least ten people were left injured from the mass shooting, which remains under investigation, according to the department.”

In a statement, the fast food chain said: “In-n-Out is heartbroken as we mourn the tragic loss of three innocent lives, one of them being our Associate Ashley Garibay.”

News.title: ‘Distress’ as pedestrians targeted with liquid from passing cars across Surrey
News.content:
‘Distress’ as pedestrians targeted with liquid from passing cars across Surrey

There's been several incidents reported to police in the town in recent weeks where pedestrians said passing cars either squirted or chucked a liquid at them

View Image There's been several reports of similar incidents in Surrey in recent weeks (Image: Google Maps)

An investigation has been launched in Surrey after pedestrians were reportedly targeted with liquid from passing cars.

‌



At around 8pm on Thursday, a runner reported a black Audi slowed down to throw a substance, believed to be water, in their face from a bottle. Surrey Police said the incident occurred on College Road, Epsom, and the victim was not injured.

‌



It comes after several similar incidents reported in another Surrey borough. In Elmbridge, a liquid-filled glass bottle was reportedly thrown at a pedestrian on Esher Road, near the Molesey Road roundabout, from a black SUV at 10.42pm on July 17, Surrey Police said. There were no injuries reported.

‌



A further two incidents were also reported in Cobham, a village in Elmbridge, on May 6, The Express reports.

A victim said liquid was thrown at them from a passing car at around 5.55pm in Leigh Corner. Another reported they were also doused in liquid the same day, at about 7.50pm in Tilt Road. The roads are about 150 metres apart.

‌



Elmbridge Borough Commander Inspector Chris Thoday said: “We recognise the distress and alarm incidents like this can cause.

“While thankfully no injuries have been reported, this type of behaviour is completely unacceptable.

“We are actively investigating and ask anyone with information to come forward.”

Article continues below

Surrey Police asked for other potential victims, witnesses and anyone with dashcam or video footage to contact the force quoting PR/45260086397 for Elmbridge or PR/45260095129 for Epsom.

News.title: Mum loses 9 stone and drops from size 22 to 6 but 'operation wasn't a magic fix'
News.content:
Mum loses 9 stone and drops from size 22 to 6 but 'operation wasn't a magic fix'

Amy Salmon had spent years comfort eating and despite trying countless diets, she couldn't shift the extra pounds

View 5 Images Amy Salmon in March 2024

A mum has shed half her body weight to completely transform her looks – and her health. Amy Salmon spent years comfort eating, and despite attempting "countless" diets, she struggled to shift the excess weight – eventually tipping the scales at 18 stone and squeezing into a size 22.

‌



But following a breakup two years ago, the mum-of-two resolved to finally put herself first, embarking on a determined mission to get fit. Now, Amy is virtually unrecognisable, having dropped half her body weight to slip into a trim size 6, and having injectables "everywhere" to enhance her facial appearance.

‌



"The biggest difference isn't what I see in the mirror – it's how I feel," said the aesthetics practitioner from Hertfordshire. "Life has changed massively.

‌



"I finally feel confident in myself, and I no longer hide away from photos or avoid social situations. I struggled with my confidence for a long time, and food became something I turned to when I was stressed, overwhelmed or unhappy.

View 5 Images Amy Salmon in April 2024

"Looking back now, I realise I wasn't just carrying extra weight physically, I was carrying a lot emotionally too."

‌



The mounting pressures of motherhood, a hectic lifestyle, and a deteriorating relationship drove Amy to use food as a crutch.

She regularly snacked on high-calorie, processed foods such as chocolate and sweets, while also indulging in takeaways like McDonald's and pizzas, piling up oversized portions with little regard for their nutritional content.

While she was dissatisfied with her appearance and attempted diets such as Slimming World and weight loss shakes, it wasn't until her 2023 separation from her former partner encouraged her to begin putting her own health first that Amy decided enough was enough.

‌



She said: "I reached a point where I realised I wasn't living the life I wanted. I wanted to be healthier, more confident and, most importantly, able to keep up with my children as they grew up.

'The operation was not a magic fix'

"I knew something had to change, not just for how I looked, but for how I felt." After finding dieting unsuccessful, she underwent gastric sleeve surgery in Egypt in June 2024 to help her with her weight loss.

Within 12 months, she had shed nine stone – cutting her body weight in half. She said: "I always say that the operation was a tool, not a magic fix.

‌



View 5 Images Amy Salmon

"It still required a huge amount of commitment, learning healthier habits and changing my mindset. During this time I focused on prioritising protein, exercising regularly, building muscle and creating sustainable habits rather than chasing quick fixes.

"Now, my diet is centred around protein and whole foods. A typical day might include eggs on sourdough or Greek yoghurt with protein and berries for breakfast, chicken with salad or some form of omelette for lunch, and lean meat or fish with vegetables for dinner.

‌



"I still enjoy treats in moderation, but my relationship with food is completely different. I eat to fuel my body rather than to cope with my emotions."

The impact on the young mum's life has been nothing short of remarkable. She said: "I have so much more energy, I can be far more active with my children and everyday tasks that once felt exhausting are now effortless.

"I spend less on takeaways – they were costing me a fortune – and my mood is happier as I feel better in my own skin. My confidence has completely transformed and that's had a huge impact on both my personal life and my career.

‌



"It's also inspired the mission behind my business, because I know what it's like to lack confidence and I love helping other women feel better about themselves too." Amy has been documenting her transformation on TikTok, where her videos have racked up over one million views.

View 5 Images Amy Salmon in July 2026

Yet it isn't solely her weight loss that has captured people's attention, but the extraordinary shift in her overall appearance. Never one to "gate keep", Amy revealed she "religiously" undergoes treatments every four weeks, which have helped shape and maintain her striking new look.

‌



She places particular focus on skincare, receiving skin boosters including hyaluronic acid injections, as well as polynucleotides – the infamous salmon sperm treatment – under her eyes, in her lower face and neck.

Amy also has Botox across her face, along with lip and chin filler. She said: "I went from looking completely unhealthy.

"[I was] physically overweight, my face looked puffy and tired, and overall I feel it made me look older than I actually was. To now [I'm] looking a lot healthier, more put together and less tired.

‌



View 5 Images Amy Salmon in June 2026

"People have also said I look younger." However, she insists that appearance isn't her primary focus.

Amy added: "If there's one thing I'd want people to know, it's that losing weight doesn't automatically fix every problem in your life – but it can give you the confidence to start changing everything else. The physical transformation is obvious, but the mental transformation has been even bigger.

Article continues below

"I'm proud of the weight I've lost, but I'm even prouder of the woman I've become through the process. And if sharing my story helps even one person believe that change is possible, then it's worth it."

News.title: Tributes to 'wonderful' dad, 44, who died after being hit by six vehicles on busy A40
News.content:
Tributes to 'wonderful' dad, 44, who died after being hit by six vehicles on busy A40

Tributes have poured in for a much-loved dad remembered as a “wonderful” man after the fatal A40 incident in Carmarthen.

View Image Gerard Trojanowski (Image: Dyfed-Powys Police)

Tributes have been paid to a “wonderful" and "generous” husband and father who died after being hit by several vehicles on a major A road.

‌



Gerard Trojanowski, 44, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to the A40 in Carmarthen at around 9.50pm on July 28.

‌



Dyfed-Powys Police said officers had responded following concerns for the safety of a pedestrian. Several vehicles, including a marked police vehicle which was on patrol, collided with Gerard, according to the force.

‌



Gerard, who lived in the Merthyr Tydfil area, has now been named by police.

In a tribute reported by Wales Online, his family said: “Gerard was a loving husband and father. A wonderful and generous person with a good heart. He will always be in our memories.

‌



“As a family we ask for privacy during this difficult time.”

A section of the A40 in Carmarthen remained closed for almost 24 hours following the fatal incident.

Dyfed-Powys Police made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is a statutory requirement following incidents of this kind.

Article continues below

Officers have also appealed for witnesses or anyone with information about what happened to come forward by calling 101.

News.title: Another hosepipe ban starts today - what is exempt and what you can't do in your gardens
News.content:
Another hosepipe ban starts today - what is exempt and what you can't do in your gardens

Another water company has imposed a hosepipe ban on millions of customers as low rainfall and another incoming heatwave puts pressure on water supplies

View 3 Images New hosepipe restrictions are coming into force (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

A new hosepipe ban has started for nearly 2 million people today as the UK braces for a fifth heatwave.

‌



Most of south-west England will be hit following a prolonged period of dry weather, as South West Water announced the restriction. All customers in Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset and the Isles of Scilly will be subject to the temporary conditions, which started from 1am today.

‌



The water company said a dry summer, significantly below average rainfall and high demand had increased pressure on the local water resources and led to the temporary ban.

‌



Met Office issues heatwave verdict and names two regions facing 36C on Thursday READ MORE :

View 3 Images Aerial view of dry fields at the Falmouth Golf Club, in Cornwall, on July 31 (Image: Getty Images)

What will people not be allowed to do?

Restrictions have been placed on non-essential activities like filling swimming pools or paddling pools, watering gardens, washing cars, boats, patios and windows.

People will still be allowed to use water for washing, cooking, drinking and flushing toilets. Customers can also carry out activities without a hosepipe - like using a watering can on flowers and plants.

‌



What are the exemptions?

The hosepipe ban does not apply to certain customers, which includes:

Blue Badge holders

People on the water company's Priority Services Register and unable to make reasonable adjustments due to a health condition or disability

Cases where human health and safety need to be protected

Water is needed for animal welfare, including pets, livestock and fish

There is also an exception for people who are not using water from the mains supply, for examples if it has been taken from a recycled water storage system.

‌



View 3 Images Dried land at Glastonbury, Somerset, on July 31 (Image: Getty Images)

Why has the new ban come into force?

South West Water said a dry summer, significantly below average rainfall and high demand had increased pressure on the local water resources and led to the temporary ban.

The water company added that rainfall in the region has been considerably below the seasonal average for several months. South West Water said this temporary restriction will "ensure a resilient supply of water to its customers".

‌



Last month was the driest July for England and Wales since records began in 1836, according to provisional figures released by the Met Office.

What else have customers been asked to do?

South West Water has asked people in the impacted region to take shorter showers and turn off the tap while brushing their teeth. Customers can also rub washing machines and dishwashers only with full loads.

Sam Bottomley, South West Water, said: "Our teams have been working tirelessly to protect supplies for customers. We've maximised water production wherever possible, increased leak detection and repairs, moved water around our network and introduced a wide range of operational measures to make the best use of the water available."

Article continues below

Bottomley added: "Every litre saved now will help protect our rivers and water resources while drought conditions continue. By making small changes to how we use water, our customers can make a real difference."

Which other water companies have restrictions in place?

Some companies have had bans in place since mid-July. Nine water companies have temporary bans in place: Affinity Water, Anglian Water, Cambridge Water, Essex and Suffolk Water, Southern Water, South East Water, South West Water, Dŵr Cymru Welsh Water and Thames Water.

This comes as new heat alerts are to come into force as the UK braces for its fifth heatwave of the year, bringing scorching highs of 36C. The Met Office said temperatures will climb through the weekend, with a high of 36C expected in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by Thursday.

News.title: Brian Reade: 'Farage said Brexit would stop the boats - we must ignore his cynical fantasies'
News.content:
When I was growing up I often heard sarcastic claims that ­winning the Second World War was the worst thing that had happened to Britain. Relatives who had survived the Blitz or fought abroad would ponder the point of their generation’s sacrifice when the German and Japanese ­economies were booming and ours was bust. Today I see a different downside to that vital victory over Nazism.

It has locked a huge group of Britons into a mental straitjacket, unable to let go of a war that has been eulogised out of all proportion. The blind fools, nearly all of whom were not alive in the early-1940s, are manipulated by right-wing ­opportunists who profit from viewing every event through the prism of Dunkirk or D-Day.

This week Nigel Farage tried to shake off questions about his dubious finances and his war of ideas with a bin when he announced he would stop the boats by marshalling the Royal Navy to drag them all back to France through “Operation Fortress”, which would be “the largest military operation in the English Channel since World War Two”. Despite the fact that we don’t possess a fully-functioning Navy (even the warship on the front of Reform’s Operation brochure was flogged to Brazil eight years ago) and military experts and French authorities all mocked his stunt as a ludicrous non-starter, Farage went up in the opinion polls. Because so many naive Brits swallow his cynical fantasy that the only way this country will be great is by turning the clock back 80-odd years.

‌



When France described Farage’s plan as a violation of its sovereignty, Reform MP Sarah Pochin tweeted: “Pity the French did not show the same resolve in defending their sovereignty in June 1940.” Which is lamentable in every sense of the word, especially in its ignorance. As many as 570,000 French people died in the Second World War, more than half of them civilians. The total of Britons killed was 450,000.

For years the Right has profited from peddling the insulting myth that British sacrifice alone defeated Hitler, therefore, we are superior to the rest of Europe. That lie won Brexit. Remember Vote Leave buses blaring the soundtrack to The Great Escape, billboards urging drivers to “Halt ze German advance! Vote Leave,” and Tory Mark Francois claiming: “My father was a D-Day veteran. He never submitted to bullying by any German. Neither will his son.” All tragic garbage.

But back to “Operation Fortress”. How come we need it when last summer Farage assured us that Reform’s mass deportations would end the small boats crisis? Wasn’t Brexit supposed to make Britain a border-secure fortress? Surely with Labour cutting Channel crossings by 44% this year, do we really need to distract what’s left of our Navy from monitoring ­Britain’s real enemies?

When you operate in Forties Fantasy World you don’t need to answer such questions. You just grab your dog whistle, claim the root of everyone’s problem is immigration, spout Churchillian rhetoric and tell the mugs that if you elect Reform, Britons never, ever, ever will be slaves. Which bumps up your popularity and reinforces the illusion that Britain can be magicked back to some glorious, all-white, problem-free past if we just put our trust in a dodgy salesman in a Union Jack suit with a boot full of snake oil. Snake oil sold in Spitfire-shaped bottles with instructions to be slugged back like a large glass of Vera Lynn.

‌

News.title: 'I spent night at Travelodge and woke up covered in 100 bites – people say I look diseased'
News.content:
'I spent night at Travelodge and woke up covered in 100 bites – people say I look diseased'

Travel blogger Hannah Stephenson has managed to largely avoid bugs during her trips to Asia and Africa, but she was left with more than 100 bed bug bites during a night at a Travelodge

View 5 Images Hannah Stephenson was left covered in bites (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

A woman who spent a night at a Travelodge hotel woke up covered in more than 100 bed bug bites that she says have left people fearing she has a disease.

‌



Travel blogger Hannah Stephenson, 31, had been expertly dodging creepy crawlies while travelling around Asia and Africa, but it was a night in Cambridge that proved her undoing.

‌



She was staying at the Newmarket Road branch of the budget hotel firm on July 26 after a day out with a friend.

‌



Hannah woke the next day feeling itchy before discovering her arms were covered in red spots.

She soon discovered blood stains and black dots on her pillow before finding bed bugs crawling in the bedding.

The horrified customer soon discovered more bites appearing across her chest, back, face and legs.

‌



View 5 Images Hannah says people think she has a disease (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

She complained to reception but alleged she was simply told to contact Travelodge's customer services by email. They assured her that hotel room would not be let that night.

Travelodge has since apologised to Hannah for the "distressing" incident and claim they have "resolved the matter to her satisfaction".

‌



They also confirmed there were bed bugs in Hannah's room and claim they are retraining housekeeping at the hotel.

Hannah, from Bassingbourn, Cambridgeshire, said: "I was horrified and shocked. I didn't expect it from a Travelodge, I always thought they are pretty reliable. The swelling has gone down. Now it looks like I have chicken pox.

"People have been horrified, they've said I look like I have a disease. Everyone is saying how bad it looks."

‌



View 5 Images Hannah found bed bugs crawling over the sheets (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

Hannah admits the incident left her "embarrassed" to attend her cousin's wedding earlier this month. She was forced to cover up the bite marks with foundation while she also switched outfits to a dress with long sleeves - not ideal given the current hot spell.

She added: "I felt really embarrassed going to a wedding. They're on my hands, which are hard to cover up, I feel very self-conscious. People are going to think I'm dirty or something.

‌



"I don't usually wear foundation but I went to buy one to cover up for the wedding, I couldn't wear my original outfit which had no sleeves."

Hannah, who has travelled in Asia and Africa, says she's never experienced anything like it anywhere else in the world.

View 5 Images The blogger has managed to avoid creepy crawlies during her travels (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

‌



She called 111 who advised her to visit a pharmacy, where she was given steroids and antihistamines to tackle the bites.

But she is still scratching after a week while the incident is making her want to avoid hotels - especially other Travelodge branches.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson’s experience and recognise how distressing an incident like this can be.

‌



"The safety of our customers is our priority and we maintain stringent, expert-led measures to prevent and manage pest issues, including training our housekeeping colleagues to be vigilant and to spot early signs wherever possible.

View 5 Images Hannah doubts she will ever stay in a Travelodge again (Image: Kennedy News/@thecapetownblog)

"Bed bug activity affects the wider hospitality sector and is completely unrelated to hygiene or cleanliness standards.

Article continues below

"In the rare instance that an issue is reported in one of our hotels, we immediately take affected and surrounding

rooms out of service for inspection and treatment by independent pest control experts. We have apologised directly to Ms Stephenson and resolved the matter to her satisfaction."

News.title: What are legal rights when neighbour's car alarm goes off all day and night
News.content:
What are legal rights when neighbour's car alarm goes off all day and night

A car alarm that repeatedly sounds throughout the day can quickly become a nuisance, but is there anything legal you can do to stop it?

View 3 Images There are approximately roughly 36 million licensed cars in the UK (Image: Getty Images)

A car alarm going off every now and then is something most people can accept. But when it keeps sounding throughout the day or repeatedly wakes you during the night, it's easy to wonder whether there's anything you can do to end it once and for all.

‌



While the noise can be frustrating and painful, a faulty car alarm does not automatically mean the owner has broken the law. Whether action can be taken depends on how often it happens, how long it lasts and whether the noise is considered serious enough to amount to a statutory nuisance. According to the UK Government, local councils have powers to investigate complaints about excessive noise.

‌



Environmental health teams assess noise complaints on a case-by-case basis rather than relying on a fixed legal limit. GOV.UK says councils will consider factors including the volume of the noise, the time of day, how frequently it occurs and how it affects nearby residents when deciding whether it amounts to a statutory nuisance.

‌



View 3 Images The noise can be more than just frustrating - it can be a nuisance (Image: Getty Images)

If the council decides a statutory nuisance exists, it can serve an abatement notice requiring the person responsible to deal with the problem. Failing to comply with that notice without a reasonable excuse can result in prosecution or financial penalties under the Environmental Protection Act 1990.

‌



In some cases, councils also have specific powers to deal with vehicles whose alarms continue sounding for long periods when the owner cannot be contacted. Under the Clean Neighbourhoods and Environment Act 2005, authorised officers can arrange for persistent vehicle alarms to be silenced in certain circumstances.

Before making a formal complaint, however, official guidance recommends trying to resolve the issue directly with your neighbour if you feel comfortable doing so. They may not realise the alarm is repeatedly sounding, particularly if the vehicle is parked away from their home or they are out at work.

View 3 Images Car alarms go off due to a real threat or a false trigger, most commonly caused by faulty sensors (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

If the problem continues, it can help to keep a record of when the alarm sounds, how long it lasts and how often it occurs. This information may assist the council if it decides to investigate whether the noise amounts to a statutory nuisance.

It is worth remembering that a single false alarm or occasional malfunction is unlikely to lead to formal action. Councils generally focus on persistent or recurring noise that has a significant impact on people living nearby.

Although a neighbour's car alarm can be highly disruptive, it does not automatically mean any laws have been broken. However, where the noise becomes persistent enough to amount to a statutory nuisance, councils have powers to investigate and, where necessary, take enforcement action.

News.title: Royal Mail could 'suspend' post for millions of homes
News.content:
Royal Mail could 'suspend' post for millions of homes

Royal Mail is urging potentially millions of households to act - or risk their post being disrupted

View Image Royal Mail has shared what people should do (Image: coldsnowstorm via Getty Images)

Royal Mail is urging potentially millions of households to take specific precautions or risk having their post "suspended".

‌



The warning comes after thousands of postal workers were attacked by dogs over the past year, with some suffering life-changing injuries. The delivery giant has issued a direct appeal to pet owners: "please help us protect your postie", warning that mail deliveries could be temporarily halted if a dog is found roaming loose outside a property. Owners are also being advised to keep their pets away from the door when answering it, and to consider fitting letter cages or external postboxes to prevent bites through the letterbox.

‌



Kirsteen Hobson, a postwoman of ten years, suffered severe facial injuries following a savage dog attack. She said: "The gentleman I was delivering to was standing, kind of half hanging, outside his door. I got about two thirds of the way and next thing I know there's a dog on my face and it ripped my lip off.

‌



"I didn't see the dog come at me, my first view of the dog was when it was attached to my face ... Somehow I managed to get the dog off me, and then it lunged at my face again, biting me under the eye and on my forehead.

"I somehow got the dog off me again and I turned around to get away from it, and it sunk its teeth into my leg, into my thigh", she continued, detailing how the traumatic event continues to affect "every aspect of my life".

Article continues below

Kirsteen went on to say: "It's not something that I'd like anyone else to experience, which is why I wanted to share this so it hopefully doesn't happen [again], it can be prevented."

To stop similar incidents occurring with other dogs, the Royal Mail website offers a downloadable postcard that can be printed and displayed in a door or window. Royal Mail explains: "This lets anyone delivering to your property know that you have a dog and asks them to wait whilst you secure your dog before opening the door."

The postal service also advises: "If we are delivering to your home address and you have a dog, help us deliver safely by keeping it secure and out of the way before your postie arrives."

News.title: Widdecombe police reopen investigation into incident at Farage's home, BBC understands
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the killing of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident at Nigel Farage's south London home, the BBC understands.

It is understood to relate to what the Reform UK leader described as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox in April 2025.

Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London said it was looking into an "attempted burglary" at a property as part of the Widdecombe murder investigation, but did not confirm the home was linked to Farage or why it might be connected to the killing of the former MP.

CTP London has also referred itself to the police watchdog over how the initial investigation into the Farage incident was handled.

Police said at the time that "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

Both CTP London and the Metropolitan Police were involved in enquiries. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

But on Friday, CTP London said a new line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said it had "decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier [on Friday]".

A statement continued: "The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025."

CTP London said it would "full engage" with the watchdog's investigation, adding: "The victims and families in both investigations have been updated today, and we continue to support them."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover' when he was general secretary
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: Hunter Biden tells BBC his pardon was 'not good' for America or his father's legacy
News.content:
Hunter Biden has told the BBC he is "the most privileged person there is" after receiving a presidential pardon from his father, former US President Joe Biden, acknowledging it was not a good choice for America or his father's legacy.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC's Newsnight, Hunter Biden defended the controversial pardon, revealed his father's "painful" cancer has spread, ruled out seeking elected office and spoke about helping others recover from addiction.

Asked about the 2024 pardon, he said he understood the criticism but noted: "What would you have thought of my dad if he did not do that for me."

"It's something that is easily criticised and for good reason," he added.

"It's not fairâ¦ All I know is that I'm grateful that he did it for me," he said, acknowledging the pardon was "not good" for the American people, the Constitution - or his father's legacy.

He argued to the BBC that his father ultimately acted out of concern that he would become a target under Donald Trump's incoming administration.

"I was the only one in the world that could have gotten what I got from the only person in the world who could give it, my father."

Hunter Biden also insisted he and his father had never discussed the possibility of a pardon before it was granted.

"There is no way that you can have those kinds of discussions that would not become public," he said.

President Biden granted his son a full and unconditional pardon in December 2024, despite repeatedly saying beforehand that he would not use the powers of the presidency to intervene in his son's legal cases. In announcing the decision, the former president said his son had been "selectively and unfairly prosecuted".

The pardon covered his son's federal gun conviction, a tax case he'd pled guilty to and any federal offences committed between 2014 and 2024.

News.title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
News.content:
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.

"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.

"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."

Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".

Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.

"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."

Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.

"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."

His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.

While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.

But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".

She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
News.content:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

News.title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back and 'a bit more real'
News.content:
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.

The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention â "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.

He's right â digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.

There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18â30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.

So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?

For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".

She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.

"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.

That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids â where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image â are also popular on socials right now.

With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.

"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.

"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."

News.title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
News.content:
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.

"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.

By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.

Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.

"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.

So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?

Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.

"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.

But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" â like someone might experience with drugs, for example â and how best to deal with it.

Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.

This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.

Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.

This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.

The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.

News.title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
News.content:
Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner Kevin Southworth has acknowledged that failures to remand Levy in custody during court hearings in May and June 2025 left him free to commit further offences.

BTP confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.

Crime and policing minister Sarah Jones said the situation "raises serious questions".

"The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning."

Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect.

"In particular, there were points where we could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail, based on the information available."

Victims' Commissioner for London Andrea Simons called for a "multi-agency review" over the "litany of failures to manage such a prolific offender".

She told BBC Breakfast that public services "have to get better at recognising patterns of offending" before attackers become "emboldened".

She continued: "There was a lack of restrictions that could have been placed on him and a failure to monitor him appropriately - so all of those things, I think, we need answers to now."

Lisa Squire, whose daughter Libby was murdered by a man who had previously committed a string of sex crimes, told the BBC that a "catalogue of disasters" had led to Levy's murders.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme "the patterns were there, he was flying those red flags", and said there were "precursor offences" for which he could have stopped by police.

"At the moment, the message going out, in my opinion, is that women's safety is not important," she continued.

ZoÃ« Billingham, a former independent police inspector who pushed for reforms on how violence against women in girls is policed, said that "too often in cases like this the dots aren't being joined up".

She added: "It's not one or two missed opportunities that could have brought him to justice, that could have had him locked up and behind bars and no longer a threat to women and girls. It was an extraordinary succession."

News.title: Police failings revealed as sex offender left free to murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was all right, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent BTP investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Woman attacked by bed bugs during Travelodge stay
News.content:
Thirteen days after Hannah Stephenson stayed a night in a Travelodge hotel, she is still itching with red lumps over her body - a nightmare she would not wish on her "worst enemy".

The 31-year-old from Bassingbourn had been out with friends in Cambridge and decided to book a one-night stay at the hotel on Newmarket Road on 26 July to save money instead of getting a taxi home.

The next morning, she woke up to a "horrible realisation", feeling itchy with red lumps over her body and blood spots smeared on the bedding â the tell-tale signs of bed bugs, she said.

A Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for Ms Stephenson's experience and how distressing an incident like this can be."

Stephenson said a lovely evening with friends had turned into a horrible morning.

"It was just a lovely wholesome time of Cambridge sightseeing and pubs, and now it is tarnished by these bedbug bites," she said.

"It wasn't until I saw the blood and the bugs that I realised what had happened."

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: How asylum protests brought disorder to Thetford
News.content:
At the nearby St John's Way estate, the houses are arranged in circular terraced blocks with large courtyards.

On the corner of one is a house that protesters believe was home to five asylum seekers.

According to Norfolk Police, there were reports that a group of people, who did not live at the address, were "attempting to get inside and smashed a window, and damaged a fence panel and letterbox".

"A resident of the same property reported a group of between 30 and 50 people trying to get into the house," the force added.

Eyewitnesses described police drones buzzing in the area.

More stories of interest:

A crowd of about 100 people were gathered outside, said neighbour Chelsea Goodwin, but she said she did not see any disorder.

Her objection to the arrivals is that "you don't know who they are".

"I don't feel safe having undocumented illegal immigrants here," she said.

"If it was a family with kids and they were trying to get away from some war-torn country, then that's fine," the mother-of-two added.

"But it's a just group of middle-aged men."

Her perception, which we heard from numerous locals, was that women and children were not safe because of "cultural differences".

She did not specify which culture she had concerns about.

The property is now empty, with locals reporting that the occupants were escorted out by the police.

Once again, the BBC was unable to confirm who these individuals were - or where they came from.

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: How mum joined ‘rising number of hidden homeless’ after fleeing with daughter
News.content:
When Jodie and her daughter had to flee their hometown, they could only take what they could carry - two black bin bags filled with their belongings.

Jodie, then aged 30, found herself in Margate, Kent, with a seven-year-old child to take care of and no place to live.

"I had to leave everything," Jodie said. "The bags were mainly my daughter's clothes and her dolls."

She chose the seaside town because they had been there on summer and half term holidays, but it meant leaving her family and friends behind.

"I wanted to go somewhere that wasn't very alien for my daughter," said Jodie, now 42.

"It was still scary, but I had to be the strong one and protect her. I had to do it so that my daughter could have a life."

After a brief stay in council emergency accommodation, she said they spent a year sleeping on the sofas and floors of people she had met in Margate.

Passengers are facing travel chaos at Bristol airport after a runway defect suspended operations for hours leading to cancellations and delays.

Passengers were left stranded on Friday after the airport’s runway was closed at around 6pm. It remained shut, with no flights coming in or out, until 8am on Saturday, but operations have now resumed.

Though the runway has reopened, passengers are now facing hours of delays, with multiple flights affected.

An updated statement on the airport’s website said: “Flights have resumed at Bristol Airport this morning. There will be some disruption to some flights today and customers are advised to refer to their airlines with any flight queries. We apologise for any inconvenience caused.”

Earlier, the airport said that it had suspended operations to assess and repair a “defect on the runway.”

If you have been affected by the runway closure at Bristol airport, please get in touch by emailing daniel.haygarth@independent.co.uk

Among the many flights to be delayed this morning, according to the airport’s online departures board, are the 5.55am service to Faro, which is scheduled to take off at 10.40am, and the 6.20am flight to Menorca, which is expected to depart at 11.30am.

Cancelled or delayed flights: What are my rights to a refund? Check here

Paul Smith, who was due to fly to Glasgow on Friday for his son's 20th birthday but had to cancel the holiday, told the BBC: "The communication, advice and support for passengers has been really poor”.

Mr Smith said there were no announcements for more than an hour on Friday and claimed that he was only getting information from EasyJet staff in the departure lounge.

On X, responding to a passenger asking if flights have been cancelled today, airline Jet2 said: “Our flights have not been cancelled. They are currently delayed, and are expected to fly later today when the runway re-opens.”
