World.title: Abiodun announces arrest of four more kidnappers of Ogun students, commissions road
World.content:
Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun, on Friday commissioned the 3.3-kilometre Adesan Road in Mowe, Obafemi-Owode Local Government Area, as he announced the arrest of four additional suspects linked to the abduction of seven students of Gateway ICT Polytechnic, Saapade.

Governor Abiodun described the rescue of the students and the arrest of the suspects as a major victory in the state’s war against criminality, declaring that Ogun State would never become a safe haven for criminals.

It would be recalled that two members of the kidnapping gang were arrested on Thursday during the operation that led to the successful rescue of the students.

Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, the governor expressed appreciation to the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS), the National Association of Ogun State Students (NAOSS), and other student bodies for their patience, understanding, and support throughout the period of the students’ captivity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He attributed the successful rescue operation to the coordinated efforts of security agencies, including the Nigeria Police Force, the Department of State Services (DSS), the Nigerian Army, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), the Ogun State Security Network Agency (Amotekun Corps), local hunters, and vigilantes.

Governor Abiodun also acknowledged the support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Inspector General of Police, and the Director-General of the DSS.

“Sometime before the end of July, some of our students were kidnapped by unscrupulous elements. To the glory of God, with the cooperation and collaboration of our law enforcement agencies and the support we received from Mr. President, the Inspector General of Police and the Director-General of the DSS, we worked night and day.

“Yesterday, we rescued all seven students alive. We have arrested four more of the kidnappers, while the remaining suspects are still on the run. We will arrest them as well,” the governor said.

Reaffirming his administration’s zero tolerance for criminality, Governor Abiodun stressed that Ogun State, as Nigeria’s industrial capital and gateway to the nation, would not permit criminals to operate within its borders.

“Ogun State will not allow crime or criminality. Those who come here to test our resolve will be tracked down, smoked out, arrested, and made to face the full weight of the law,” he declared.

Highlighting his administration’s infrastructure achievements, Governor Abiodun disclosed that 42 roads have been constructed or reconstructed across Ogun Central Senatorial District since 2019, with 12 of them located in Obafemi-Owode Local Government Area. He added that about 1,600 kilometres of roads have been completed across the state’s three senatorial districts.

According to him, roads completed in Obafemi-Owode include the Abeokuta–Sagamu Interchange Road, Panseke–Adigbe Road, Journalists’ Estate Road in Arepo, Siun–Owode Road (Phase I), the revived Mowe–Ofada Road, Iyana-Oloke Junction–MAPOLY Road, Adesan Road, Kuforiji–Olubi Road, Adigbe–Laderin–Train Station Road, Sagamu–Ofada–Papalanto Road, and Magboro–Makogi Road.

“In Ogun Central, within the last seven years, we have reconstructed 42 roads, and we are still constructing more.

“When we assumed office on May 29, 2019, we made several promises. Today, it is gratifying to look back and see how far God has helped us in fulfilling those promises.

“Even as we wind down this administration, we still have more roads to award and complete. There are additional roads in Obafemi-Owode, including the road linking Magboro, that will soon be commissioned. We will remain a promise-keeping administration,” he said.

The governor observed that Obafemi-Owode, being a border local government and the food basket of Ogun State where the renowned Ofada rice is cultivated and processed, deserves sustained investment in infrastructure to support its growing population and expanding economic activities.

He urged residents to protect the newly commissioned road by ensuring its proper use and maintenance.

Earlier, the Commissioner for Works and Infrastructure, Ade Akinsanya, described Adesan Road as a strategic economic corridor that would improve connectivity between adjoining communities and the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, enhance commerce, and ease transportation.

Also speaking, the Chairman of Obafemi-Owode Local Government, Mr Adesina Ogunsola, commended Governor Abiodun for his sustained investment in infrastructure, noting that the road would greatly benefit traders, students, motorists, and other road users.

He disclosed that the local government had complemented the state’s efforts by constructing the 1.6-kilometre Adigbe–Ita-Baale–Idi-Mangoro–Police Post Road and the one-kilometre Ogidan–Gele Odun Road, while additional roads have been earmarked for reconstruction.

The member representing Obafemi-Owode State Constituency in the Ogun State House of Assembly, Hon Damilola Soneye Kayode, thanked the governor for fulfilling a long-standing request for the reconstruction of the road, noting that it serves about six communities and would significantly enhance transportation and economic activities.

Also, the member representing Obafemi-Owode, Odeda and Abeokuta North Federal Constituency in the House of Representatives, Hon Olumide Osoba, applauded the governor for delivering yet another strategic infrastructure project, describing it as a reflection of the administration’s commitment to inclusive development.

In his remarks, the Olu of Mowe, Oba Oriyomi Yahaya, commended Governor Abiodun for fulfilling his campaign promise to the people of Mowe and appealed to him to also reconstruct the town’s market to further stimulate commerce and economic growth.

World.title: Infantile Infantino should exit for trying to sell the World Cup, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
In reality, the Infantino gang tried to commercialise the soul of football, a unifying force of humanity. He had dangled a $40 million award to every association that voted for his plans, promising that an advance $30 million would be made available to each of the federations by 1 January, 2027.

Gianni Infantino, the Federation Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) President who stole into office a decade ago on the back of a coup against Sepp Blatter, may be on his way out. He has become like an orphan caught with his hand in the till.

The 2026 World Cup was quite successful. It was also a commercial success, with FIFA raking in a record revenue of $13 billion to $15 billion. The World Cup, which had thirteen teams at inception, has expanded to a record 48 teams and a total of 104 matches. This has led to high-volume ticket sales. Broadcasting rights alone in 2026 generated about $4.2 billion. Sponsorship and hospitality added to the income.

Admittedly, FIFA’s costs also went up. For instance, a higher $871 million was allocated to the teams, including a $655 million base prize. The champions, Spain, took $51 million; runners-up, $34 million; and third place, $30 million. Also, holding the competition in three venues – the United States, Mexico and Canada – increased the logistical overhead. But, overall, it was a hugely successful tournament.

However, as the world celebrated and discussed the games, the Infantino leadership decided to take advantage of the euphoria by sneaking in a partial privatisation package.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

As it turned out, without consultations with the regional bodies, the leadership created a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise, with which it was going to sell a 20-30 per cent stake in World Cup commercial rights to private investors led by Joshua Kushner, brother of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared. Infantino said the plan was to raise a minimum of $20 billion.

In reality, the Infantino gang tried to commercialise the soul of football, a unifying force of humanity. He had dangled a $40 million award to every association that voted for his plans, promising that an advance $30 million would be made available to each of the federations by 1 January, 2027.

However, an immediate rejection came from the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), the umbrella body of 55 members of FIFA’s total 211. The region also runs the world’s most lucrative league.

The UEFA knockout punch was its decision to boycott FIFA if the Infantino team went ahead with its greedy plans. The implication of such a boycott is that FIFA may be split and Europe can hold a parallel World Cup with teams that ally with it. The North American confederation, CONCACAF, also joined UEFA in rejecting the FIFA plan.

UEFA declared the attempted privatisation of the World Cup unacceptable and a line that football’s governing institutions must not cross. It added that: “UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.”

To underscore the seriousness with which it is handling the matter, UEFA sent FIFA a preservation letter. It demanded that the world body preserve all evidence, as this may turn out to be a lawsuit.

The UEFA knockout punch was its decision to boycott FIFA if the Infantino team went ahead with its greedy plans. The implication of such a boycott is that FIFA may be split and Europe can hold a parallel World Cup with teams that ally with it. The North American confederation, CONCACAF, also joined UEFA in rejecting the FIFA plan.

Equally, the Asian Football Confederation, AFC, declared it stands in solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF, describing the FIFA leader’s actions as “totally unacceptable.”

However, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) did not take a concrete position on the matter, preferring to keep the door open, which is an indirect endorsement of the plan.

However, things began to crumble around Infantino. Some officials of FIFA distanced themselves from the plan. FIFA’s head of global football development and famous coach, Arsene Wenger, said he was “not aware” of the Infantino gambit.

In conceding defeat, Infantino and FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström issued a joint statement after a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, stating that: “We acknowledge mistakes were made in the process of the proposed establishment of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). It was certainly not the intention for the FIFA Council and FIFA Member Associations to feel excluded from the process and it should have been handled differently.” They followed with a clarification and a warning: “Furthermore, as already known, the proposal, which would have been subject to the approval of the FIFA Member Associations and the FIFA Council, is now off the table. With the project withdrawn, FIFA will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.”

Another alternative way to replace Infantino is to wait until the 77th FIFA Congress scheduled to be held in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March, 2027, where he can be voted out. FIFA was established on 21 May, 1904, and the first World Cup was held in 1930, with Uruguay defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final to win the maiden edition. As it stands, Infantino is a danger to world football.

But the warning appeared to have had little effect. UEFA, looking beyond the FIFA statement, declared that although Infantino has beaten a retreat, this “must not be the end of the story. The proposal has gone. The task of rebuilding trust in FIFA has only just begun.”

It implied that Infantino must fall. Equally, the AFC, looking beyond the Infantino backdown, demanded that FIFA’s future actions must be “shaped through proper consultation.” This is an indication that a post-Infantino FIFA era should commence. What the Infantino team tried to carry out was like a coup, and there are implications for a failed coup.

The options for Infantino’s welcome replacement include impeaching him. This will require a minimum of 41 member associations calling for an extraordinary congress, where an impeachment motion would need a simple majority to pass.

A second alternative is for his case to be tabled at the FIFA Independent Ethics Committee, which is empowered to remove a FIFA president, as was done to the immediate past president, Sepp Blatter.

Another issue of ethics that Infantino faces is taking dictation from United States President Donald Trump, who personally called him to have the red card issued to USA striker, Folarin Balogun, at the 2026 World Cup be overturned. Balogun was expected to miss the last-16 clash against Belgium after picking up a red card for an unsportsmanlike challenge of Bosnia’s Tarik Muharemovi. FIFA, in compliance with Trump’s political directive, suspended the ban, clearing Balogun to play against Belgium. The latter beat the USA 4-1 in the 6 July match.

Infantino had also been accused of removing two chairmen and all but two members of the Ethics Committee, which implied that he did not want the body to investigate corruption against the FIFA governing body. He was also accused of influencing the candidature of Ahmad Ahmad as CAF president.

Another alternative way to replace Infantino is to wait until the 77th FIFA Congress scheduled to be held in Rabat, Morocco on 18 March, 2027, where he can be voted out. FIFA was established on 21 May, 1904, and the first World Cup was held in 1930, with Uruguay defeating Argentina 4-2 in the final to win the maiden edition. As it stands, Infantino is a danger to world football.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside fragile chain holding Kano, Gombe’s immunisation systems together
World.content:
Under the harsh April sun, the heat was oppressive in Fagge Local Government Area of Kano State. But 56-year-old Uma Usman kept walking from one compound to another, calling out familiar names, knocking gently on half-open doors and asking after children she had come to know over the years.

She is not an employee of the local Galadima Primary Health Centre. Her name does not appear on any government payroll. Yet, she has become one of the most important links in the community’s immunisation system.

Her job is to find children who missed their routine immunisation appointments.

“I know the community very well, so I follow them house by house,” Mrs Usman told PREMIUM TIMES. “If the parents don’t come, we check the register and trace the households.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

For Mrs Usman, behind every missed appointment, there is a story.

Sometimes a child is ill. Sometimes a mother cannot raise money for transport. Sometimes parents are occupied with work or family responsibilities.

“When you reach a house, you find it is not that they don’t want to come,” she said. “Something just stood in the way.”

Mrs Usman’s daily routine illustrates a broader reality observed in a PREMIUM TIMES investigation in Kano and Gombe states.

Contrary to the widespread assumption that vaccine shortages are the biggest obstacle to routine immunisation, frontline workers in the two states described a different problem. Vaccines are usually available. The challenge is ensuring children complete the immunisation schedule.

However, for many families who spoke with PREMIUM TIMES, the barrier is not acceptance but access. Long distances to health facilities, transport costs, delayed outreach activities and the daily struggle to earn a living often interrupt follow-up visits. As a result, many children receive their first vaccine but never complete the doses needed for full protection.

The consequences extend far beyond individual families.

This investigation examined routine immunisation efforts and challenges in Kano and Gombe between 2023 and 2026, drawing on field visits, interviews, official records and data from health authorities and development partners.

The period captures the continuing struggle to reach children who have never received a vaccine, as well as those who start their vaccination schedule but fail to complete it.

According to UNICEF, Nigeria has one of the world’s largest populations of zero-dose children, those who never received a routine vaccine. Its latest data shows that only about 67 per cent of surviving infants receive the third dose of the diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTP3) vaccine, while coverage for the second dose of the measles vaccine is about 35 per cent.

Although routine immunisation coverage has improved in recent years, many children still receive no vaccines at all or fail to complete the schedule.

Behind those national figures are thousands of individual stories like the ones Mrs Usman encounters every week.

But the investigation found another, less visible reality.

Across communities in Kano and Gombe, routine immunisation continues largely because health workers, volunteers and community mobilisers bridge gaps created by delayed funding, difficult terrain and overstretched primary healthcare systems.

Many spend their own money to reach remote settlements. Volunteers without formal employment trace children from house to house. Outreach activities continue even when operational funds arrive months late.

Different communities, same struggle

The pattern seen in Fagge extends far beyond one community.

In Takai LGA of Kano State, reaching children who miss vaccination appointments often means travelling long distances across scattered settlements. Health workers say routine clinic sessions alone are not enough; repeated outreach visits are essential to find children who fail to return.

“There is never a time when people come and we do not have vaccines,” said Muhammad Ali, the officer-in-charge at Gamawa Health Post.

Field records reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES and interviews with frontline workers showed that children scheduled for follow-up are not always reached as planned.

Health workers explained that outreach teams frequently face transport constraints, limited time, and difficult terrain, making it impossible to visit every household listed for follow-up during a single outreach exercise.

“We don’t refuse to go,” one health worker said. “But sometimes the list is longer than what we can physically cover in one outreach.”

Many children miss vaccine doses because follow-up visits could not be completed.

In Billiri LGA of Gombe State, the pattern is the same.

Health workers and volunteer mobilisers spend almost as much time searching for children who missed appointments as they do on administering vaccines.

Across these locations, one pattern persists: children often begin immunisation but fail to complete the schedule because of family challenges.

A system sustained by people

For Ignatius Essien, general manager of eHealth Systems Africa, the difficulty families face getting to health facilities helps explain the introduction of the Zero Dose Support Programme.

Mr Essien said the programme gives transport support to caregivers who bring their children for immunisation. It applies to children coming for either their first dose or subsequent doses.

“The funds are not tied to routine immunisation outcomes,” he stated.

He explained that the idea grew from what health workers repeatedly saw in the field: families who wanted to vaccinate their children but lived too far from health facilities or could not afford the fare to get there.

“Some say they cannot even afford transport fare to the clinic,” he said. “That is what stimulated the stipend.”

The support started at N500 but has since increased from N1000 to N2500 depending on the vaccine type as transport fares and the cost of living rose.

At Sansani PHC in Billiri LGA, routine immunisation sessions typically attract between 30 and 45 caregivers.

Behind those clinic days, however, lies another routine that is rarely captured in official reports —tracing children who do not return.

The facility’s Head of Immunisation, Elias Ezekiel, said health workers use immunisation registers to identify children who miss appointments from the catchment seven communities.

“From the register, if anyone misses, we follow up,” Mr Ezekiel told PREMIUM TIMES.

That work depends on outreach funding.

The health centre receives about N35,000 monthly for outreach activities, but the money is released quarterly by the State Primary Health Care Development Agency.

When PREMIUM TIMES visited, more than three months had passed without any release.

Mr Ezekiel said the delays are routinely reported through local government health authorities.

“If we stop outreach, the children will miss their vaccines,” he said.

So, staff members buy fuel and pay transport costs from their own pockets while waiting for the fund.

His account echoed those of several frontline workers interviewed across Kano and Gombe.

Vaccines are generally available, they said, but getting them to children in remote communities often depends on health workers absorbing the cost whenever operational funding is delayed.

That challenge is more difficult for facilities serving scattered settlements.

A quiet crisis in the North

The challenges confronting health workers in Kano and Gombe reflect a much wider crisis across northern Nigeria, where hundreds of thousands of children remain unreached by routine immunisation.

In April 2025, UNICEF estimated that about 53,000 children in Gombe State had never received a routine vaccine. More than half of them were in five high-risk LGAs, including Akko, where health authorities were contending with poor access to healthcare, low awareness and vaccine hesitancy.

To address the problem, the Gombe State Primary Health Care Development Agency, with support from UNICEF, launched the Fathers’ Response Team in 2024 to encourage greater male involvement in decisions about child health and immunisation.

Even so, many children continue to miss life-saving vaccines.

The challenge is even greater in Kano.

UNICEF estimates that more than 300,000 children are zero-dose, accounting for half of the burden across Kano, Katsina and Jigawa states.

UNICEF’s Chief Field Officer in Kano, Rahama Farah, said more than 600,000 children across the three states have yet to receive their first routine vaccine dose.

Many of these children live in remote or underserved communities where access to healthcare remains inconsistent.

“This is a basic fundamental child right,” Ms Farah noted.

She also warned that missed vaccinations increase vulnerability to outbreaks of preventable diseases and urged caregivers to complete immunisation schedules.

Why Kano and Gombe tell different stories

Although Kano and Gombe face similar immunisation challenges, the underlying pressures are different.

In Kano, the greatest obstacle is scale. With a population of more than 17 million people and over 600,000 births every year, health facilities operate under constant pressure.

The 2021 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) found that about 30.2 per cent of children in Kano are zero-dose, while only about 48 per cent complete the full routine immunisation schedule by their first birthday. National estimates indicate dropout rates of up to 31 per cent between the first and third doses of routine vaccines.

In Gombe, where the population is less than a third of Kano’s, geography plays a larger role. Communities are more dispersed, distances are longer, and access to health facilities often requires significant time and effort.

Estimates place Gombe’s zero-dose prevalence between 18 and 22 per cent, with only about 36 per cent completing full immunisation in some datasets.

Where the system weakens

The investigation found that the biggest weakness in routine immunisation is not getting children into the system.

It is keeping them in it.

Across health facilities in Kano and Gombe visited by PREMIUM TIMES, workers consistently described a system that performs relatively well at administering first doses but struggles to retain children through the full vaccination schedule.

Nationally, dropout rates between early and later vaccine doses range from about 12 to 30 per cent, depending on location.

At the Galadima PHC in Kano, Hauwa Isa, the assistant head of the facility, pointed to a solar-powered vaccine refrigerator stocked with vaccines.

“We have complete vaccines in the fridge,” she said. “We conduct immunisation three times a week and spend other days on outreach.”

“The real issue is not availability. It is continuity.”

That continuity depends on a governance system in which responsibility is shared but accountability is often blurred.

Primary health centres are under local governments, while state Primary Health Care Development Agencies oversee much of their staffing and operations. The federal government sets national policy and supports key immunisation programmes through partnerships with development agencies.

Health workers told PREMIUM TIMES that when outreach funding is delayed or operational gaps emerge, it is often difficult to determine where responsibility lies.

Money, priorities and the field reality

Over the past five years, both Kano and Gombe have recorded sharp increases in their budgets.

Official budget documents show Kano State’s spending plan rose from N221.24 billion in 2022 to N1.47 trillion in 2026, while Gombe’s grew from roughly N154.96 billion to N617.95 billion over the same period.

Those figures suggest governments have greater financial capacity to deliver public services, including primary healthcare.

Yet interviews with frontline workers across both states tell a more complicated story.

For them, the size of the budget does not matter when operational funds do not arrive when they are needed.

Outreach funding illustrates that gap.

It is the money that helps vaccines to reach children in remote communities. Health workers say when those funds are delayed, outreach activities depend on staff members improvising.

In Fagge and Takai LGAs of Kano State, workers told PREMIUM TIMES that each PHC is allocated about N7,000 a month for outreach transport.

Several months’ allocations are often paid together in arrears at the end of a quarter, long after many of the outreach visits.

In Gombe State, PHCs receive N35,000 a month for outreach transport, but the money is likewise paid quarterly.

The situation is even more difficult at health posts.

Unlike PHCs, they receive no dedicated transport allocation, according to workers interviewed by PREMIUM TIMES. Yet they are responsible for tracing children who miss appointments and carrying vaccination services to remote settlements.

When priorities compete

Funding pressures extend beyond the health sector.

Budget documents reviewed by PREMIUM TIMES show that both Kano and Gombe have made substantial allocations to debt servicing in recent years.

In the 2026 fiscal year, Kano budgeted about N69.84 billion for debt repayment, while Gombe allocated roughly N37.23 billion.

Those obligations are met before many operational funds are released to sectors such as PHCs, reducing the fiscal space available for routine service delivery.

Health workers say they experience those pressures in delayed outreach, postponed field visits and reduced operational flexibility.

Government spending priorities are also visible elsewhere.

In Kano, the state approved the purchase of 41 sport utility vehicles (SUVs) for members of the House of Assembly in 2024 at a cost of about N2.6 billion, alongside other vehicle purchases for the executive and security agencies.

In Gombe, similar procurements included 41 SUVs for lawmakers and commissioners in 2023, while more than N2 billion was allocated for vehicles for the judiciary in 2025.

Government officials have defended such purchases as necessary for governance and movement across challenging terrains.

For health workers travelling across the same terrains, however, the contrast is difficult to ignore. Many outreach teams continue to rely on motorcycles, commercial transport, or long walks to reach remote communities.

Where the system holds

Despite its weaknesses, northern Nigeria’s routine immunisation system continues to function because thousands of frontline health workers, volunteers and community mobilisers return to the same communities, often with limited resources, determined to find children who have missed their vaccines.

But sustaining that effort requires more than commitment, according to public health expert Abdulhameed Adediran, who warned that children who miss subsequent vaccine doses remain vulnerable to preventable diseases.

“A child is supposed to have three doses but has only the first dose. That child is not 33 per cent protected. That child is not protected because the first dose is supposed to last for a particular period before the next one is administered to have a complete effect,” he told PREMIUM TIMES via phone interview.

Mr Adediran said inadequate financing for PHC undermines the entire immunisation system. According to him, when outreach activities are poorly funded, children in distant communities are more likely to miss vaccinations, leaving dangerous gaps in disease prevention.

He traced many of the problems to systemic weaknesses, including poor funding, shortages of health workers, weak accountability, and inadequate infrastructure. In many facilities, he noted, community health extension workers shoulder responsibilities beyond their intended roles because of years of limited recruitment.

Mr Adeniran said immunisation programmes must be designed around the realities of the communities they serve rather than through one-size-fits-all approaches.

“People sit in Abuja and take decisions for people in those villages, and those decisions don’t necessarily work for them or are not necessarily applicable to them,” he explained, adding, “We need to start looking at a tailored, people-centred approach to our health institutions.”

Government responds

Responding to the findings, the Gombe State Primary Health Care Development Agency acknowledged that delays in releasing outreach funds sometimes occur, attributing them to administrative procedures, financial reconciliation processes and the timing of support from development partners.

The State Immunisation Officer, Abdulkarim Aliyu, said routine immunisation outreach is funded through a combination of government resources and donor support, with disbursements passing through several approval and accountability processes before reaching health facilities.

While acknowledging the effect of delayed releases, Mr Aliyu praised frontline workers who continue to provide outreach services despite funding constraints.

“We also recognise and appreciate the dedication of frontline health workers who often go the extra mile to ensure that vaccination services continue even when resources are delayed,” he said.

He said the agency has strengthened defaulter-tracking systems, expanded community mobilisation through Ward Development Committees, Community Health Influencers, Promoters and Services (CHIPS) agents and the Mama-to-Mama initiative, while holding regular review meetings to identify communities with high dropout rates and deploy targeted interventions.

Mr Aliyu added that the agency was pursuing workforce training, supportive supervision, and strategic staff deployment to address staffing shortages, while routine data validation and quality assessments are used to monitor immunisation records and identify children who miss scheduled vaccinations.

Looking ahead, he said the agency would focus on strengthening outreach services, improving community engagement, and expanding efforts to identify and vaccinate zero-dose and under-immunised children.

In Kano, the Director-General of the State Primary Health Care Management Board, Salisu Ibrahim, said outreach stipends are paid through a performance-tracking system supported by Acasus, a routine immunisation partner that monitors outreach sessions conducted by service providers.

Mr Ibrahim explained that payment delays sometimes occur because service-delivery records must first be verified before payments are processed.

He said the state has adopted several measures to reduce vaccine dropout rates, including ensuring that planned immunisation sessions are conducted, expanding public awareness campaigns, and addressing practices that contribute to missed vaccination opportunities.

While acknowledging financial pressures, he said the current administration of Governor Abba Yusuf increased outreach stipends from N1,000 to N4,000 per session to help health workers cope with rising transportation and operational costs.

He added that the board also conducts monthly data validation exercises, review meetings and independent surveys to identify service gaps and strengthen routine immunisation in underserved communities.

Whether those efforts will be enough to reduce the number of children missing vaccines remains uncertain.

What is clear, however, is that across communities in Kano and Gombe, routine immunisation continues to depend heavily on the persistence of health workers, volunteers and caregivers who keep showing up despite funding delays, staffing shortages and the difficulties of reaching remote settlements.

For many children, completing vaccination depends on that fragile chain.

This reporting was completed with the support of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

World.title: Osun Decides: I’ll block leakages, expand revenue – Oyebamiji
World.content:
By Clifford Ndujihe & Juliet Umeh

The All Progressives Congress, APC, governorship candidate in the August 15 Osun State election, Asiwaju Munirudeen Bola Oyebamiji, AMBO, in this interview speaks on his chances, allegations of political violence, his plans to stabilise the state’s finances, expand revenue through technology, reduce government spending, implement local government autonomy, and deliver on his administration’s prosperity agenda, if elected.

On why he is running

I am a credible alternative to the current administration in Osun State. I served as the Commissioner for Finance under the administrations of Governors Rauf Aregbesola and Adegboyega Oyetola. Before then, I served as the Managing Director of the Osun Investment Company Limited, now known as Omoluabi Holdings Limited.

To properly situate why Osun deserves a better deal at this time, the last allocation received by the APC administration of Governor Gboyega Oyetola from the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) stood at approximately N2.6 billion. Today, the average monthly allocation to the state is about ¦ 16 billion without commensurate values to the state and her citizens.

In fact, few of the infrastructure projects delivered by the current administration were awarded in secrecy to incompetent contractors while many of such projects have failed before commissioning.

I am contesting to arrest the current drift in the state. Our Prosperity Agenda has continued to gain widespread acceptance among the people of Osun. So far, we have taken our campaign to all the 30 local government areas of the state. As a party, our firm belief is that the primary responsibility of any government, as provided in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, is the security and welfare of its citizens. Consequently, our Prosperity Agenda is built on seven key pillars:

P – Poverty Alleviation, Workers’ Welfare, and Job Creation; R – Responsive, Accountable, and Transparent Governance; O – Opportunities for Economic Growth, Support Programmes for Small and Medium-Scale Enterprises (SMEs), and Youth and Women Empowerment; S – Security, Safety, and Social Protection; P – Productive Agriculture Through Public-Private Partnerships and Rural Development; E – Education, Skills Development, and Targeted Investment in Healthcare Delivery; and R – Renewed Investment in Infrastructure to Drive Inclusive Growth, Culture, and Tourism.

In line with our campaign promises, within our first 100 days in office, we will undertake a comprehensive review of all outstanding entitlements owed to active and retired workers and commence immediate payment. We are equally committed to ensuring that the Dagbolu Dry Port becomes fully operational. In addition to these, through strategic partnerships, we will commence the training and empowerment of not fewer than 10,000 young people in information and communication technology.

We will also institutionalise monthly meetings of the State Security Council involving security agencies, traditional rulers, and local government leaders. Furthermore, we will launch pilot off-grid renewable energy projects in selected public institutions and rural communities. Similarly, we will conduct a comprehensive fiscal sustainability review covering state revenue, expenditure, and debt obligations. We will also undertake a state-wide infrastructure audit to identify priority economic roads and other critical infrastructure needs. These, among others, are the initiatives that we consider essential within our first one hundred days in office.

We want to reassure Osun people and Nigerians that both the APC and I have been victims of the persistent political violence in Osun State. During the 2022 governorship election, more than 25 members of our party were allegedly murdered by members of the political party in power in Osun. In my own local government area for example, the Chairman of Irewole Local Government, Remi Abass, was killed within the council secretariat. Our party has also documented several other politically-motivated attacks and killings, for which we continue to seek justice through the courts.

The ongoing political violence in the state has all the signs of the government in power on it. Just recently, the Inspector-General of Police visited Osun State and publicly raised allegations concerning individuals accused of criminal activities being housed within the Government House. Reports also emerged a few days ago concerning the arrest of a suspected criminal within the private residence of the Secretary to the State Government in Osogbo. Furthermore, reports on Sunday night indicated that some of our members were attacked in Ede, the hometown of Governor Ademola Adeleke.

As an opposition party, these are some of the experiences of members of our party. Ironically, it is the Accord party and the government of Adeleke that would cry foul while our members bear the scars of political violence.

What are the conditions that will guarantee a free and fair governorship election in Osun State?

For us, first of all, we are going to abide by the rule of law, especially relying on INEC rules and security rules. If I have to take you back to the memory lane, the antecedents of APC in this country is not about violence.

Violence is synonymous to the opposition. Especially if you look at all the states that APC has governors, there has not been any violence propelled, driven, or initiated by the APC government.

It is not in our character and it is the same in Osun. About three-four months ago, we wrote to the IG, the policy commissioner, the director of DSS and the Commander of Civil Defence Corp, the opposition had designed, customised vehicles in APC colours and used those vehicles to perpetuate criminal activities.

We are privileged to have that information and we inform them accordingly. All those criminal activities that have been perpetrated in Osun are being initiated by the Accord party.

And we have written to the INEC and the security operators.

It is important for them to take that into account.

On his chances of winning the election

Politics is about numbers. This time around, we have the numbers on our side.

On how he would get funds to execute his prosperity agenda

We have done it in the past during the Rauf Areghesola regime when I was the Commissioner for Finance. I came in May, by July, I had stabilised the finance of the state.

The first thing is to block the leakages and cut the cost of governance. We won’t witch-hunt anyone

The second one is to expand the revenue base. We have done it in the past.

During Oyetola’s regime, the World Bank gave an award to the state as the best managed and profitable revenue enhancement state. We will deploy efficient technology to expand the finance base of the Osun State.

On his plan for local government autonomy

The Supreme Court has ruled, local government autonomy is here to stay. Even before the autonomy of the local government, during Oyetola’s tenure, we had never been involved in the activities of the local government.

Is the zoning formula in Osun State in your favour?

On zoning, what we have in Osun is one APC, and the current governor is from the West, I’m also from the West. So, I can confidently say that come 15th of August, I will win that election.

On his assessment of Governor Ademola Adeleke’s performance

Our position is that the current administration has not justified the enormous resources at its disposal. This assessment is based on publicly available information regarding federal allocations, intervention funds, and other revenues received by the state.

The critical question is whether those resources have translated into visible improvements in the lives of ordinary people. When governments receive substantial revenues, citizens expect corresponding progress in education, healthcare, infrastructure, agriculture, employment and economic development.

We believe there are legitimate questions regarding priorities, project implementation and overall outcomes. Have schools improved sufficiently? Has healthcare become more accessible? Have roads and other public infrastructure been upgraded? Have enough jobs been created?

These are not partisan questions. Every citizen has the right to demand accountability because public resources belong to the people.

Our campaign is centred on measurable performance, responsible governance and a clear vision for the future of Osun State.

You have criticised some infrastructure projects undertaken by the government. What are your concerns?

Our concerns centre on value for money, transparency and quality of execution.

Infrastructure is important, but citizens deserve assurance that public funds are being spent responsibly. Whenever huge sums are committed to projects, the government should be transparent about costs, procurement processes, implementation timelines and expected outcomes.

We have also raised concerns about aspects of some road and bridge projects, including questions about construction standards and project delivery. Infrastructure should be built to last and should serve communities for generations.

Our criticism is not opposition for its own sake. We simply believe every naira spent should produce measurable value for the people.

If elected, transparency, accountability and value for money will guide every infrastructure project undertaken by our administration.

What distinguishes your campaign from that of your opponents?

Our campaign is distinguished by its focus on governance and practical solutions. We are not interested in propaganda or personal attacks. Our emphasis is on issues that affect ordinary citizens every day, job creation, infrastructure, education, healthcare, agriculture and economic development.

We believe politics should be about offering solutions rather than trading insults. That is the approach we have adopted, and it is the approach we intend to sustain if elected.

His take on political violence in Osun State

Political violence remains a serious concern, and it should worry every stakeholder regardless of political affiliation. Democracy thrives only when citizens can freely express their opinions, participate in political activities and vote without fear.

Our party has repeatedly raised concerns over attacks on some of our members and supporters. Over the years, APC members have reportedly been attacked, injured, and, in some cases, killed. We have consistently brought these incidents to the attention of security agencies because every allegation of violence deserves proper investigation.

In 2022 alone, we lost 25 members to political violence. That is now history, but it is a painful reminder that no political office is worth the life of any citizen.

Political competition should never degenerate into violence. Regardless of political differences, we remain members of the same communities and citizens of the same state.

I believe political leaders have a responsibility to promote peace. They must be careful with their words and actions because supporters often take their cue from them. We should encourage dialogue, tolerance and respect for differing opinions.

The APC is not a violent party. Violence is not part of our political culture. We intend to win the confidence of voters through our ideas, performance and programmes rather than intimidation. Unfortunately, from what we have witnessed, those currently in government appear determined to deploy violence as a political tool.

But your opponents argue that the APC is responsible for tension in the state.

We reject that narrative completely. Elections should be decided on governance, policies and performance, not on allegations or hostility. We have, on several occasions, received intelligence about planned acts of violence and alerted the appropriate security agencies to what we believe the Accord Party intended to do. Whatever is happening in Osun today is being propelled by those in power.

Our focus remains on presenting our programmes while allowing voters to make informed decisions. Democracy works best when citizens have clear choices based on facts and performance.

The party in office is the one harbouring political thugs to attack us.

You have made allegations regarding criminal activities and security issues in the state. Can you elaborate?

Our position has always been that the rule of law must prevail.

Where individuals are accused of criminal offences, investigations should be thorough, transparent and allowed to run their course without political interference.

We have expressed concern over reports that some criminal cases were discontinued because such developments naturally raise public questions. Citizens deserve confidence that justice is being administered fairly.

No one should be presumed guilty without due process, but serious allegations should never be ignored.

Law enforcement agencies and the judiciary must remain independent and professional. Political considerations should never interfere with the administration of justice because public confidence depends on the integrity of these institutions.

What message do you have for security agencies ahead of the election?

My message is simple: remain professional, impartial and committed to the rule of law.

Security agencies have a constitutional responsibility to protect every citizen regardless of political affiliation. Their duty is to maintain peace, prevent violence and ensure that voters can exercise their democratic rights without fear.

Every reported case of violence or intimidation should be thoroughly investigated, and anyone found culpable should face the law.

Accountability is essential to maintaining public confidence.

We do not require federal might to win the Osun governorship election. We believe the people of Osun will freely choose the candidate they consider best prepared to govern the state.

World.title: Tinubu deserves praise for works across Nigeria – Onanuga
World.content:
Bayo Onanuga

Presidential spokesperson Bayo Onanuga has said that President Bola Tinubu deserves praise for expanding infrastructure across the country.

Onanuga stated this during an inspection tour of the Makurdi–Otukpo–Obolo-Affor–Enugu dual carriageway by the Renewed Hope Ambassadors Presidential Media Team.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the team led by Onanuga is being conducted round completed and ongoing federal and state infrastructure projects across Benue State.

Speaking to newsmen along the corridor, Onanuga described the expressway as a landmark project that would strengthen connectivity, boost commerce and foster national integration.

“From what we have seen so far, even though we have not even completed this road, it has shortened the travel time between Makurdi and Otukpo.

“From what I gathered, the road was so bad that from Makurdi to Otukpo it used to take about three hours. But now, just about one and a half hours or so, we are in Otukpo.

“So, this is a commendable project and I think President Bola Tinubu deserves a lot of applause for touching almost every part of Nigeria, giving them one road or bridge or one infrastructure or the other,” he said.

Onanuga added: “This road is linking the North Central and the South East for you.

“If you are able to link all parts of Nigeria, it shows you that we are improving the connectivity across our states.

“This will no doubt boost, not just passenger traffic, also business as people will be able to move goods across all the borders, all the state borders”.

Speaking on the project, the Federal Controller of Works, Benue State, Mukaila Danladi, said the 258-kilometre dual carriageway had been divided into five sections to facilitate construction.

He explained that the project traverses Nasarawa, Benue, Kogi and Enugu states, forming a strategic transport corridor linking major economic and commercial centres across the regions.

According to the controller, about 178 kilometres of the highway fall within Benue, while the section under inspection covers 50 kilometres on each carriageway, totalling 100 kilometres.

Danladi said construction had progressed to about 86 kilometres of binder course on both carriageways, describing the achievement as significant in spite of prevailing weather-related challenges.

He attributed the slower pace of work to the rainy season, noting that some earthworks could not be undertaken under unfavourable weather conditions common during construction.

The controller, however, said work had not stopped, with contractors concentrating on hydraulic structures and drainage installations along the alignment pending improved weather conditions.

He reiterated the Federal Government’s assurance that the project would be delivered within the 48-month contract period, with completion expected by December 2027.

Danladi recalled that the highway is the second phase of the Abuja-Akwanga-Nasarawa-Makurdi corridor, extending the dualisation from Makurdi through Otukpo and Obollo-Afor to Enugu.

He said the project is funded through a combination of the China EXIM Bank loan and Federal Government counterpart funding, while China Harbour Engineering Company is executing the works.

NAN reports that the highway is expected to improve road safety, reduce travel time, ease movement of agricultural produce and strengthen trade and economic integration across the affected states.

(NAN)

World.title: Osun account: Law mandates EFCC to serve court order – State counsel
World.content:
Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke

Counsel to the Osun State Government, Prof. Mubarak Adekilekun (SAN), has argued that neither the state government nor First Bank was served with any court order accompanying the directive that restricted access to the state’s statutory allocation account.

Adekilekun made the claim on Friday during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today, while commenting on the controversy surrounding the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission’s action on the account.

According to him, the law requires that a court order be obtained and properly served, particularly on the bank involved, before such a restriction can take effect.

He explained that the EFCC initially wrote to First Bank, and the letter was later forwarded to the Osun State Government, but the bank indicated that no court order was attached to the correspondence.

“You will recall that after the letter was written to First Bank in Osun, which in turn transmitted the letter to the state government, the requirement of the law in this regard is that a court order must be issued and served on, especially, First Bank.

“The letter was forwarded to Osun State Government, where First Bank confirmed that no court order was attached to it,” Adekilekun said.

The senior advocate acknowledged that the EFCC possesses statutory powers to act in cases involving suspected financial crimes, but maintained that those powers must be interpreted together with the provisions of the Money Laundering (Prevention and Prohibition) Act.

“They were trying to justify their action that if they do not do it, the account could be compromised. Yes, we agree there are some provisions of the law that say EFCC can, but if you interpret this in conjunction with Section 7 of the MLA, it says that there must be a court order served on that party.

“You can’t just go in and say, ‘Er, we are using our power vested in the Chairman of EFCC to now put a PND on the State Government’s statutory account,’” he said.

When asked whether the commission could impose a restriction for up to 72 hours before obtaining a court order, Adekilekun rejected that interpretation and insisted that judicial authorisation must come first.

“See, in this regard, EFCC must get a court order. The laws are there. If you read the provision I’m talking about, Section 7 of the Money Laundering Act, it stipulates that court order must be served. It is there,” he insisted.

He also dismissed allegations that the account was linked to money laundering, stressing that it had only been used to receive allocations from the Federation Account.

“You can’t do an act of this magnitude and just say you are transmitting a letter to put a PND on a state government account. The only money that is being transferred to that account is from the Federation Account, pure federal domain. That’s one of the requirements,” he said.

His comments came shortly after human rights lawyer and Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Femi Falana, defended the EFCC’s action, saying the commission did not act unlawfully.

Falana argued that the EFCC has the authority to freeze a state government account, provided it secures a court order within the legally prescribed period.

He referred to a 2022 Court of Appeal decision involving the Benue State Government and the EFCC, which he said confirmed the commission’s power to place a Post No Debit restriction for a maximum of 72 hours before obtaining judicial approval.

Amid the dispute, President Bola Tinubu directed the EFCC to return to court to seek the vacation of the order and discontinue the action, citing concerns over the timing of the restriction ahead of the August 15 Osun governorship election.

Responding to a question on whether the Osun State Government would continue with its legal challenge despite the President’s intervention, Adekilekun said the next step would be determined by his client.

“Well, it depends on what my client thinks, which is the Osun State Government. If they give us the go-ahead, but I think and I believe that it should be tried,” he said.

World.title: Nigeria VS Cameroon: Justin Madugu and his 200 million assistants
World.content:
Madugu

By Douglas Baye-Osagie

[email protected]

The Super Falcons are in the Quarter finals and are up against the Lionesses of Cameroon for a Semi Final spot and an automatic World Cup ticket in the ongoing WAFCON.

We have a pattern in this country. The moment things get uncomfortable, we conclude that the local coach “doesn’t know his work.” Every Nigerian is tactical and can read a match. We rate foreign coaches higher by default, even when the results and context are the same. If this were a European coach with the same record, we would be calling it “rotation” and “tournament management.” Justin Madugu is not being judged on tactics alone. He is being judged because he is Nigerian.

The truth is, African women’s football has come of age. The gap is closing fast. Who would have thought Nigeria would be needing calculators to qualify from a WAFCON group that has debutants Malawi and Egypt? Both teams were only in the tournament because it expanded from 12 to 16 teams. Yet they made us work.

That is not because Nigeria got worse overnight. It is because everyone else got better. Cameroon, Zambia, South Africa, Morocco — they are all professional now. They have structures, data, and players in Europe. The days of walking through group stages are gone.

In April I wrote an article that went viral titled “ SUPER FALCONS DESERVE BETTER.” I expressed doubt that the NFF had set this team up to succeed. Here are two paragraphs from that article:

“Elite performance is built on elite preparation. Friendlies are not just warm-ups. They are tactical laboratories where coaches test formations, bed in new talent, and measure their squad against varied styles of play. Right now, the Falcons’ 2026 calendar shows just a double-header vs Cameroon in February and March. That is a recipe for rust, not readiness.”

“The concern is sharper because the rest of Africa is not standing still. Nigeria no longer wins games by default. Women’s football on the continent has undergone a quiet revolution in the last 5 years. Investment, structure, and belief have spread. The days of Nigeria walking through WAFCON are gone. The competition is now a fight.”

You could see the effect of that poor preparation in the first three games.

Three games. Three different lineups. That tells you everything. Madugu is not playing mind games. He is using the tournament to find his first eleven because he was not given the time to do it before the tournament. When preparation is rushed, the coach experiments in public.

That is why the Esther Okoronkwo case keeps coming up. Yes, she has the reputation. Yes, she is quality. But she is also coming back from injury. Rhythm is not something you switch on. You build it with minutes, and sometimes the safest way to build it is off the bench.

Fans see 20 minutes of brilliance and ask why she didn’t start. Coaches see training data, recovery markers, and tactical matchups and decide to protect the player. Remember, Esther herself benefits when she is not rushed back into 90 minutes too early.

The criticism is also loud because we are Nigeria. We expect to dominate. But this WAFCON is different. Teams sit deep. They press. They analyze. You cannot just throw your “best XI” on paper and expect chemistry. Chemistry is built, and Madugu is building it under live fire.

Let us be honest about the lineup changes too. Is it ideal? No. But is it necessary when you had poor preparation? Yes. The coach is trying combinations. He is testing who can link with Oshoala, who can cover defensively, who can break a low block. That is what tournaments are for when pre-tournament work was not done. The good thing is there are goals in this team and we have different leaders in every department.

We have been here before. Shuaibu Amodu qualified us for two World Cups, in 2002 and 2010. Fans and administrators screamed “tactically deficient.” They sacked him both times. We went to those World Cups with new coaches and flopped. We regretted it. And Nigerian football has not fully recovered from that culture of panic.

Amodu was not perfect. But he understood the players, the terrain, and the pressure. We threw that away for the illusion that a foreign name would solve everything. We are repeating that script with Madugu.

Now we face Cameroon in the quarterfinals. A World Cup ticket is on the line. This is not the time for experiments or fan selections. This is the time to back the man in the dugout, even if we disagree with one or two decisions.

What the Super Falcons need now is not more noise about who should start. They need ruthlessness in front of goal. They need to take the half-chances. They need the midfield to control tempo. Those are coaching points, but they are also player execution.

Esther Okoronkwo will have her role. Whether she starts or comes on at 60 minutes, her impact is still needed. A player of her quality changes games either way. The goal is not to start 11 stars. The goal is to win and qualify.

Madugu deserves respect for navigating this mess. He inherited a team with no proper build-up, a fan base expecting 2010 football, and opponents who no longer fear us. Yet we are still in it.

So to the fans: criticize, yes. Debate, yes. But don’t burn the house down because one player is on the bench. Don’t confuse rotation with incompetence. Don’t confuse a Nigerian coach with a bad coach.

African women’s football has grown up. Our expectations must grow up too. The pitch against Cameroon will answer more questions than Twitter will.

For now, let Justin Madugu guide this team. He has the experience to navigate the storm. Let Esther get to full rhythm. If the Falcons are clinical another trophy is possible.

Because if we sack, insult, and undermine our way through every tournament, we will keep repeating the Amodu story.

And we cannot afford to regret this one too.

World.title: Two Nigerian women held in India after cocaine seizure worth N380m
World.content:
Two Nigerian women have been taken into custody by railway police in Delhi, India, after officers allegedly recovered 2.28 kilograms of cocaine estimated to be worth about Rs20 crore, roughly N380 million.

The suspects were identified as 43-year-old Chikanso James and 41-year-old Happiness Okoye. They were arrested during a patrol operation on Platform One of Hazrat Nizamuddin Railway Station, according to The New Indian Express.

Police authorities said the women attracted suspicion because of their conduct, prompting officers to search under the provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act.

During the operation, officers reportedly recovered 11 packets containing the suspected cocaine from James.

The substance was subsequently examined by members of the crime team and forensic specialists, who confirmed it was cocaine.

Investigators further alleged that the drugs were linked to an interstate trafficking operation believed to be active between Mumbai and the Delhi-NCR region.

Police said James informed investigators that the consignment had been picked up from Vikaspuri. Authorities added that efforts are ongoing to identify other individuals connected to the alleged network and to trace its financial and supply channels.

Following the arrest, James was remanded in police custody, while Okoye was placed in judicial custody as investigations continue.

World.title: Military rescues 363 victims, kills 69 terrorists in one week – DHQ
World.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi

Following sustained land, air and sea offensives against criminal elements in all theatres of operations by gallant Nigerian troops in the last one week, 69 terrorists elements were neutralised in gunfights and air interdiction, over 360 kidnapped victims rescued while 49 suspects were arrested.

During operations against economic saboteurs, three reactivated illegal refinery sites were discovered and dismantled while a total of 251,600 litres of stolen crude were recovered and 12 dug-out pits for storage were destroyed.

Major General Michael Onoja, Director of Defence Media Operations, while making this known, noted that sadly, one soldier was killed in action while another sustained injury in action.

Detailing the encounters, Onoja said, “In the North East, troops of Operation Hadin Kai deployed at Dutsen Kura while sustaining robust operation, on 31 July 2026, foiled terrorists’ attempt to abduct civilians along the Buratai-Kamuya Road in Biu LGA of Borno State.

“Troops pursued the fleeing terrorists towards Mangari-Dora and rescued 31 persons, comprising 22 adult males, 5 adult females and 4 children. Four vehicles and one motorcycle belonging to the terrorists were also confiscated.

“On the same day, a suspected terrorist informant was apprehended at Garaha Market in Hong LGA of Adamawa State.

“On 1 August 2026, troops on routine clearance patrol near Amuda Bridge in Gwoza LGA of Borno State rescued two women and two children who had been held since the 2023 farming season at a terrorist enclave.

“The victims were subsequently handed over to the community head of Ngoshe.

“Between 2 – 4 August 2026, several family members of suspected terrorists surrendered while some were intercepted in Gwoza, Konduga and Bama LGAs of Borno State.

“Additionally, a group of 20 persons surrendered to troops at Kwuari in Konduga LGA of Borno State.

“On 3 August 2026, troops arrested two suspected terrorist logistics suppliers at Monguno LGA of Borno State, recovering assorted foodstuffs and provisions destined for terrorists in Kukawa LGA of Borno State.

“Similarly, another terrorist logistics supplier was arrested at Gwalaram Village in Magumeri LGA on 4 August 2026.

“In a separate operation conducted on 3 August 2026, troops rescued Miss Blessing Tuggur, an 18-year-old victim abducted in November 2025 at Dogoba Kopre axis in Askira Uba LGA of Borno State.

“The victim was subsequently reunited with her family after receiving medical attention.

“On the same day, a suspect was arrested at Kan Lamba village in Darazo LGA of Bauchi State, for allegedly attempting to procure firearms.

“Similarly, a suspected terrorist informant was arrested at Dzangola Kilba in Hong LGA of Adamawa State, on 5 August 2026.

“In the North West, troops of Operation Fansan Yamma on 2 August 2026, responded to the movement of suspected terrorists transiting through Giwa LGA of Kaduna State, from Hadeija.

‘Following a snap operation, the troops successfully intercepted and arrested 21 persons attempting to cross into Birnin Kebbi.

“Upon profiling the arrested persons, five suspects were identified as terrorists and handed over to the Department of State Services, while the remaining passengers were released to continue their journey.

“On 6 August 2026, troops arrested four suspects at Darusa Village Market in Gudu LGA of Sokoto State. Items recovered from the arrest include six rustled cattle, mobile phones and the sum of ₦165,000 believed to be proceeds of the intended sale.

“In a major air interdiction operation, the Air Component of Operation Fansan Yamma conducted surveillance over Kampani Bobi and Beri Settlement in Mariga LGA of Niger State, on 6 August 2026.

“This was followed by a precision air strike that neutralised scores of terrorists who had assembled with about 15 motorcycles in preparation for hostile activity.

Battle Damage Assessment confirmed the neutralisation of the terrorists, with secondary explosions indicating the destruction of additional logistics and equipment, including explosive ordnance.

“In the North Central, troops of Operation Whirl Stroke, in sustained operations against armed criminal elements in Benue, Nasarawa and Kogi States, apprehended a suspected gun runner, Mr Victor Idoko, at North Bank in Makurdi LGA of Benue State, on 31 July 2026.

“This led to the recovery of two locally fabricated pistols and other items at his residence.

“On the same day, troops rescued seven kidnapped victims in Ukum LGA of Benue State. The victims, who are all indigenes of Tela Village in Gassol LGA of Taraba State, had been abducted along the Wukari-Zaki-Biam Road on 13 July 2026. All rescued victims have since been reunited with their families.

“On 1 August 2026, troops destroyed a hideout linked to a terrorist leader named Mathew aka “Full Fire” at Sabongida Leke village in Ukum LGA, and arrested five persons suspected to be associates of the wanted terrorist leader.

“Relatedly, a coordinated operation by troops on 5 August 2026 at Gbede village in the same LGA led to one terrorist neutralized.

“On 1 August 2026, troops intercepted a motorcycle conveying two women at Yelwa village in Doma LGA, Nasarawa State, and recovered ten AK-47 magazines with 551 rounds of 7.62mm ammunition, while a separate arrest at Doma town also led the discovery of twelve rounds of AK 47 ammunition. Both cases were handed over to the Police for further action.

“In Kogi State, troops foiled a kidnap attempt along the Lokoja-Okene Road in Adavi LGA on 2 August 2026, where a civilian sustained a gunshot wound and was evacuated for treatment.

“On the same day, troops and local security groups responded to a kidnap incident at Oke Ere community in Yagba West LGA. Troops engaged the terrorists and neutralised one while the others fled, thereby rescuing two of the four abducted victims unharmed.

“However, a member of the local security group was tragically killed in action. Efforts are being made to rescue the remaining two victims.

In the North Central geopolitical zone, troops of Operation Savanna Shield recorded a major rescue success in a joint operation within the Kainji Lake National Park, Borgu LGA of Niger State.

“This feat was achieved on 5 August 2026, where Three Hundred and Eight abducted victims, mainly women and children, were rescued.

“One Hundred and Sixty-Three of the victims were indigenes of Woro village, Kwara State, while One Hundred and Forty-Five were from Niger State.

“In another operation on 4 August 2026, troops arrested a suspected terrorist informant at Nuku community in Kaiama LGA of Kwara State.

“Similarly, from 5 – 6 August 2026, troops conducted operations at Kamfanin Bobi village in Mariga LGA of Niger State, and engaged terrorists moving from Zamfara State with the intent of launching a reprisal attack on a military base.

“The ensuing engagement forced the terrorists to withdraw and resulted in one terrorist killed and nine motorcycles confiscated, with no casualties recorded by troops.

“Troops continue to operate in the area to deny the terrorists any freedom of action.

“Troops of Operation Enduring Peace in continued efforts to stem communal and terrorist-related violence, on 6 August 2026, arrested a youth leader named Zakari Yahu Adamu at Fadan Chanwei in Kauru LGA of Kaduna State, in connection with the recent terrorist attack on Naridon community.

“The suspect is currently undergoing further investigation to establish the full circumstances of the attack.

In the Niger Delta, troops of Operation Delta Safe on 30 July 2026, responded to a kidnap incident along the Lagos-Benin Road in Ovia North East LGA of Edo State, pursuing the perpetrators and rescuing 11 victims unhurt, who were subsequently reassured before being encouraged to continue their journey.

“In a sustained maritime offensive under Operation Delta Sentinel, troops dismantled three reactivated illegal refining sites in the Ogba-Egbema-Ndoni Axis of Rivers State between 1 – 2 August 2026.

“An approximated 61,000 litres of stolen petroleum products, comprising 43,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and 18,000 litres of illegally refined Automotive Gas Oil, concealed within 12 dugout pits and reservoirs, were discovered at the site and handled.

“On 5 August 2026, troops discovered 85,300 litres of crude oil products in Ogba-Egbema-Ndoni Axis of Rivers State.

“Furthermore, on 6 August 2026, OPDS troops conducted an offensive operation to Oteghele Axis of Delta State, where 105,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil products were discovered and handled in accordance with the OPDS Mandate.

“In the South East, following sustained pursuit after an ambush on troops on 4 May 2026, that resulted in the death of one soldier and injury of another, troops of Operation Udoka conducted offensives that led to the arrest of one Mr Abire on 30 July 2026, in Port Harcourt, Rivers State.

“Information obtained from the suspect led to further operations in Opaebe, Oleh, in Delta State on 31 July 2026, where the principal suspects, Mr Albert Tony (aka Chiboy), Temple Eburua (aka Marathon) and Vitalis Eburua (aka Onowu), were apprehended.

“The suspects subsequently led troops to camps at Ohaji/Egbema and Umudike Plantation, where weapons used during the earlier ambush, alongside additional arms and ammunition, were discovered and confiscated.

“On 1 August 2026, a militant leader known as Comedy voluntarily surrendered a cache of arms buried in Egbema, Imo State, through the State Amnesty Chairman.

“On the same day, troops conducted a search operation near Ihuonyia community in Ezeagu LGA of Enugu State, following an earlier attack on Fulani herders, arresting five suspected members of the Indigenous People of Biafra and destroying their hideout at Amansioda Ndiagu Oghe Forest.

“In a follow-up operation, troops confiscated two General Purpose Machine Guns with ammunition and an Improvised Explosive Device.

“On 4 August 2026, troops foiled a kidnap attempt along the Nsukka-Obollo road in Udenu LGA of Enugu State. The victim’s abandoned vehicle was discovered while the perpetrators were engaged with weapon’s fire, thereby forcing the criminals to abandon their victim and flee.

“Furthermore, Major General Onoja said, “The Chief of Defence Staff, General Olufemi Oluyede extends his profound appreciation to troops across all theatres of operation for their discipline and commitment to the defence of the nation.

“He commends the sustained collaboration between the Armed Forces and other security agencies, including the local security groups and other stakeholders, which has continued to yield positive results in the ongoing campaign against terrorism, kidnapping and other forms of criminality.

“The CDS further commends the media for their continued professionalism and balanced reportage of military operations, and urges members of the public to continue providing useful information to troops to enhance the security architecture nationwide.

“The CDS assures all Nigerians of the resolve of the Armed Forces to sustain the current tempo of operations until peace and stability are fully restored across all theatres.”

World.title: Alcohol: Nigerian children caught in deadly trap
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna

At the age when most children are still learning how to spell their names, count money and tell the difference between right and wrong, nine-year-old Ade already knows the taste of alcohol. He does not hide it. Neither does he consider it unusual.

Read Also: 25 children from Kebbi, Kwara, Niger died in terrorists’ captivity — Lawmaker

The provided text describes the serious issue of underage alcohol consumption and the environmental factors that contribute to it. It highlights stories of young children being introduced to alcohol by family members and the normalized presence of alcoholic substances in their daily lives.

Underage drinking poses significant risks to a child’s physical and mental development. Early exposure to alcohol can lead to dependency, impaired judgment, and long-term health complications. Public health experts and child advocates emphasize the importance of parental supervision and the enforcement of laws to protect minors from accessing regulated substances.

For those seeking help or more information on protecting children from substance use, resources are available through local child welfare services and public health organizations dedicated to substance abuse prevention.

me to buy as usual and an uncle I met there offered to buy one for me. He said he wanted to know if I could drink it or not. So, I proved him wrong that I could take alcohol,” he recalled. “Since then, each time I go to buy, he will buy for me. That is how it all became an everyday thing.” Today, Chibuike said he drinks two to three sachets of alcohol a day, sometimes buying it with his own savings.

When errands become dangerous

The stories of Ade and Chibuike expose a troubling reality in Nigerian society. Children are often expected to obey adults unquestioningly, especially when sent on errands, yet little attention is paid to what they are being sent to buy, deliver or do. It is a practice deeply rooted in African family and social structures. Parents, older relatives and other adults exercise authority over children, while society often interprets obedience as a virtue.

In religious settings, children are similarly taught to obey their parents and elders. But what happens when obedience becomes a pathway to danger? What happens when the child sent to buy alcohol eventually becomes the child who drinks it? Across Nigeria, children are exposed to alcohol not only through friends and social gatherings, but through their homes, relatives and neighbourhood shops. Some are introduced to it by adults they trust. Others obtain it themselves from retailers who do not ask their age. The result is a disturbing cycle in which some children encounter alcohol years before they can understand its implications.

The disturbing numbers

A 2021 national survey conducted by Research and Data Solutions Limited, Abuja, for the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, and the Distillers and Blenders Association of Nigeria, DIBAN, found widespread access to alcohol among minors and underage persons. The study covered 1,768 respondents in six states representing the six geopolitical zones. Respondents below 13 years were classified as minors, while those aged 13 to 17 were classified as underage.

The findings showed that 54.3 percent of minors and underage respondents obtained alcohol by themselves. Nearly half, 49.9 percent, accessed alcohol through friends and relatives, while 43.9 percent obtained it at social gatherings. Another 21.7 percent had access to alcohol in their parents’ homes.

Among those who procured alcohol themselves, 57.2 percent of minors and 48.8 percent of underage respondents bought drinks in sachets, while 41.2 percent of minors and 47.2 percent of underage respondents procured alcohol in PET bottles.

The survey also found that 63.2 percent of minors and 54 percent of underage respondents consumed alcohol occasionally, while 9.3 percent of minors and 25.2 percent of underage respondents reported drinking daily.

The state-level analysis reveals disturbing variability of alcohol use by the survey; Gombe, Kaduna, the Federal Capital Territory, Anambra, Lagos and Rivers, Rivers recorded the highest procurement of alcohol in sachets and PET bottles among minors and underage persons, with 68.0 percent and 64.5 percent respectively. Lagos followed, with 52.3 percent procuring alcohol in sachets and 47.7 percent in PET bottles, while Kaduna recorded 38.6 percent and 28.4 percent respectively.

The figures show that the problem is not confined to one region or one type of community. In neighbourhood shops, markets, motor parks, social gatherings and even homes, alcohol can be within easy reach of children.

The health warning

But the danger, according to health experts, goes beyond access. The World Health Organisation, WHO, warns that alcohol use during childhood and adolescence can interfere with the normal development of the brain and increase the risk of problems involving learning, memory, judgment and decision-making. Early initiation of alcohol use is also associated with a greater risk of developing alcohol-use disorders later in life.
