World.title: Kärt Pormeister: The charm and pain of AI in the legal field
World.content:
One thing is when non‑lawyer participants in proceedings trust artificial intelligence too much, but far more frightening is when real lawyers — or even attorneys — fall for AI hallucinations, writes Kärt Pormeister.

I once tried using AI to help write an opinion piece. I wanted to know whether there were any scientific studies that confirmed or disproved certain hypotheses. The AI wrote me beautiful answers in fluent English, complete with citations. The answers were full of all sorts of interesting claims.

I then started asking one by one: what is the source of this specific claim? Sometimes the answer was: "Sorry, no source actually says this exactly. My mistake, thank you for pointing it out." Other times the AI gave a citation, but when I checked it, it turned out the source did not support the conclusion at all.

When I pointed out that the claim did not match the source, the AI politely apologized again and thanked me for drawing attention to its error. After several rounds of this back‑and‑forth, I began to feel that I was helping the AI, not the other way around. I felt like the AI's teacher or coach, pointing out its shortcomings.

Of course, AI tools vary greatly in quality, and you shouldn't expect top‑tier service for a bargain price. I've had the chance to test a more advanced, law‑focused AI solution whose citations and analysis genuinely impressed me. So I'm not trying to claim that AI cannot be useful in law — it certainly can; just like a weapon can be useful for self‑defense, provided you don't shoot yourself in the foot through poor handling.

Regardless of price or quality, you must always be source‑critical when using AI. That doesn't just mean checking whether a source exists, but also diving into its content. AI can help find sources, provide ideas and inspiration, and give feedback on work already done, but it cannot — at least not yet — replace human thinking.

For a long time now, especially from the United States, we've seen news about AI hallucinations ending up in court filings. The problem is much worse there because their legal system is based on precedent.

In a precedent‑based system, judges create new legal rules through their decisions. US law textbooks are often built around case analysis because the rules arise from court practice. In such a system, AI hallucinations have far more room to cause trouble. But even here in Estonia, examples are quietly emerging of AI causing problems in court proceedings.

After Midsummer, the Supreme Court announced (link in Estonian) that at least one such AI‑related case has now reached a final resolution. A group of people had filed a complaint in administrative court to challenge a logging permit. They submitted a document citing scientific studies on clear‑cutting impacts. According to the Supreme Court's press release, the court discovered that the Estonian researchers mentioned in the citations did not actually exist, and the described studies could not be found.

"But even here in Estonia, examples are quietly emerging of AI causing problems in court proceedings."

In essence, false factual claims had been submitted to the court. The administrative court fined one complainant €150 and nine others €50. The complainants didn't like this. They argued that using AI is not prohibited and they did not intend to mislead the court. Of course it's not prohibited — but the person submitting a document is responsible for its content, regardless of whether they used their neighbor or an AI to help write it.

The administrative court emphasized that if a complainant cites scientific sources, they must be sure those sources actually exist and contain the information claimed in the filing. That seems obvious and logical. But the complainants didn't think so and appealed to the Circuit Court. The Circuit Court agreed with the lower court. The Supreme Court refused to hear the case, and the fines became final.

Rightly so. If a complainant without legal training makes legal mistakes when turning to court, that is completely understandable — applying the law correctly is the court's job, especially in administrative court. But if someone presents factual claims to the court, citing scientific studies that do not exist, that is entirely their own fault.

Tallinn Administrative Court's president Kaupo Kruusvee explained that administrative proceedings do not require legal knowledge from the person — it is enough for them to describe their real‑life problem and desired solution, and the court must help them formulate a proper claim to protect their rights. He added that for the sake of both the participants' and the court's workload, it would be better if people did not submit AI‑generated, confusing documents, but instead turned to the court directly and in their own words.

One thing is when non‑lawyers trust AI too much. Far more frightening, in my view, is when actual lawyers — even attorneys — fall for AI hallucinations.

"Regardless of price or quality, you must always be source critical when using AI."

Earlier this year, the Tartu Circuit Court issued a decision in a criminal case in which the court scolded the defense attorney for submitting an appeal full of errors that were clearly just AI hallucinations. The attorney had cited supposed Supreme Court decisions that do not exist (the case numbers simply do not exist). In addition, the attorney made several claims about Supreme Court rulings that did not match their content.

One amusing example: "According to the appeal, Supreme Court decision No. 3‑1‑1‑67‑14 deals with the seriousness of threats. In reality, that decision concerns operating without an environmental permit, control measurements, traceability of measurement results, and calculating environmental damage." (Tartu Circuit Court decision of 17.02.2026 in case No. 1‑24‑5343, para. 31)

The Circuit Court summarized its devastating analysis by stating that none of the numerous Supreme Court decisions cited by the defense contained the legal positions claimed in the appeal. The court concluded that the text was AI‑generated and the attorney had not bothered to check it.

The attorney had requested state legal aid compensation corresponding to 4.5 working hours. As a sort of "punishment" for submitting an appeal full of AI hallucinations, the circuit court found it justified to compensate only 1.5 hours — three times less.

I don't know whether the attorney was also called before the Bar Association for this conduct, but I sincerely hope so. Being a member of the Bar should at least theoretically be a mark of quality. If an attorney allows themselves to make such a crude mistake as submitting AI hallucinations in a court filing, the Bar as a professional body should respond with full seriousness.

World.title: Fixed or market‑price electricity? What to consider ahead of an unpredictable winter
World.content:
Whether it makes sense to choose a fixed‑price or market‑price electricity package for winter depends largely on a person's consumption habits, electricity sellers say. Some also said customers have increasingly begun to prefer fixed prices.

The market price of electricity is unpredictable, but one thing is clear: electricity is more expensive during cold and dark periods. Last winter, the situation became difficult for customers buying electricity at market price in January and February, when price spikes repeatedly rose to several dozen cents per kilowatt‑hour. The average price in both January and February was 15.4 cents per kilowatt‑hour (without VAT).

In 2025, only one month — February — had an average price above 15 cents per kilowatt‑hour.

No one knows exactly what the coming winter will bring, because as electricity sellers themselves say, the market price is always unpredictable and that is nothing new. And if you think about it, the market would not make sense if the price were known in advance.

But ahead of this winter, there are more factors than usual that influence electricity prices and make them even harder to predict, electricity sellers said.

Timo Tatar. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"This year we can expect periodically high peaks due to red flags on global markets, and futures prices reflect this — they are at similar levels to last winter or even slightly higher. But in the end, this is crystal‑ball gazing because predicting the coming winter's weather today is impossible," said Ignitis Eesti head Timo Tatar.

In such a situation, the question arises: is it wiser for a household to choose a price package tied more closely to the market or one that offers greater independence from market fluctuations? There is no clear answer, because the best solution depends on how a person uses electricity.

"If electricity costs are not a major part of the household budget — for example, someone lives in an apartment and consumption is low — then it does not make much difference whether you choose a fixed or market package. The financial difference is small. Choose what feels right. You might win or lose, but the stakes are not high," Tatar said.

With a heat pump, fixed price is better

But if electricity costs are a major expense — for example, if a heat pump is the main or only heating source — then a fixed price is recommended because it provides predictability and helps avoid large bills caused by price spikes, he said. "You might pay more than the market at times, but you might also pay significantly less. For you, cost management is what matters," Tatar said.

And if consumption can be significantly controlled — for example, charging an electric car, or having an alternative heating source, battery storage or other flexible consumption — then a market‑price package makes sense because cheap hours or periods can be used to your advantage, Tatar said.

Eesti elektrijaam Auveres. Autor/allikas: Rene Kundla/ERR

Enefit board member Tiit Hõbejõgi also said each person should choose an electricity package based on their risk tolerance and consumption habits.

"A fixed‑price package is best for those who do not adjust their consumption according to market prices. It is also more suitable for those who value predictable costs and want to avoid possible price spikes," he said.

"A market‑price package may be suitable for those who are willing to accept price fluctuations and can shift their consumption to cheaper hours," Hõbejõgi added.

Winter determines which choice is sensible

Looking back at previous winters, there is no single answer to whether fixed or market‑price packages were cheaper for consumers, Hõbejõgi said. First, it again depended on the household's consumption: if electricity was used more during peak hours, fixed‑price customers saved money; those who managed their consumption more actively benefited from market‑price packages.

"Looking back, there have been winters when the average market‑price package cost was lower than fixed prices, but there have also been periods when fixed‑price customers avoided very high spikes. For example, last winter, due to exceptionally cold months, fixed prices stayed lower than the average market price," Hõbejõgi said.

And it is important to remember that the goal of a fixed‑price package is not always to achieve the lowest possible average price, but to provide price security and predictability, he added.

"The advantage of a market‑price package may appear over a longer period, but its users must be ready for potentially higher bills during winter months," Hõbejõgi said.

"Choosing between fixing the price or staying with the market price should primarily be seen as a risk‑management decision. More and more of our customers are treating it exactly that way," Tatar said.

Alexela Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

Alexela: people increasingly prefer fixed prices

At Alexela, the fluctuating electricity price has already pushed customers to prefer fixed‑price packages more since spring, said Alexela residential segment manager Ester Ausmees.

"In June and July this year, nearly 20 percent more new customers chose fixed‑price electricity packages compared to a year earlier. We see the same trend among existing customers, who increasingly prefer price security," Ausmees said.

As of June, about 60 percent of electricity packages chosen by Alexela customers had fixed prices.

"What is interesting is that usually interest in price security increases at the end of summer and beginning of fall, but this year we saw it already in spring — in April and May," Ausmees said.

She said this suggests people's expectations have changed: although a low price is still very important, customers are also looking for certainty that next month's electricity bill will not be shocking.

"In practice, we see that people have become more aware and want to decide for themselves how much they want to risk with electricity price fluctuations," Ausmees said.

Because the coming winter is expected to be more unpredictable in electricity prices than before, Ausmees recommended reviewing your electricity package before winter. "Not necessarily to change anything, but to make sure your current solution is still the right one," she said.

World.title: Canadian Estonian family still thriving 30 years after return to homeland
World.content:
The Viinalass family recently celebrated 30 years in Estonia, reflecting on how a temporary move to their homeland became permanent, coming full circle after generations.

The family marked the milestone with a gathering of about 150 relatives and friends, who shared memories from their early years after moving from Canada.

"Our mom was in charge of the Facebook event," recalled Joshua James Viinalass, a real estate broker with Arco Vara.

"She accidentally sent the invite to everyone," added his brother, musician Daniel Levi. "And everyone responded that they're coming."

Like in many diaspora Estonian families, the Viinalass brothers' grandfather was a World War II-era refugee, who first fled to Germany in 1944 before reaching and later naturalizing as a citizen in Canada.

Their father, Linden Viinalass, was born and raised in Canada, where his children were also born and spent the first few years of their lives. After their grandfather's death in the 1990s, however, their father came across an ad in a Canadian Estonian diaspora newspaper seeking English teachers in Estonia.

"He immediately knew that [opportunity] was meant for him — like it spoke to him almost supernaturally," Daniel Levi said.

The plan was simple: move to Estonia for a year and then return to Canada. Thirty years later, the family is still here and thriving.

Adjusting as kids

Joshua James and Daniel Levi were just 3 and 8 years old when their family moved to Tartu, and some of their earliest memories are of life in and around the Soviet-era prefab apartment buildings in Annelinn.

Viinalass family photos. Source: Viinalass family/ERR

Joshua James said he picked up Estonian simply playing with other kids on the playground and in kindergarten.

Daniel Levi recalled his father giving a neighbor's child a soccer ball, which prompted an unexpected gift to the Viinalass family in turn.

"The family was so touched that they gifted us a drinking horn brought all the way from Georgia in return," he said, adding that the horn is still proudly displayed at their parents' home.

The musician acknowledged that the move from Canada to Estonia took some getting used to for all of them, but added that the younger you are, the easier it can be to adjust.

"Speaking of adjusting, just today I was talking to someone about what our favorite parts of kindergarten had been," said Joshua James. "I remember I couldn't understand a word at first, but when meals were served, that was the best part of the day."

Both brothers praised Estonian food, agreeing that one of their favorite Estonian dishes is still hakklihakaste — a simple creamed ground meat often served with potatoes and popular both in Estonia and the diaspora.

Years after a previous appearance on ETV's "Ringvaade," however, Daniel Levi admitted he still can't bring himself to eat sült, or meat aspic.

Brothers Daniel Levi Viinalass and James Joshua Viinalass. August 2026. Source: ERR

'Three men sitting in a sauna'

Asked whether Estonia lives up to its digital image, the Viiinalass brothers pointed out that the contrast is evident when they talk to friends in the U.S. who still have to deposit physical paychecks in person at the bank, or grapple with filing tax returns that in Estonia take literally just a few clicks to do.

They also agreed Estonians seem to be warming up to things like hugging, although the perception that Estonians are typically reserved and need their personal space persists.

"Estonians like their fresh air and pure nature, and I think that sense of personal space goes beyond just that question of hugging," said Daniel Levi.

"I think it's very healthy," Joshua James countered, prompting his brother to quip that it's clear he was raised in Estonia. "That little bit of personal space is really welcome sometimes."

The real estate broker described his post-workout sauna at the gym earlier that day, calling it a perfectly Estonian example.

"Three men sitting in a sauna: no one says a word, no one makes eye contact, no one says 'Tere,' nothing," Joshua James said. "No, when I handed the water bucket over to one of the other guys in the sauna, he said, 'Aitäh.'"

World.title: Unaligned MPs mulling presidential candidates
World.content:
Unaffiliated members of the Riigikogu are discussing who they will vote for at the upcoming presidential election on September 2, and the coalition will need their support to elect their chosen candidate.

Estonia's president is elected by the parliament, not directly by the public. A candidate needs to win at least 68 votes from the 101-seat Riigikogu.

Reform Party secretary general Kristo Enn Vaga told ERR's "Aktuaalne kaamera" that the Social Democrats, the Reform and Eesti 200 support Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise's candidacy. The three parties have 66 votes between them, in theory.

"At least three" unaligned MPs would also be willing to support Madise, he added.

"And by simple arithmetic, that makes 69 votes in total. I can't speak for the others. And between us, some MPs from both the Center Party and Isamaa have said that they too would support Ülle Madise. On paper, there are more than 68 votes," Vaga said.

The MPs who are not part of parliamentary groups held discussions on Friday. Tõnis Mölder said that while Ülle Madise is a strong candidate, the unaffiliated MPs will wait to see whether candidates might also be put forward by Isamaa or the Center Party.

Kristo Enn Vaga Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"And if no additional candidates emerge from there and Ülle Madise gives her consent, even informally, to run as a presidential candidate, then we are ready to meet with her and form our position. We will wait for Tuesday's meeting of the Council of Elders and after that we will meet again to discuss a common position," Mölder said.

On Thursday, Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas said Madise has 67 votes, as MP Züleyxa Izmailova, who left Eesti 200 and joined the Social Democrats, does not support her candidacy.

Izmailova said that as the vote takes place by secret ballot, the election of the president will not depend on her. However, she believes there must be discussion before the vote rather than pressure on the opposition to make a quick choice.

"In my assessment, this is simply an attempt to divert attention from the coalition's own inability to manage this process, and I am not at all convinced that the alleged votes and signatures they say they have actually exist," Izmailova said.

Vaga said the members of the three parliamentary groups would vote for Madise if she agreed to run, and they also want to collect at least 68 signatures to nominate her as a candidate.

"Everyone can of course act according to their conscience. Ülle Madise has been Chancellor of Justice for 11 years, everyone knows her and is familiar with her, and she is seriously considering it," he said.

The first round of the election is on September 2.

World.title: Estonian pilgrim swaps work stress for freedom on Camino journey
World.content:
Seeking relief from work stress and the weight of nonstop responsibility, Estonian pilgrim Rebeka Neitsov found unexpected freedom while walking Spain's Camino de Santiago.

The Camino de Santiago is a popular, centuries-old network of pilgrims' ways that lead to the shrine of the apostle James at Santiago de Compostela Cathedral in Galicia, Spain.

Neitsov said the idea to take on the famous journey came after talking with several friends who had done the pilgrimage themselves. At the time, she was navigating a particularly stressful period in her communications job at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.

"I had to make a lot of decisions each day," she recalled. "I felt like I needed time where I didn't have to make a single decision."

Friends described the Camino as a journey that "carries you along" and where your next steps are already laid out for you.

The ministry employee said the trip also offered a chance to step back from the weight of constant responsibility.

"I wanted confirmation that not everything is constantly mine to decide or carry," she said, adding that she was leaving things in part back up to the universe.

In all, Neitsov walked just under 300 kilometers, and said the experience helped her sort through thoughts that truly mattered while letting go of distractions. Some ideas and emotions she realized she'd need to keep working through afterward.

She also formed friendships with fellow pilgrims, many of whom she remains in touch with today.

An emotional end

The only disappointment came near the end of the route, when the final 100 kilometers became noticeably more crowded as hikers completed the minimum distance required to earn the official Compostela certificate.

Although some fellow pilgrims dropped out due to injuries or exhaustion, Neitsov said she never considered quitting. About two kilometers before reaching Santiago, she began crying instead.

"I felt so good on this journey; I was able to let go and simply be exactly who I am," Neitsov said, noting that it had been an incredibly emotional experience.

She added that she already plans to return to the Camino one day.

World.title: Another 26 kilometers of Estonia's border infrastructure completed
World.content:
Construction of the infrastructure on the southeastern border has reached the final stretch after two sections totaling almost 26 kilometers were completed this week.

Estonia has been strengthening its eastern border for several years, building fences and installing surveillance equipment.

The newly completed sections stretch from the Koidula road border crossing point to Saatse. Construction cost €12 million and was co-financed by the European Union, the Ministry of the Interior said in a press release.

"I think the Estonian taxpayer can be satisfied that the right investment was made. If we think about all the challenges neighboring countries here have faced with illegal migration attacks, then we certainly have proper border infrastructure in place to repel that," Minister of Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said during a visit.

Surveillance equipment will be installed on the 30-meter-high masts, which will guard and protect the border.

Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) for border guard affairs, said: "The masts have very good technical solutions that can handle the load required to ensure the security of the entire border. Then there will be conventional surveillance systems, radar systems and counter-drone – or rather, drone surveillance systems. And electronic jamming equipment for counter-drone purposes can also be fitted on top of these masts."

All construction work on the €180 million eastern border infrastructure is expected to be completed next year.

"The land border is now 80 percent covered by infrastructure, and by the end of the year, when the next two sections with a total length of 20 kilometers are completed, this will already reach 90 percent," Taro added.

The minister said a separate decision needs to be made on the final 14 kilometers of the land border. "Originally, there were no plans to build it because the area is naturally difficult – bogs and wetlands that already act as obstacles themselves. However, given the current situation with migration pressure, I nevertheless see that this too needs to be built," Taro said.

"This requires €18 million, of which €14.5 million would be spent on infrastructure and €3.5 million on surveillance equipment. Then there will no longer be any uncovered sections on our land border," he added.

Estonia's eastern border separates the country, and the EU, from the Russian Federation, while its long southern land border with Latvia is an internal EU frontier. Source: Ministry of the Interior

World.title: Clinton compares Trump’s White House to former Iraqi dictator Saddam’s palaces
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has compared President Donald Trump’s White House renovations to former Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein’s palaces, remembering her own travels to Baghdad after his ouster.

Clinton, speaking on journalist Kara Swisher’s podcast, compared Trump’s White House decor to meetings she attended in Saddam Hussein’s former palaces while serving as a US senator.

“They were quite reminiscent of what we are seeing in our own White House,” she said.

Her remarks come amid wider criticism of Trump’s renovations and architectural decisions, such as heavy gold décor within the Oval Office, plans for a new White House ballroom, and a projected triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

Clinton called the improvements “tacky” and suggested that the president was focusing too much on cosmetic initiatives when the US confronts substantial foreign policy, economic, and technological issues.

She also criticized the process around Trump’s planned ballroom, stating that she was not opposed to the White House having such a facility but was concerned about the architecture and how the project had been handled.

Given Clinton’s past with Iraq, the connection to Saddam was especially relevant.

She was a member of the United States Senate during the 2003 war that deposed Saddam Hussein and subsequently became Secretary of State under President Barack Obama.

During his reign, Saddam was noted for building multiple extravagant presidential palaces around Iraq, many with elaborate interiors and significant use of marble, chandeliers, and gold-colored décor, despite the country’s international sanctions and economic difficulty.

Trump has defended his White House restoration plans, which are part of a larger push to renovate and enhance Washington’s important federal buildings and sites.

Clinton’s parallel brings Iraq and one of Saddam’s most recognizable emblems into the increasingly heated political argument over Trump’s White House moves.

World.title: Apple officially enters Iraq under new digital services framework
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Apple has legally joined Iraq’s regulated digital market, having met the country’s standards for digital platforms and services, according to the Communications and Media Commission (CMC).

According to the regulator, Apple has been categorized as a trusted digital service provider in Iraq, which includes the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Apple Arcade, and Apple Ads.

The certification means Apple’s digital services may now function under an official Iraqi regulatory framework, having passed the CMC’s technical and legal standards.

Iraqi officials said the decision is anticipated to boost the country’s digital economy and enhance the investment climate for multinational technology firms.

The development also corresponds with a significant step toward Apple’s physical presence in the Iraqi market. Asiacell has reached a direct arrangement with Apple to include iPhones in its retail network across Iraq.

As part of the cooperation, Asiacell will provide real Apple products with valid warranties throughout its network, while retail personnel will undergo Apple-approved training.

The regulatory permission and Asiacell deal represent a substantial change in Apple’s position in Iraq, pushing both digital services and official device distribution further into a market of over 46 million people.

The move is another indication of Iraq’s quickly emerging technology and consumer market, as Baghdad attempts to lure global corporations, legalize digital services, and promote increased investment in the country’s information technology industry.

World.title: Al-Ghodwa deploys Linde warehouse equipment in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Linde Material Handling of Germany has completed a new warehouse technology project in Baghdad with its official Iraqi partner, Al-Ghodwa Group, as modern logistics systems gain traction in Iraq.

The project was completed in early August, and it comprised the installation and commissioning of two Linde Very Narrow Aisle (VNA) trucks built for high-density warehouse operations.

As part of the turnkey project, Al-Ghodwa installed the guiding system, calibrated and tested the equipment, and taught the local operators.

The technology enables firms to store more items in their current warehouse space by running equipment securely in tighter lanes, which increases productivity and reduces space needs.

The project combines Linde’s German warehouse technology with local installation, maintenance, and after-sales services in Iraq.

Linde Material Handling is a subsidiary of Germany’s KION Group, one of the world’s biggest producers of industrial vehicles and a leading supplier of warehouse automation systems.

The Baghdad installation comes as Iraq’s logistics and distribution industry grows, amid investment in manufacturing, retail, transportation, and private-sector growth.

World.title: Saudi renews invitation to Iraq PM as Baghdad, Riyadh seek to repair ties
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Saudi Arabia has extended an invitation to Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi to visit Riyadh as the two countries try to regain momentum in ties after a dangerous escalation involving Iran-backed militias operating from Iraqi soil.

Al-Zaidi met with Saudi intelligence head Khalid bin Ali Al-Humaidan in Baghdad on Friday, with the Saudi official conveying a message from the kingdom’s leadership extending the offer and discussing greater security cooperation, according to the Iraqi government.

The meeting is notable since Al-Zaidi canceled a scheduled visit to Saudi Arabia last month in response to US-Saudi airstrikes on Iran-aligned armed groups in Iraq.

These operations followed a series of drone assaults on Saudi Arabia.

Riyadh claimed that Iran-backed militias fired drones from Iraqi territory, attempting to damage oil installations in the Eastern Province and targets near Riyadh, and publicly urged Baghdad to prevent its land from being used as a launchpad for assaults against the country.

Saudi Arabia then launched operations with US troops against Iran-backed militia strongholds in Iraq, increasing pressure on Baghdad to bring armed organizations operating outside of effective official control under its authority.

During Friday’s meeting, Al-Zaidi underlined Iraq’s refusal to allow its land to be used for attacks on Saudi Arabia or any other country, emphasizing Baghdad’s commitment to sovereignty, good neighbor relations, and regional security.

According to the Iraqi statement, the two sides agreed to maintain information sharing and security cooperation, with Baghdad aiming to avoid future assaults that may prompt another military reaction on Iraqi soil.

The outreach coincides with Saudi Arabia’s efforts to deepen regional security relationships.

On Friday, Riyadh, Ankara, and Islamabad signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which states that any military assault on one of the three nations is considered an attack on all.

Saudi authorities are also apprehensive about additional strikes by Iran-aligned forces.

For Al-Zaidi, the repeated Saudi invitation provides a chance to mend ties with one of Iraq’s most significant Arab neighbors while also displaying Baghdad’s determination to prevent Iran-backed forces from dictating its regional connections.

The implications extend beyond security. Iraq has been pursuing more Saudi and Gulf investment as part of a larger push to diversify its economy, attract foreign money, and enhance trade and infrastructural ties with its Arab neighbors.

As a result, Friday’s meeting constitutes a crucial step in moving Baghdad-Riyadh relations past last month’s dispute. However, continued progress is likely to be strongly dependent on Iraq’s capacity to show that attacks on its neighbors would not be launched from its territory in the future.

World.title: Spain imposes border checks on Italy as migrant showdown grows
World.content:
Madrid – Spain announced on Friday it would introduce temporary border checks on travellers from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass migrant rush into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until September 7, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the European Union and NATO allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s North African territory on July 30-31 in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy which imposed a one-month suspension of its visa free-travel Schengen deal with Spain.

The Spanish government slammed the measure Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity.”

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” the government said.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

– ‘Creating rifts’ –

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before August 15, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

“Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control,” Meloni’s office said in a statement.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered,” it read.

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from the Iberian country.

The move announced on July 31 was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups however estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH) and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta — including hundreds of unaccompanied children — face dire living conditions with little access to food, water, and shelter.

World.title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan sign defence pact amid regional war
World.content:
Riyadh – Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a joint defence agreement on Friday amid violence in the region from Houthi attacks and the US-Iran war.

Riyadh is looking to strengthen its security ties against the backdrop of war between the United States and Iran, which has drawn in surrounding nations and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

The war has emboldened Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, both of which have attacked Saudi Arabia, while analysts say Washington is now seen as an increasingly unreliable partner.

In a joint statement published by the official Saudi press agency and Pakistan’s foreign ministry, the three countries announced the signing of the “Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”.

They declared a “shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security and stability in the region and beyond”.

Pakistan’s foreign ministry said the pact meant an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all, adding it was “intended to strengthen collective deterrence”.

Ankara nonetheless said later that the agreement was “not aimed at any particular country”, according to a post on X by the presidency’s communications director.

It added that “the agreement is not in contradiction with the commitments of Turkey’s existing international alliances, including those at the heart of NATO,” according to a post on X by the government’s anti-disinformation service.

Riyadh said “the agreement does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc”.

“Nor is it linked to any nuclear ambitions or arms race, rather it is focused on building sustainable capabilities,” Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said on X.

The “does not constitute a threat to the security of any country in the region”, he added.

– ‘Layers of security’ –

Since the onset of the regional war, Saudi Arabia has grown closer to Turkey, Egypt and Pakistan, which have been pushing for mediation and a resolution to the conflict.

Umar Karim, an expert on Saudi foreign policy at the University of Birmingham, England, said the alignment “is clearly oriented towards Iran and meant to address Iran’s new strategic approach which is geared towards dominance of the broader Gulf region”.

The fact that Turkey and Pakistan border Iran means they could “exercise a different kind of leverage” on Tehran, he added.

A source close to the Saudi military and government told AFP before the signing that although the agreement had been under discussion for a long time, “the latest developments in the region expedite it”.

Andreas Krieg of King’s College London said the deal showed a clear desire to diversify alliances beyond the United States.

“Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan are not trying to replace the United States,” he said.

“They are building the capacity to protect their interests when Washington cannot or will not do so.”

Riyadh, in particular, he added, “wants several layers of security rather than one American umbrella”, after the shock of the Iran war.

The deal will support Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to become an organiser of regional security and diversify its defence umbrella, said Krieg. Turkey and Pakistan gain political clout and access to potential Saudi investments, he added.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Mecca on Friday, the Turkish presidency said on X, sharing an image of the meeting.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir also travelled to the Gulf kingdom for the signing.

– Renewed Houthi attacks –

Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already announced a mutual defence pact in 2025, a move that drew attention because Pakistan is the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state.

The deal also comes as a truce between Riyadh and the Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen has broken down. The Houthis have launched attacks on Saudi soil and declared a maritime blockade against Saudi Arabia, which they have attempted to enforce by attacking Saudi tankers.

The Houthis, backed by Iran, have added pressure to Gulf energy exporters — already under strain from Tehran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz — by threatening Red Sea shipping.

Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis since 2015.

A truce was agreed four years ago which largely held until hostilities broke out again in recent weeks.

On Thursday, the Houthis killed at least 58 Yemeni government troops in missile and drone attacks, a military source said, in one of the conflict’s deadliest days in years.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate continues to rise in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar compared to the Iraqi dinar rose on Thursday in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, and the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Erbil.

The US dollar exchange rate slightly rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,523.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,520.5 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,530 Iraqi dinars and 1,520 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also rose, fluctuating between 1,525.5 and 1,525 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq to increase production from Kirkuk oil fields
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair announced on Thursday plans to increase oil production from the Kirkuk oilfields.

The decision intends to capitalize on a recent agreement with Turkey for exporting oil to the port of Ceyhan.

This move also aims to circumvent the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and increase Iraq’s oil exports via ports on the Mediterranean.

The instruction utilizes the recently expanded Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline deal, with the goal of increasing exports from 180,000 barrels per day to approximately 750,000 barrels per day.

Khudair stated that increasing production lays the groundwork for boosting export volumes through Turkey to 1.5 million barrels per day.

Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) has officially partnered with British Petroleum (BP) to bolster cooperation in oil and natural gas projects in Kirkuk oilfields.

In 2025, BP reached a deal with Iraq’s North Oil Company (NOC) to develop oil fields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk, with investments projected to reach $25 billion.

The step is part of the Iraqi government’s attempts to optimize energy sector investments, increase oil output, and minimize gas flaring.

The enhanced output directly addresses the Iraqi government’s growing deficit as a result of continued maritime restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

By producing more petroleum from Kirkuk, Baghdad reduces internal shipping expenses from southern fields while increasing supplies to global markets via outlets on the Mediterranean.

World.title: 'Changing colours like a chameleon': Mayawati hits Akhilesh over 'Pandit' twist in SP's PDA formula

World.title: 'Keep your curiosity alive': PM Modi addresses IIT Delhi graduates; highlights rapid tech shift
World.content:
PM Modi told students to always remember their mentors

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday addressed IIT Delhi's 57th Convocation Ceremony, urging graduating students to embrace change, keep learning and remember the mentors who shaped their journey.Addressing more than 3,000 graduating students, including 587 PhD scholars, as the chief guest, PM Modi congratulated them on completing their studies and asked them to embrace the next phase of their lives. "From orientation to convocation, you must be satisfied with your journey, but also excited about the start of a new chapter," Modi said.He asked students to "live this moment to the fullest", noting that many were preparing to start their first jobs, move to new cities, launch startups or appear for competitive examinations.The Prime Minister also urged them not to forget their time at IIT Delhi or the people who supported them. "Carry them as an asset; don't forget them. Before you leave, make sure to meet every member here," he said.Speaking about the rapidly changing world and technology, the Prime Minister asked students to keep their curiosity and learning instinct alive."Today, the world is changing rapidly. Nobody can say what will happen 20-30 years from now.Keep your curiosity alive in life... Keep your learning instinct alive. Those who learn, win," he said.He said people who remain open to new situations and challenges can turn difficulties into opportunities. "Challenges become chances for those with courage to find new solutions," Modi said, adding that this was among the things students had learned at IIT Delhi."The global power balance is changing every moment and the biggest force behind it is the speed of technology," he said.The PM also spoke about India's push for self-reliance and the emergence of new sectors for the country's youth. Referring to the semiconductor sector, he said India had begun production at its first semiconductor unit. "I firmly believe that from chips to ships, everything will be made here by your hands," he added.The Prime Minister also presented IIT Delhi's top honours, including the President's Gold Medal, Director's Gold Medal, Shankar Dayal Sharma Gold Medal and Perfect Ten Gold Medals, to meritorious students.He said he was proud of the graduating students but that there should have been "more" girls among them. "Just as your families are feeling proud today, I, too, am proud of all of you," he added.Union Education Minister Prahlad Joshi, who was also present at the ceremony, said PM Modi's vision had made India's education ecosystem "learner-centric, research-driven, and future-ready".Earlier, the Prime Minister inaugurated Param Pragya, an AI-powered high-performance supercomputing facility at IIT Delhi's Sonipat campus. According to the PMO, the facility will strengthen the institute's capabilities in AI, data science, advanced computing and interdisciplinary research.

World.title: ‘Honey-trapped’ IAF officer held for allegedly sharing classified defence data
World.content:
The arrest followed specific inputs shared by the IAF intelligence wing with the Delhi Police

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: An Indian Air Force (IAF) Wing Commander has been arrested for allegedly leaking sensitive defence information after being honey-trapped through social media by Pakistani intelligence operatives, officials said.According to an ANI report, the officer was under surveillance by the IAF intelligence wing before he was arrested and handed over to law enforcement agencies. Delhi Police sources said he is currently in judicial custody and has been booked under provisions of the Official Secrets Act for allegedly sharing classified information and confidential defence-related documents.IAF officials said, "He was under active surveillance and was handed over to the suitable law enforcement agencies. Due to proactive measures, he was caught. The IAF has zero tolerance for such activities."Sources said the officer allegedly fell victim to a honey trap operated by Pakistani intelligence personnel through social media. He is also accused of installing data-stealing software on a colleague's mobile phone in an alleged attempt to gain access to the device.The arrest followed specific inputs shared by the IAF intelligence wing with the Delhi Police, sources said.Further investigation into the case is underway.The incident comes amid continued concerns over attempts by Pakistani intelligence operatives to target Indian personnel and civilians through social media-based honey traps.Last year, Rajasthan Police arrested an Alwar resident, identified as Mangat Singh, for allegedly spying for Pakistan's intelligence agency ISI. Police said a surveillance operation had been launched in the state following Operation Sindoor, during which Singh's activities in the cantonment area of Alwar were found to be suspicious.According to police, Singh had allegedly been honey-trapped by a female Pakistani handler using the pseudonym Isha Sharma. The handler reportedly offered him money in exchange for cooperation. Police said Singh had remained in contact with Pakistani handlers through social media platforms for around two years.

World.title: Sick teen dies as ambulance gets stuck in mud for hours in J&K's Rajouri
World.content:
J-K's Rajouri landslide

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A 17-year-old girl died while being taken to hospital in Jammu and Kashmir's Rajouri district after the vehicle carrying her remained stuck in mud for nearly three hours. The district administration has suspended a government engineer and ordered an inquiry into the incident.The girl, a resident of remote Methyani village, had fallen seriously ill on Friday and was being taken to Government Medical College (GMC), Rajouri, when the vehicle became stranded following a mudslide at Chak Methyani, officials told news agency PTI.Volunteers later managed to pull the vehicle out, but the girl's condition deteriorated and she died while she was being taken to the hospital, according to officials.The incident occurred on the Chak Methyani-Panglar-Kotecharwal road, which serves as the only road link for several remote villages in the area. The road was washed away near Methyani during last year's monsoon and had subsequently been restored temporarily.The same stretch was hit by another mudslide around two weeks ago, leaving the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) road unmotorable, officials said.According to the report submitted by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (ADC), Kotranka, the girl had been suffering from an illness for nearly a month and had previously been admitted to Government Medical College Hospital, Jammu. She was discharged around two weeks ago, but her condition worsened again, prompting her family to take her to GMC Rajouri.The ADC's report said the blocked road resulted in a delay of nearly two to three hours. It also found that the stretch remained in "extremely poor condition" due to landslides and deep ditches, making it unfit for vehicular movement.The report further noted that residents of Narla Bamble, Kotecharwal and Panglar continued to face difficulties in transporting patients, food grains and fertilisers.The district administration said the executive engineer, PMGSY division Rajouri, had informed officials through an official WhatsApp group that the road had been restored and was "trafficable". However, subsequent verification by the ADC found otherwise.Taking note of the report, district development commissioner (DDC) Rajouri Abhishek Sharma ordered the immediate suspension of the assistant executive engineer (AEE), PMGSY Sub-Division Kalakote, who was in charge of the road project, pending an inquiry.The DDC said the failure to restore the road despite repeated directions indicated "prima facie negligence and non-compliance with official instructions".The executive engineer has also been asked to explain why disciplinary proceedings should not be initiated against him for allegedly misreporting the road's status and failing to ensure its timely restoration. His salary has been withheld pending consideration of his explanation.The additional district development commissioner (ADDC), Rajouri, has been directed to conduct a detailed inquiry and submit a comprehensive report within seven days.

World.title: Centre seeks Meta's action on deepfakes, awaits legal opinion on further steps
World.content:
Centre has asked Meta to take action against deepfake content, while it examines whether the social media giant is complying with intermediary provisions under Indian law, sources told PTI.

A legal opinion on further action is expected after the government reviews the outcome of its meetings with the company.

Centre is likely to seek responses from other social media platforms as it examines whether they meet the definition of intermediaries under the country's law, sources said.

Sources also said that if Meta and other social media platforms exercise control over what content is shown to users, their role could be viewed as akin to 'publishing', making them responsible for the content and actions on their platforms.

The development comes a day after the government held technical discussions with the social media giant, during which Meta outlined its plans to address the Centreâs concerns over deepfakes, child sexual abuse material and unlabelled synthetically generated content on its platforms, sources said.

The technical discussions followed two days of meetings in which IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw questioned Metaâs team, led by global affairs head Joel Kaplan, over its content recommendation algorithms and compliance with Indian laws.





During the third round of talks, Meta explained how its systems operate and presented proposed measures to tackle the concerns raised by the government. The company said it had solutions to address deepfakes, CSAM and bot accounts, and explained how the measures could be deployed on its platforms, the sources said.

Sources had earlier said Meta acknowledged that there were "serious issues" and assured the government that it would take continuous steps to address them.

The government, meanwhile, will continue to push the company to undertake sustained measures and improvements to address its concerns, they added.

Metaâs global team met IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and IT Secretary S Krishnan on both days after the government summoned the company over the temporary restriction of Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs Facebook post.

During Thursdayâs meeting, the Meta team was questioned on its compliance with Indian laws, content recommendation algorithms and the safeguards in place to ensure that constitutional and legal requirements are met.

The social media giant assured the government that it was taking the concerns seriously and was "working hard" to address issues related to deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, bot accounts and synthetic content.

On Wednesday, Meta apologised for the temporary removal of PM Modiâs post and acknowledged failures related to child sexual abuse content and deepfakes, as well as the promotion of certain content after being paid "a lot of money".

World.title: When ‘healthy’ is just a label
World.content:
âNaturalâ, âhealthyâ, âorganicâ, âheart-friendlyâ, âhigh proteinâ and âzero maidaâ often persuades a shopper before the packet is even turned over. In a spate of notices sent in the past month, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (

) has asked several brands whether their front-of-pack promises say more than the product can support.

FSSAI has issued notices to food businesses across categories including breads, chocolates, juices, cooking oils, noodles, supplements, packaged water and caffeinated drinks. The claims questioned range from â100% naturalâ and âorganicâ to immunity, detoxification, disease reduction and energy-boosting promises. Since these are notices rather than final rulings, the issues remain subject to the companiesâ replies and regulatory examination.

TOI reached out to FSSAI over e-mail, but was yet to receive a response.

The scrutiny comes as Indiaâs health-and-wellness food market expands and brands compete for shoppers seeking healthier choices. Experts say the front of a packet increasingly functions as advertising, while the information needed to judge the product â ingredients, sugar, fat, sodium and additives â is usually on the back.

Former FSSAI CEO Pawan Kumar Agarwal says consumers rarely read or fully understand the mandatory information panel.





Marketing teams therefore have a powerful incentive to foreground attractive words, sometimes stretching the meaning permitted by regulation. For large companies, he argues, penalties may need to be linked to turnover or the commercial gain from a misleading claim rather than treated as a routine cost.

Nutrition experts call this the âhealth haloâ effect: one positive phrase can make the entire product appear healthier and reduce the buyerâs inclination to examine it critically.

A packet labelled ânaturalâ can still be high in sugar or sodium. âSugar-freeâ does not automatically mean low-carbohydrate. âOrganicâ requires certification; it is not merely a lifestyle description. Disease-treatment or prevention claims require scientific and regulatory support.

AIIMS dietician Monita Gahlot advises shoppers to start with the ingredient list, which records ingredients in descending order by weight.

The nutrition panel should then be checked for total and added sugars, saturated and trans fats, sodium, protein and carbohydrates. Serving sizes deserve particular attention: a modest-looking number can be based on a portion far smaller than what people normally consume.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The clearest warning sign, food-testing expert Ashwin Bhadri says, is a bold front claim that is not supported or adequately explained elsewhere on the label.

The simplest consumer rule is therefore to turn the packet over before deciding.

Food author Krish Ashok argues that companies are not acting in a vacuum. Consumers increasingly seek a purchasable shortcut to good health. Products labelled âhigh proteinâ, âlow GIâ, âA2â or âheart-healthyâ can offer the feeling of making a healthy choice without the slower work of eating fewer ultra-processed foods, increasing fibre and protein, exercising and sleeping well.

That is why tighter enforcement alone will not end the health halo. Brands must make precise, evidence-backed claims, but consumers must also stop treating the front of a packet as nutritional advice.

World.title: QR code, no queue: 25 crore OPD registrations go digital
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The long wait at hospital registration counters is slowly giving way to a QR code. In a sign of India's growing digital health footprint, patients have now completed 25 crore outpatient (OPD) registrations through the ABHA-based 'Scan and Register' service under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), with nearly four lakh people using the facility every day.

Introduced in October 2022, the service allows patients to register for an OPD consultation by simply scanning a QR code displayed at participating hospitals through an ABDM-enabled health app. Once they give consent, their ABHA-linked details are shared with the hospital, eliminating paperwork and reducing waiting time at registration counters.

The service is now available in 30,800 hospitals and healthcare facilities across 36 states and Union Territories and 756 districts, making it one of the country's fastest-growing digital public health services.

More than 24,000 government facilities and 6,400 private hospitals have adopted the system.

The biggest users of the platform are in Bihar, which has recorded over 7.3 crore digital OPD registrations, followed by Uttar Pradesh (4.09 crore), Andhra Pradesh (3.38 crore) and Jammu & Kashmir (1.39 crore).

Among hospitals, AIIMS New Delhi has emerged as the country's busiest digital registration centre, recording over 54.29 lakh Scan and Register transactions.





It is followed by AIIMS Bhopal (29.1 lakh), AIIMS Bhubaneswar (23.93 lakh), AIIMS Patna (19.62 lakh) and AIIMS Raipur (18.63 lakh).

Officials said the service has particularly eased hospital visits for senior citizens, pregnant women and patients requiring frequent follow-ups by cutting time spent at registration counters and doing away with repeated form filling.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

"This milestone reflects the growing trust that citizens and healthcare providers have placed in India's digital health ecosystem.

By simplifying one of the most common touchpoints in healthcare, OPD registration, the service has enhanced patient convenience while improving efficiency for hospitals," National Health Authority CEO Dr Sunil Kumar Barnwal said.

The National Health Authority said the service is now operational across AIIMS, central and state government hospitals, medical colleges, district hospitals, ESIC and railway hospitals, as well as private healthcare facilities, and is expected to expand further as more hospitals adopt ABHA-enabled digital services.

World.title: Akal Takht panel asks Punjab govt to address objections before anti-sacrilege talks
World.content:
Akal Takht panel flags Punjab govt response, seeks compliance report on anti-sacrilege law

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The expert panel appointed by the Akal Takht on Friday asked the Punjab government to first submit a compliance report on the objections raised by the Sikh temporal seat before any further talks on the proposed anti-sacrilege law.The panel, formed to discuss the Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act, 2026 with the state government, held its first meeting on Thursday.The panel said the Punjab government's July 29 response did not address the main concerns raised by the Akal Takht, especially those related to possible interference in Sikh religious matters.On June 29, Akal Takht Jathedar Giani Kuldip Singh Gargajj had given the state government one month to respond to his objections to the anti-sacrilege law.In a statement on Friday, the Akal Takht secretariat said the government's response, submitted just before the deadline, was an attempt to avoid the main issues. It said the concerns of the Sikh community had already been conveyed to the Punjab assembly Speaker and members of the state Cabinet on July 31.The secretariat also accused the Bhagwant Mann-led government of not taking a constructive approach towards resolving the sensitive issue.It said that despite being given enough time, the Punjab government had not formed its own panel to discuss the matter.Earlier, Jathedar Gargajj had rejected the government's response as "unsatisfactory" and announced a five-member expert panel to hold discussions with the Aam Aadmi Party government.The panel includes retired judges Rupinder Singh Sodhi and Mohinder Mohan Singh Bedi, senior advocate Puran Singh Hundal, and Sikh scholars Dr Kehar Singh and Prof Jagmohan Singh.The Jathedar had also written to Punjab assembly Speaker Kultar Singh, Sikh MLAs and state ministers, asking them not to discuss or amend the anti-sacrilege law without a wider "Panthic" consensus.He had directed Sikh MLAs and Cabinet ministers to ensure that no discussion on the law takes place during the assembly session that began on August 3 until an agreement is reached with the Akal Takht and the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC).The issue came up after AAP MLA Inderbir Singh Nijjar submitted the Punjab government's response to the objections raised by the Akal Takht over the proposed anti-sacrilege legislation.

World.title: e-KYC updation: Special camps to be held at all ration shops in Virudhunagar district
World.content:
Updation of e-KYC for all the members of the family in the ration card can be done at the ration shops on August 2.

The updation can be done through the ‘point of sale’ machine by using finger prints or iris.

All ration shops in Virudhunagar would take up special camps, Virudhunagar Collector N.O. Sukhaputra said in a statement.

He said that all the members whose names were mentioned in the family cards should take up e-KYC updation.

Those family members who live out-station can visit their nearest ration shop for updating e-KYC, the statement said.

World.title: Tender for waste-to-energy plant at Coimbatore’s Vellalore dump yard postponed after residents’ representation
World.content:
The tender process for the proposed 1,200-tonnes-per-day (TPD) waste-to-energy (WtE) plant at the Vellalore dump yard, intended to process municipal solid waste from Coimbatore and Tiruppur, has been postponed by a month.

The tenders, which were scheduled to be opened on July 31, were deferred following a representation submitted to Tamil Nadu Prohibition and Excise Minister K. Vignesh by the Kurichi–Vellalore Pollution Prevention Joint Action Committee, and Poovulagin Nanbargal.

The representation sought withdrawal of the proposed WtE project, permanent closure of the Vellalore dump yard, scientific removal of legacy waste through biomining and implementation of decentralised solid waste management in line with the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026. It contended that residents had been affected for years by air pollution, foul odour and groundwater contamination caused by the dump yard.

“We requested the Minister to withdraw the proposed Waste-to-Energy project and stop the tender process. After hearing our concerns, he assured us that the tender scheduled to be opened on July 31 would be postponed by a month and that he would consult the concerned officials before taking a decision,” said K.S. Mohan, secretary of the Kurichi–Vellalore Pollution Prevention Joint Action Committee.

“We welcome the assurance and hope the government will review the proposal in line with the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, and adopt decentralised waste management instead of a waste-to-energy plant,” he added.

World.title: Police constable booked on charges of harassing a woman and setting fire to her car near Tiruchi
World.content:
The Kollidam police have registered a case against a police constable for allegedly harassing a woman and setting fire to her car at Sankara Nagar in Kollidam Tollgate area on the outskirts of Tiruchi city recently. The case was booked on a complaint preferred by the 41-year-old woman resident of Sankara Nagar.

The police said the woman lodged a complaint on July 29 suspecting the involvement of the police constable P. Sathiyaraj, 42, attached to the Kollidam police station, in setting fire to her car that was parked in front of her house.

The woman had alleged that the constable knew her as she was an LIC agent and harassed, intimidated, and abused her after she rejected his sexual advances and did not answer his phone calls. She suspected that he was behind the incident and lodged a complaint.

The woman had parked her car and left for Thanjavur a few days ago leaving her son at home. During her absence, a person wearing a helmet broke open the car door and set it on fire and fled the spot. The fire spread to another car parked adjacent to it.

The incident was captured on nearby CCTV cameras. The firefighters doused the flames. Sources said the constable had not been arrested and investigation was on.

World.title: Erode district bags Elite World Records recognition for mass reading event
World.content:
The Erode district administration has been recognised by Elite World Records for organising the largest simultaneous book-reading event across multiple venues as part of the 22nd Erode Book Festival.

Elite World Records adjudicator A. Sangeetha presented the world record certificate to District Collector S. Kandasamy at the Collectorate here on Friday (July 31).

The record attempt was organised by the district administration and Milky Mist Dairy Food Limited, in association with the School Education Department and Makkal Sinthanai Peravai, to promote reading habits. A total of 2,06,760 participants read books simultaneously at 519 locations across the district from 9.30 a.m. to 9.52 a.m. School and college students, along with government officials, participated in the event.

The organisers submitted documentary evidence from all the venues to Elite World Records, which verified the records before officially certifying the achievement under the category, “Maximum participants reading books simultaneously at multiple venues.” Earlier, a book-reading session was held at the Collectorate conference hall as part of the 22nd Erode Book Festival celebrations, with the District Collector participating in it.

Among those present were Corporation Commissioner Arpit Jain, Superintendent of Police D.V. Kiran Shruthi, District Revenue Officer S. Santhakumar, Chief Educational Officer E. Manvizhi, Personal Assistant (General) to the Collector V. Thenmozhi, Makkal Sinthanai Peravai president T. Stalin Gunasekaran, Milky Mist Dairy Food Limited Assistant General Manager (Human Resources) Sathyaraj, and senior officials from various government departments.

World.title: Police seize 292 kg of ganja headed for Sri Lanka, arrest three
World.content:
The Q Branch police seized 292 kg of ganja that was being taken for smuggling to Sri Lanka near Ramanathapuram and arrested three persons.

Based on a tip-off received by the Ramanathapuram Q Branch police, a team led by Q Branch Inspector Jeevamani Dharmaraj, along with head constables Rajendran, Senthilkumar, Raju, and Raja, was conducting surveillance early Friday morning.

At that time, near the Pudumadam bus stop close to Uchippuli, they intercepted a goods vehicle heading towards the coast. Upon inspecting it, they seized 292 kg of ganja contained in 146 parcels (2 kg in each of 8 sacks) along with vegetable sacks.

Following this, they arrested Thangaraj, 25, from Kottanatham village, Vilathikulam taluk in Thoothukudi district, who drove the vehicle; Sekar, 50, from Kumarasakkanapuram, Vilathikulam; and Senthilvelan, 50, from Melatheru, Perungulam in Ramanathapuram district.

During further inquiry, it was revealed that they had procured the ganja from a gang in Madurai and then loaded vegetables from the Paravai market.

It was also found that they had planned to smuggle the ganja to Sri Lanka from the Pudumadam coastal area through Senthilvelan.

The Q Branch police handed over the 292 kg of ganja and the three arrested persons to the Ramanathapuram Anti-Narcotics Intelligence Unit.

World.title: Kin stage road blockade at Poomparai after murder of SC youth
World.content:
A 25-year-old man from Arunthathiyar community was allegedly hacked to death with a sword by a caste Hindu man in Poomparai village in upper Kodaikanal hills in Dindigul district on Thursday night. A 16-year-old boy, who was with the victim, was also injured in the attack and he has been admitted to Kodaikanal Government Hospital for treatment.

Police said Ramar, 25, was cultivating crops in a small piece of land and rearing a horse. A year ago, his horse reportedly destroyed the crop cultivated by Ragu, 23, of Prabakaran Street. Ragu scolded Ramar over this.

On Thursday evening, Ragu came to Ramar’s house and urged him to take away his horse which was grazing in his field.

When Ramar went there with two friends, Ragu allegedly pulled out a sword and attacked Ramar, inflicting multiple injuries on him. With severe blood loss, Ramar was rushed to the Primary Health Centre in Poomparai, where the doctor declared him brought dead.

As the news spread, villagers gathered in large numbers and squatted on the ghat section road on Friday morning. Traffic on the road was paralysed for a few hours, and officials held talks with the protesters, but to no avail.

Meanwhile, some relatives of Ramar and local youth set Ragu’s two-wheeler on fire, prompting the police to post pickets in the area.

The protesters demanded immediate arrest of the accused, a government job to one of the family members of the victim, and due compensation to the family.

Dindigul Superintendent of Police Jeyakumar, Revenue Divisional Officer Keerthana and others assured the protesters of proper action, following which they allowed Ramar’s body to be taken for a post-mortem at Government Dindigul Medical College and Hospital.

A case had been registered and the prime accused held, a senior officer said. Further investigation is on.

World.title: One dead, two missing as fishing boat capsizes off Neendakara
World.content:
A fishing expedition turned tragic after a boat capsized in rough seas, leaving one person dead and two others missing. The victims belong to the same family and the search for missing persons is on. The deceased has been identified as 76-year-old Rajeevan, a fisher and the boat’s owner residing at Puthanthura. Search operations are currently underway to locate his relatives, Radhakrishnan, 47, and Gautam Krishna, 26.

​The accident occurred on Friday morning near the Neendakara groyne (pulimuttu). The fishing vessel named ‘Meomi’, carrying 14 crew members, was hit by violent waves and overturned. Nearby fishers immediately rushed to the scene to initiate rescue efforts. Upon receiving information, teams from the Coast Guard, the Fisheries department, Marine Enforcement, and the Fire Force arrived to carry out a coordinated search operation. Rajeevan was pulled from the water in critical condition and rushed to a nearby hospital, but his life could not be saved.

​Eleven other crew members, including five migrant workers, were successfully rescued from the capsized vessel. Preliminary investigations suggest that turbulent sea conditions and strong crashing waves caused the boat to flip. ​This incident marks the second major fishing boat accident in the region within three days. On Wednesday morning, another vessel met with an accident near the Tangasseri breakwater, claiming the life of a fisherman named Royson, whose body was recovered the following night.

World.title: Differences in Kerala’s ruling front over PM SHRI out in the open
World.content:
The differences in the United Democratic Front (UDF) over the PM SHRI (Prime Minister’s Schools for Rising India) scheme are coming out in the open.

A day after UDF convener Adoor Prakash said at a press meet following a UDF State coordination committee meeting that the government would continue with the scheme, Minister for Industries P.K. Kunhalikutty denied any discussions on PM SHRI at the meet. At the same time, he denied reports of any differences in the UDF, of which his Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) is a constituent, over PM SHRI.

Addressing mediapersons on Friday, the Minister said reports that the Congress and the IUML expressed different opinions during discussions on PM SHRI in the UDF were incorrect.

Once the Cabinet subcommittee constituted to study the scheme submitted its report, the government would announce a final decision.

The subcommittee would recommend how to get out of an agreement signed by the previous Left Democratic Front government or if there were any ways to go ahead without accepting the conditions of the Union government. “Their conditions related to curriculum or school selection will not be implemented in Kerala. There should be no doubts on this. If such a situation arises, we will take a decision then,” Mr. Kunhalikutty said. The IUML had earlier strongly opposed the PM SHRI scheme.

A volte-face

Put on a spot over Mr. Kunhalikutty’s statements, Mr. Prakash did a volte-face and denied that the PM SHRI issue had been discussed in the UDF. “Only if there were a discussion would a dispute arise.” Denying he had said the government would go ahead with the scheme, Mr. Prakash said the UDF had taken no such decision. A final decision would be taken on the basis of the report of the subcommittee, he said.

Meanwhile, former Minister for General Education V. Sivankutty accused Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan of stating falsehoods. “The Chief Minister is now saying the opposite of what he said as the Leader of the Opposition,” Mr. Sivankutty said.

‘Clear reasons’

He pointed out that no government or aided school in Kerala had been selected for the scheme and that the funds received were Right to Education (RTE) entitlements through the Samagra Shiksha Kerala.

He said there were clear reasons why the PM SHRI scheme should not be implemented. For one, only seven months remained for the scheme period to conclude. School selection and other technical processes related to sanctioning of funds would also take time. This would likely leave only three months for the PM SHRI scheme, since its duration ended in March 2027.

Meanwhile, a clutch of educational and cultural activists have demanded that the UDF government withdraw from the scheme. In reply to a query from Abdul Wahab, MP, the Union government had stated that States could withdraw from the scheme. This should be taken at face value. Why was the government getting ready to spend 40% and implement a scheme that would end in March 2027, they asked. After the project ends, the schools would have to be taken over by the States concerned, resulting in full financial burden.
