The Pentagon is investing more than half a billion dollars to expand an Australian critical mineral project poised to become the world's first scandium mine, US President Donald Trump has announced.

The $US400 million ($560m) loan to Sunrise Energy Metals' Syerston scandium project in central west NSW is expected to shore up America's supply of the "increasingly critical mineral" used in aerospace, defence and automotive sectors.

Scandium is already used widely for defence, aerospace and energy applications, but nearly all supply comes from China, Russia and Ukraine. The US has not mined scandium since 1969.

The Pentagon's Office of Strategic Capital (OSC) said while there was currently no primary mine-source scandium supply globally, it was harvested through by-products of other industrial or resource extraction processes.

Donald Trump's announcement was part of a slew of investments in critical minerals and battery projects. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

It said "foreign competitors" accounted for about 80 per cent of the world's mining production and nearly all scandium processing.

The OSC said the mine's production would "support warfighting capabilities" as well as "strategically important economic sectors" including data centres, semiconductors and automotives.

Under the proposed financing, the US Department of War would receive a right of first offer on the mine's output.

Sunrise Energy Metals said its project near Fifield, about 350 kilometres west north-west of Sydney, aimed to deliver "the world's first primary source of mine-able, high-grade scandium".

It is set to have an initial capacity of 60 tonnes a year of scandium oxide, starting production in the first half of 2028.

In February, the company's chief executive Sam Riggall said the project, backed by mining billionaire Robert Friedland, was expected to contribute to a US critical minerals stockpile worth $US12 billion ($16.9b).

Last year, the company signed a five-year deal with US defence contractor Lockheed Martin granting it to buy up to 15 tonnes of scandium oxide from its Syerston project.

The deal came days after Mr Trump and Anthony Albanese inked a critical minerals pact during the prime minister's visit to Washington.

Albanese and Trump ink deal for 'dominance' of critical minerals Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have inked a deal for "critical mineral and energy dominance" in a new partnership that will tip billions into mining projects in the US and Australia.

Resources Minister Madeleine King welcomed the decision, calling it a "significant vote of confidence" in Australia's capacity to supply the US and its partners with the critical minerals they need.

"The Sunrise scandium project hosts the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource, which has a range of vital aerospace, defence and clean energy applications," she said.

"No one country alone can create secure, end-to-end supply chains in critical minerals and rare earths.

"In working together, Australian mining companies can create more jobs and investment opportunities here at home, and more jobs and investment in the United States."

Madeleine King says the Sunrise project has the world's largest and highest-grade known scandium resource. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

OSC's senior managing director Peter B Zuckerman said the conditional loan was a "decisive step toward creating a US-aligned scandium value chain, ensuring our warfighters and manufacturers no longer depend on adversaries".

Mr Trump announced the loan on Friday, local time, alongside a slew of other local investments in critical minerals and battery projects totalling $US3 billion ($4.2b).

Speaking at a State Department event in Washington involving more than 200 mining executives, educators and investors, Mr Trump said the US was reclaiming its place as "the minerals superpower of the world".

"Critical minerals are the raw materials of American strength that power everything from advanced weaponry to automobiles, and we want these essential products to be mined, refined and made right here in the USA," he said.

The US has burned through large numbers of precision-guided missiles and air-defence interceptors during its five-month-long war against Iran.

Defence officials and lawmakers have warned that replenishing some inventories could take years given existing production constraints, even as the Trump administration has disputed reports of significant shortages.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Rockliff adviser, ex-minister chosen as Liberal Senate replacements
World.content:
A senior adviser to Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff has been chosen to replace outgoing Liberal Senator Wendy Askew, while a former state minister will replace Senator Jonno Duniam when he finishes up at the end of the year.

Former party president Chris Gatenby will top the Liberals Senate ticket at the next federal election, with former minister Sarah Courtney coming in second and Latrobe councillor Jacki Martin third.

Brad Stansfield, a former chief of staff to Will Hodgman, missed out on a spot on the ticket.

Senators Askew and Duniam announced earlier this year they would not be seeking preselection.

Their resignations create casual vacancies, allowing the party to appoint new senators in their place, rather than go through a by-election.

The Senate spots were determined by about 60 Liberal Senate selectors at a meeting in Launceston today.

Long-term staffer gets his chance

Mr Gatenby is a senior adviser to Premier Jeremy Rockliff and has been involved with the Liberals for years, having previously served as party president.

He was raised on a farm in northern Tasmania, and then lived in Launceston.

He has had a broad career including senior roles in policy development, advocacy and government across Australia and the UK.

The father of two ran unsuccessfully in Bass during the last election.

"I think having two attempts at the state level gives you a great grounding at the door step, understanding what people's issues are, and I'm looking forward to getting in there and making a difference," Mr Gatenby said on Saturday.

Premier Rockliff said in July 2025, during the election campaign, Mr Gatenby "brings a wealth of experience to the table, in government, in small business, in policy advocacy and in the Liberal Party, including as our previous party president.

"Chris is the next generation of the party, putting his hand up to represent his community in parliament. He already volunteers in his community, including on the board of the Launceston Harvest Market," he said.

Sarah Courtney was Tasmania's first-ever female primary industries minister, in the government of Peter Gutwein. (ABC News: Scott Ross)

Sarah Courtney was elected to the Tasmanian parliament in 2014 and appointed to cabinet in 2018.

Ms Courtney, a moderate Liberal, was viewed as a talented minister with leadership potential.

She was Tasmania's first female primary industries minister, but stepped down after starting a relationship with her department secretary, who is now her husband.

She is a trained engineer and owns a boutique vineyard in the Tamar Valley.

Ms Courtney held the health portfolio throughout the COVID pandemic, and listed the guiding of voluntary assisted dying through the parliament as a key achievement.

In 2022, Ms Courtney quit Tasmanian politics after returning from a European holiday during which she caught COVID-19.

Ms Courtney, who was education minister, was forced to isolate in France just days out from school resuming in Tasmania.

When asked on Saturday if she had learnt from that time, Ms Courtney would not comment, instead telling reporters she had a wealth of experience.

"I have enjoyed being a minister, it gave me a thorough understanding of a range of portfolios and that's the experience I bring here today," she said.

"I've got experience as a minister plus I've worked in the real world across a range of industries and that coupled together means I'm good at finding solutions.

"I'm good at working with the community and small business to make sure the policies we have here in Tasmania — and that we're advocating for in Canberra — make a meaningful difference."

Not quite for Martin, Stansfield

Jacki Martin who came third in the vote, has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary adviser to Wendy Askew.

Jacki Martin has been a Latrobe councillor since 2022 and is currently a parliamentary advisor to Wendy Askew. (Facebook: Jacki Martin)

She nominated for preselection in June and said on her social media page that she would "bring energy, discipline and relentless determination" to the role.

Representing the north of the state, she has been outspoken recently on the closure of Boags Brewery in Launceston, the Liberty Bell Bay smelter and the sale of Tasmania's largest farm, Rushy Lagoon.

Ms Martin helped campaign for Education Minister Jo Palmer, Senator Claire Chandler and Health Minister Bridget Archer.

"Small business drives me, I'm the child of a small business owner … my family drives me, your family drives me, and I'll be working every day to see that this generation that's coming up underneath us isn't any worse off than what we have been," Ms Martin said.

Brad Stansfield was unsuccessful in his bid for a place high on the ticket.

Mr Stansfield was chief of staff to former Liberal premier Will Hodgman for eight years, and former Liberal senator Eric Abetz between 2007 and 2010.

Brad Stansfield has missed out on a spot. (Supplied: Font PR)

He also advised the Tasmanian Liberals through successful state election campaigns from 2014 to 2024.

Mr Stansfield was a partner in a public relations and lobbying firm before leaving to become the owner of a polling firm and co-owner in a stable of regional newspapers.

He also commentated on Tasmanian and federal politics on a podcast which he co-hosted.

Mr Stansfield has also spoken against the federal coalition doing preference deals with One Nation, and in February wrote that the "increased voter support for One Nation is a symptom of the federal coalition’s dysfunction for much of last year".

World.title: Perth man allegedly damaged 20 cars during 90-minute rampage
World.content:
A man has been charged after he allegedly went on a car-smashing spree before leading police on a wild chase through Perth's northern suburbs on Friday.

Police allege the 45-year-old began his 90-minute rampage at midday in a Toyota Camry, which was driven through several suburbs including Mount Lawley, Perth, Inglewood, East Perth, South Perth, Carine, Madeley and Duncraig.

It is alleged that after stopping and jumping out of his car, he then used a metal pole to strike at least 20 parked or stationary vehicles, causing significant damage.

Several people were inside their vehicles at the time but no injuries were reported.

Police received numerous reports from the public about the man's alleged behaviour. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

After receiving numerous reports of the destructive behaviour, police co-ordinated a cross-district response to locate the Toyota Camry, which was spotted, from the sky, in the northern suburbs.

The man allegedly failed to stop and led officers on a high-speed chase, during which he allegedly drove recklessly and on the wrong side of the road.

He was arrested when the vehicle finally came to a stop on Lilburne Road in Duncraig.

The man, from Gosnells, was due to face court on Saturday charged with a string of offences including criminal damage, being armed in a way that may cause fear, and reckless driving to escape pursuit.

World.title: Alleged torturers to seek bail as 15yo assessed for electronic monitoring
World.content:
A 15-year-old alleged torturer will be assessed for an electronic monitoring device in an attempt to apply for bail, while the court has heard several co-accused also intend to apply for bail, after a 17-year-old with an intellectual disability was found bashed, zip-tied and wrapped in plastic in bushland.

Seven co-accused faced Townsville Magistrates Court charged with a string of offences including torture after the teenager was found in bushland in Pallarenda on July 18.

The police prosecutor told the court several people were gathered at a house when two relatives of the victim made allegations about the victim, which led to the alleged assault.

The prosecutor said the group, which had moments before been socialising, allegedly kicked the victim and whipped him with a "horse whip" leaving him "crawling out onto the road".

Police allege the assault continued, with more alleged perpetrators arriving in a vehicle and allegedly continuing to strike the victim with a bat and a metal implement and stomping on him.

The victim was allegedly dumped in bushland near Pallarenda in Townsville. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Police allege the victim was then wrapped in industrial clear plastic with his legs zip-tied together, put in the boot of a vehicle before being dumped in bushland.

Police prosecutor Harriet Hearn told the court the victim needed surgery as he had sustained a broken nose, spinal fracture, fractured tibia, friction burns, and lacerations.

Days after prior offending

The court was told the accused 15-year-old allegedly committed the torture offence the day after receiving a warning from the court for other offending.

The victim required surgery after sustaining multiple injuries. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"This is some of the most serious types of offences we might see in this court … yet alone offences that have been committed by a juvenile," Ms Hearn said.

The 15-year-old's defence lawyer, Sarah Belford, said the case against her client was "circumstantial" and that he was party to the offences, not a participant.

Police allege his fingerprints were found on the industrial plastic wrap.

'Outrageous' allegations

Police charge 11 people after teen bashed, wrapped in plastic and ‘dumped’ Eleven people have been charged after a 17-year-old boy was bashed and dumped wrapped in plastic in bushland in Townsville.

Magistrate Steven Mosch said the 15-year-old had a "limited" but "recent" criminal history and that the "exceptionally serious" new charges were an "escalation".

"The allegations are outrageous," he said.

Magistrate Mosch said it could be 12 months before the matters were finalised before the court, but he needed assurance the 15-year-old would comply with bail conditions, if granted.

The matter was adjourned to August 13 for Youth Justice to carry out a suitability assessment for the use of an electronic monitoring device for the 15-year-old.

Meanwhile, police will check the suitability of the addresses submitted by three co-accused who intend to apply for bail. Their cases were adjourned to August 10.

The cases of another three co-accused were also adjourned until August 10.

World.title: ‘Philanthropy is not neutral’: Debate swirls at university over controversial $35m scholarship program
World.content:
NationalVictoriaUniversity ‘Philanthropy is not neutral’: Debate swirls at university over controversial $35m scholarship program Jackson Graham August 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

University of Melbourne academics have voted against a university-backed plan to use $35million from the controversial Liberal-linked Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation for student scholarships, leaving the money in limbo. The scholarships, which would fund 30 students a year to study humanities subjects, come at a time when the cost of many arts degrees has surged to more than $50,000. But the conservative Ramsay Centre’s promotion of “Western culture” has raised hackles among university staff. The university is still backing the scheme, but it is unclear what can come of the money without the support of the academic board, which has the power to vote on specifics of the scholarship such as the eligibility criteria but not the overall gift. Melbourne University has accepted funding from the Ramsay Centre but plans for it have divided the academic board. Luis Enrique Ascui



“The explicit promotion of ‘Western civilisation’ excludes and denigrates other cultures, whether intentionally or not,” said University of Melbourne history professor Zoe Laidlaw, who studies the link between philanthropy and colonialism and is one of the academics who voted against the proposal. She said if the university proceeded with the scholarship plan, “it will undermine its capacity to live up to its core values of anti-racism and truth-telling” as well as “its public commitment to addressing the harm caused by its colonial past”. “Philanthropy... is not neutral.” The vote does not mean the money is off the table. It cleared the university council’s gift procedures, and university leadership is still planning to allow students to be able to apply for the scholarships later this year.



A sub-committee of the academic board will now consider the proposal, which could result in a further vote of the full board. The board voted against the proposal despite receiving a four-page explanation of the checks and balances including that the scholarship selection panel would include only one Ramsay Centre representative and three university academics. The Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation, which is chaired by former university chancellor Allan Myers and includes former prime minister Tony Abbott on its board, has been controversial in the higher education sector over its ‘bachelor of Western civilisation’ courses at several other universities. The university has previously said it is deeply committed to anti-racism and truth-telling. “Nothing about this announcement changes or compromises that commitment,” it said in May. David Gonzalez, National Tertiary Education Union branch president, wants transparent consultation over a controversial scholarship program. Joe Armao



The scholarship proposal split the academic board 39-37, with several academics arguing the money was much-needed and recognised the valuable contribution of humanities at a time when the price of many arts degrees has increased to more than $50,000 due to the Job-ready Graduates scheme. Sara Wills, a pro vice-chancellor at the university who voted for the proposal, said there were rigorous processes surrounding the scholarship that meant it did not compromise academic freedom. She wants students to understand the complex and multicultural histories that have influenced their area of study, including in western history. “There will be people at the Ramsay Centre who have views that are different from us, and we should accept that we live in a world where there are views that are different from us we may not agree with,” she said. “Really good scholarship looks beyond simple polarities.



“How do we, with integrity, take this gift and do good with it? And that’s really been my intention; to say, at the end of the day, we did not see or think that it had undue influence.” Still, some university staff take issue with how the money has been accepted and believe academics should have a greater say in gifts to the university. Related Article Exclusive

University ‘It’s about influence’: Melbourne Uni row breaks out over scholarships from Ramsay Centre “The initial discussions about this partnership took place behind closed doors,” said National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) branch president at the university, David Gonzalez. “Programs that give external organisations privileged influence or access to our students deserve transparent consultation with the people who will ultimately be responsible for delivering them.”



A University of Melbourne spokesperson said the university had gratefully acknowledged the donation and the specific scholarship arrangements were now being progressed through the standard governance processes. The university plans for five annual intakes of 30 students, with five scholarships each year for under-represented groups. As well as the stipend, it offers attendance at an international summer school, an annual regional leadership program, and a community service and volunteering program. “All philanthropic donations proposed to the University of Melbourne undergo significant and rigorous assessment at the appropriate levels before proceeding,” the spokesperson said. “The university has received other gifts of similar scale previously, and these are managed in accordance with the appropriate processes.” The university says the separation of duties – with the university council and gift committee approving donations and the academic board approving the rules and conditions of the scholarship – is a common way to make sure financial and reputation risks, as well as academic standards, are “separately and robustly reviewed”.



However, Joo-Cheong Tham, Melbourne Law School professor and NTEU Victorian assistant secretary, said the academic board should have involvement in decisions over gifts, such as providing independent advice to the university council before the money is accepted. He said the current process gave the impression of a “fait accompli”. “The governance structures are not fit for purpose,” Tham said. A spokesperson for the Ramsay Centre declined to comment on the vote, saying the administration of the scholarship was a matter for the university. World.title: Liberal Andrew Hastie faces mounting pressure from One Nation as party ramps up national expansion
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Liberal Andrew Hastie faces mounting pressure from One Nation as party ramps up national expansion Brittany Busch August 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation has launched its campaign against Liberal leadership hopeful Andrew Hastie, just days after the opposition frontbencher acknowledged his own “political mortality” in the face of the resurgent minor party. The party’s Western Australian leader Rod Caddies and Luke Herdegen, the state candidate for the impending Secret Harbour byelection, opened the Canning branch on Saturday afternoon. Andrew Hastie has backflipped on his staunch opposition to One Nation. Alex Ellinghausen Meanwhile in Victoria, freshly endorsed state leader Warren Pickering has de-emphasised his previous endorsement of conspiracy theories as the Victorian arm of the party also expands and garners fresh scrutiny ahead of the November election. At the Canning branch launch, One Nation did not announce a candidate or policies, but has vowed to run a strong opponent against Hastie. Party leadership has attacked the Coalition frontbencher for giving evidence in Ben Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation action against this masthead and his role as a potential witness in the accused war criminal’s upcoming trial.



Caddies said One Nation polled well in the area and would campaign hard. Related Article One Nation Hastie signals he might lose, hopes One Nation will preference him “But it won’t be because it’s [Hastie’s] seat. It’ll be because I’m planning to help target every seat in this state and join my federal colleagues in supporting them in making sure that we win as many seats as possible,” he said ahead of the launch. “You would be a fool not to be worried with the polling that’s been done and the support we’re getting on the street. One Nation’s momentum is massive. Anyone that says they’re not worried, I guess you can take that for what it is. But if I was the member... I would be concerned that there will be a change of representation.” A seat-by-seat analysis conducted by Redbridge for The Australian Financial Review in May predicated Hastie would lose his seat in a populist surge. The Liberal frontbencher this week signalled for the first time he could lose, saying he hoped for One Nation’s preferences after previously vowing never to “bend the knee” to Pauline Hanson.



The previous One Nation candidate, Fernando Bove, won 11.4 per cent of first preferences at the 2025 federal election, with a 6.8 per cent swing. Related Article Political leadership Hastie gets security upgrades as One Nation campaigns against him One Nation is mobilising in the region ahead of the Secret Harbour byelection, where long-term Labor minister Paul Papalia has retired. WA Labor Premier Roger Cook has warned voting for One Nation would bring “the chaos of the eastern states to Western Australia”. One Nation’s rapid expansion, with a goal to run candidates in every electorate around the country, has opened up fresh scrutiny for the minor party.





“With respect to conspiratorial type conversations, if you go a bit more into the context of those rallies and things I’d said previously, you will find that… it was in the build-up to a federal election, and surrounding things like a lot of these quotas under the pretense of sustainability and net zero. So the Paris Agreement and UN Refugee Convention , which are drafted and administered by UN and WEF [World Economic Forum] organisations. So, look, it’s not conspiratorial, but it’s also not related to a state election,” he told News24. Asked to explain his opposition to 15-minute cities, he said Victoria was removing community consultation processes on high-rise developments “under the pretense of sustainability”. “That’s the best way to describe it in the short term,” he said. Pickering also said it was “inevitable” that One Nation would continue banning news organisations after the minor party barred The Age, ABC and The Guardian from a press conference on Monday where it was announcing a handful of candidates for the upcoming state election. “It was a good move because within 24 hours, all three of those publications had managed to push out a bit of a hit piece on myself,” he told News24, referring to reporting on his embrace of conspiracy theories. World.title: Andrew Dillon stands by AFL chairman Drummond amid Geelong scandal
World.content:
AFL chief Andrew Dillon has refused to be drawn on whether commission chairman Craig Drummond should immediately step aside from his position while investigations into Geelong’s secret concussion waiver scandal are being conducted. Drummond, the Geelong president when the matter was dealt with by the club, has removed himself from league deliberations, apologising and conceding the Cats “went too far” in not seeking league approval before allowing premiership player Jake Kolodjashnij to sign a waiver that had him assuming responsibility for future on-field head injuries. AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui Amid the fallout from the scandal after Kolodjashnij identified himself on Friday as the player involved, Dillon has not ruled out calling in an independent party to lead the investigation. Pressure is mounting on the AFL to mete out heavy penalties. The league issued Carlton a $75,000 fine for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode during a game earlier this year, and also docked former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley $20,000 for taunting Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan with an aeroplane gesture in 2024.



“It is an issue at the moment that is at the AFL executive level,” Dillon said on 3AW on Saturday. “If it [the issue] gets put up to the commission … and as has happened so far … Craig hasn’t been involved in any deliberations or determinations and, obviously, he won’t be going forward.” Loading Pressed on whether Drummond’s position was untenable, Dillon replied: “Not on the information that’s in front of me at the moment”. Former Hawthorn president Andrew Newbold stepped aside from the commission amid the investigation into alleged racism at the Hawks, but Dillon would not be drawn on comparing the cases.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age “I don’t want to get into the hypotheticals ... but what we have got, at the moment, is we’re getting information from Geelong. As that information comes to light, we’ll deal with it,” he said. Dillon said he had not addressed the matter with colleague, Simon Kelleher, who was the Cats’ chief operating officer at the time before crossing to head office. In a public statement on Saturday before Dillon conducted a series of media interviews to try and shed light on the AFL’s role in the saga, Drummond apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation”. “I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024,” the AFL chairman said.



“This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board. “Jake’s welfare was central to all discussions and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days. “While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.



“Regardless of the player’s agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed.” Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract on Friday, but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Dillon would not comment on any potential sanctions or charges the Cats could face until the league receives a response from the club over what the AFL and Geelong acknowledge to be a procedural failure. Dillon denied the league had double standards when dealing with the Cats. “What we’re looking at now is getting the information from Geelong, and then we will see what we’ve got from there, and then make a decision at that stage,” Dillon said SEN.



“I know people want answers really quickly, and we’re working on that, but we want to hear back from Geelong, give them the chance to reply to that, and then we see where that goes.” Drummond and Dillon both said the waiver didn’t remove Kolodjashnij’s protections as a player under statutory health and safety laws. “As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA [AFL Players’ Association],” Drummond said. “I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations. Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij, pictured in April, has identified himself as the player involved in the agreement. AFL Photos



“I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation.” Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal speaks out Dillon said the waiver was a breach of the AFL rules and repeatedly used the word “failure” in describing the Cats’ handling of the issue. The scandal has shone the spotlight on the league’s declaration that it places player health and safety as its No.1 priority. “I don’t think the position’s weakened, but there have been failures, and they’ve been owned, and then there will be accountability,” Dillon said.



Kolodjashnij, who has a history of concussions, appeared before the AFL’s concussion panel process in 2024 and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. His twin brother Kade retired in 2020, aged 25, due to concussion issues. “There have been players who’ve gone to the panel, and the advice has been clear: you shouldn’t play. And we’ve had players retire on the back of that,” Dillon said. “We’ve had players retire as a result of concussions who haven’t gone to the panel, and they’ve come to that conclusion with their club doctor or with their independent doctor. But again, we’re very thankful for the doctors who give up their time and they serve on that panel. It’s a really important role for the game.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Deadly bird flu spreads to inland Australia, as positive cases reach 215
World.content:
The first inland case of H5N1 bird flu in Australia has been detected in western NSW at the junction of the Murray and Darling rivers on the Victorian border, in a sign the virus will spread rapidly across the continent. The NSW government announced two more cases of H5N1 bird flu on Saturday, one in Narooma on the South Coast and one near Wentworth in the far west, bringing the total number of confirmed detections across Australia to 215. The positive samples in both Narooma and Wentworth were from dead greater crested terns, that had been reported by members of the public to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline. It is the first time an Australian native bird has tested positive for H5N1 bird flu in NSW. Two deceased greater crested terns have tested positive for bird flu in NSW. Neil Bowman The highly contagious strain of avian influenza has devastated wildlife on every other continent, and arrived in Australia in June via seabirds blown off course from the sub-Antarctic flyway. As of 3pm Saturday, there had been 147 cases in South Australia, 53 in Victoria, 10 in Western Australia, four in NSW and one in Queensland, the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry said.



Previous cases have been on or near the coast, whereas Wentworth is about 400 kilometres from the nearest coast in South Australia. The “doom list” put out by the federal government earlier this week found one in five native bird and mammal species was at high, very high or extreme risk. Related Article Bird flu ‘List of doom’: Bird flu puts one in five Australian bird and mammal species at risk The NSW government said surveillance work would continue at the sites to ensure early detection of any further cases. “These positive cases are not unexpected,” NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said. “We have been preparing for a situation like this, and we remain well equipped to respond to manage further impacts.



“We are using the best available data and tools to target actions for our most at-risk wildlife species and important natural places.” In total, four birds in NSW have returned a positive result for H5N1 bird flu, with the first two being migratory petrel birds found near Port Stephens in early July. Jack Gough, chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said this was the first inland case, and the speed at which the bird flu was spreading to new species and new locations was alarming. “We now have it turning up for the first time in the Murray Darling Basin at Wentworth,” Gough said. “That should be ringing alarm bells for governments because it suggests it could soon be spreading among inland bird colonies ahead of spring breeding season.” Gough said birds in the Murray-Darling basin were already declining because of feral animals, insufficient water to critical wetlands and the loss of habitat.



Although there have been no detections of bird flu in commercial poultry flocks in Australia, the state Minister for Agriculture, Regional and Western NSW Tara Moriarty said the industry was prepared. “We are continuing to work with our industry partners, including key agricultural and wildlife stakeholders, ensuring the community have up-to-date information about our surveillance and response to detections of H5 bird flu,” Moriarty said. While humans can catch H5N1 from animals, there has been no recorded human-to-human transmission. The official advice for people who see sick or dead birds and other animals is: don’t touch, record their location, take photos and video if possible, and call the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. World.title: Won’t back down: Petty fires broadside at chief antagonist Voss in Dees’ statement win
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Won’t back down: Petty fires broadside at chief antagonist Voss in Dees’ statement win Danny Russell August 8, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Melbourne backed born-again forward Harrison Petty for his gleeful take-down of former tormentor Patrick Voss on an afternoon that the Demons announced themselves as a serious premiership threat. Petty was a crucial key forward in the finals-like MCG clash, kicking three goals to help Melbourne down top-of-the-table Fremantle by four points – 17.11 (113) to 17.7 (109). Harrison Petty kicks three goals against Fremantle. Getty Images But it was after his first goal that he made his statement, rubbing his freshly shaved head in delight – an obvious broadside at Voss for his antagonistic treatment of Petty earlier this year. Following that round-two match at Optus Stadium, Voss was charged with misconduct and fined $1500 for mocking Petty by rubbing the then defender’s hair and simulating a crying action.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Andrew Dillon stands by AFL chairman Drummond amid Geelong scandal It prompted the AFL to instruct umpires to start paying free kicks against players who rubbed the head of an opponent. But there was no taunting Petty on Saturday. He was crucial in the Demons’ fighting win – they trailed by three points a half-time, eight points at three-quarter-time and fell 15 points in arrears during a tense final term. Teammate Bailey Laurie, who kicked three valuable goals of his own, called Petty’s actions “awesome”. “Last time, I think he got his head rubbed, so I mean, he’s probably got the laugh today. So I’m sure he’ll be pretty happy with that one,” Laurie told The Age.



Coach Steven King was also full of praise for Petty. “I think it’s just him embracing who he is, being authentic. He’s on the big stage, you know,” King said. “[There’s] nothing wrong with shaving your head. I think it looks great. It wasn’t something I was aware that was going to happen. But I think that just shows where Petts is at. “He’s enjoying his footy. He’s proud of who he is, who he plays for, and yeah, it’s a good sign for him that he’s engaged in the game, and it means something to him.”



While Voss was at the opposite end of the ground to Petty, he was making a statement of a different kind. The damaging Dockers forward kicked four straight goals for the match. His teammate Jye Amiss also booted five without registering a behind. Their accuracy was unnerving for the Demons in an opening half that both sides piled on 21 goals between them in a mouth-watering shootout. At the long break, the Dockers led 11.2 to the Demons’ 10.5. “I think Kingy said we were plus-20 something in contest, and there were periods of the game we played really well, but we knew they were kicking all these goals that were pretty good. Like, tip your hat to them,” Laurie said. “But all the stats were saying that if we kept doing what we were doing, we’d be right there at the end, which we were.”



It was a game of fluctuating fortunes. Fremantle kicked four of the first five goals, Melbourne answered with the next four, the Dockers hit back with three in succession, and then Melbourne clawed their way back with four in a row. All this before half-time. Max Gawn has a fierce battle against Fremantle’s Luke Jackson at the MCG. Getty Images Then the midfields took turns in sharing dominance. For most of the afternoon it was hard to split All-Australian ruck contenders and 2021 premiership teammates Max Gawn (16 disposals and 33 hitouts) as he did battle with Luke Jackson (17 disposals and 26 hitouts).



“They’re both unique,” King said. “You could call both of them ‘unicorns’, I guess. Max has done things we haven’t seen. I think ‘Jacko’ now, the way he plays and follows up, he’s like an extra midfielder for them. “I just think they’re both unbelievable footballers, and what a privilege it was to come here today to watch them both compete against each other.” The indefatigable Gawn played out the final term without a break as he willed his team over the line – they did not hit the front until the 21-minute mark of the final term on the back of a Bayley Fritsch snap. But the Dockers had their chances. Jordan Clark and Matthew Johnson spilled marks in the last minute, while the enigmatic Fritsch was paid a mark right on the boundary line in the dying seconds that could easily have been ruled out-on-the full, allowing the Dockers one last roll of the dice. But none of that mattered to the Melbourne-dominated crowd of 40,938 who erupted in full voice as the final siren sounded.



As they belted out the theme song, Fritsch kicked a behind, bumping the final margin to four points and bringing his total for the game to 2.5. Outside of Pickett, there were crucial bit-part players everywhere for the Demons who not only landed their biggest scalp of the season and improved their MCG record this year to 10-1, but have given themselves a chance at a top-four finish. View post on X Tom Sparrow racked up 24 disposals and two goals, Koltyn Tholstrup blanketed the dangerous Murphy Reid, Harvey Langford took a mark-of-the-year contender, while hard-running wingman Harry Sharp managed three of his own, including a 60-metre bomb on the run from the boundary and a brilliant soccer goal in the pulsating final term. “I was saying to some of the boys throughout the game, as a spectator, that would have been unbelievable game to watch,” Laurie said.



“To play my part in that was nice. It was very satisfying. We’re a special group, and anything’s possible.” King agreed, beaming with pride after winning a game at the MCG with a finals-like intensity against a team they rated as “the best team in it”. “I think for us it was a scalp we needed to take,” he said. “We needed to signify to the opposition that we’re here. We’re not just shooting to play a final. We want to make it count.”

World.title: Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school
World.content:
WorldAsiaTragedy Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school Harry Jiaravongtrakul Zach Hope and August 8, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content. Bang Kruai District, Thailand: It was school work, a short study on secondhand trade, that got 15-year-old Wannapa out of class slightly early and down the elevators – to safety. She didn’t know it then, but on the sixth floor of Debsirin Nonthaburi School’s building five, one floor below her own class, a 14-year-old boy was preparing for what in minutes would be Thailand’s worst mass killing since 2022. Wannapa outside her family’s shop on the outskirts of Bangkok. Zach Hope The boy had come to his school, on the northwestern fringes of Bangkok, fresh from murdering his grandparents at their shared home earlier on Friday morning, a fact only discovered by police when they searched the place hours later.



By 10am, the second school period was almost over, and Wannapa was among a handful of students given permission to go downstairs and submit their finished work directly to their teacher’s office. She was passing by the cafe with her friends, carrying her school work, when she heard the first pop from somewhere above. “I didn’t think that much of it – I thought maybe someone was fixing something,” she told this masthead from her family’s shop, a few hundred metres from the school. The girl, who asked that her surname not be published, spoke with her parents’ blessing. A woman lays flowers and offers prayers at Debsirin Nonthaburi School on Saturday. AP “Then I heard another four or five rounds. Students were like, ‘gunshots!’”



Wannapa and about 50 others fled into the school assembly hall, as they had been told to do in an emergency, barricading the doors with chairs and opening it only to let in students frantically knocking from the outside. “I continued to hear gunshots – two or three more rounds – then I didn’t hear anything after that, but I might have been in shock,” she said. Related Article Graphic content

Mass shooting Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage The shopkeepers selling fried food about 15 metres from one of the school’s multistorey buildings heard the gunfire too. “I just thought they were dragging chairs or something,” one woman says. But then students started clambering out the upper floor windows and hiding on ledges by the outside air-conditioning compressors. “That room where the window is open,” the woman says, pointing. “That’s where one of the teachers got shot.”



The mass school shooting, something more associated with America than the “Land of Smiles”, is the talk of the country and the neighbourhood. In a nearby 7/11 store, young staff members are overheard discussing how some of the students left their phones and wallets in the classroom and couldn’t get taxis home. School shootings may be rare in Thailand, but gun ownership is not, and recent years have brought periodic, horrific killings, including the 2022 case of an ex-police officer who killed 36 people, including 24 kids, at a childcare centre in the nation’s north-east. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to review gun laws. The events at Debsirin Nonthaburi School on Friday may be a catalyst for change. The shooter had somehow got hold of his grandfather’s 9mm handgun, as he had done previously this year to show it off in an Instagram post.



For a time after killing his grandparents, the boy sat normally in class, investigators say, before suddenly pulling out the handgun and opening fire. CCTV footage circulating on social media – confirmed by Wannapa as showing her school – captures a student exiting a classroom while still firing shots inside. Two people emerge into the hallway from the classroom next door, presumably to see what is happening. The boy appears to shoot at least one of them, before running down the hallway and out of frame. Most of Wannapa’s classmates were still on the seventh floor. Many of them dashed down the stairway when the shooting began, and some evidently appeared in the shooter’s line of sight on the sixth floor. One was shot in the back. He was taken to hospital in a serious condition, and Wannapa says she heard that the wounded boy was going to survive. A schoolgirl walks past police standing guard after the shooting on Friday. AP On the fifth floor, below the initial volley of shots, 14-year-old Kwarchai and his classmates first thought someone was outside, shooting at birds. It soon became clear it was more serious.



“Everyone was shocked,” he says. “Some ran out of the classroom. Others hid under the tables.” Kwarchai chose the latter. Wannapa and the others hunkered down in the assembly hall for 15 minutes or half an hour – she isn’t sure – until police arrived. It’s unclear whether the gunman had shot himself by this stage. Authorities say he turned the weapon on himself inside another building after police had made a cordon around its perimeter. Left behind were five dead or dying staff members and close to 30 wounded, including students. A coffin containing the body of a victim of the school shooting is carried at a hospital in Bangkok on Saturday. AP The shooter’s motive or mental state is unclear but the prime minister, Anutin, and investigators said the boy had been pressured by his grandparents over his school performance.



One of the shooter’s classmates arrived at Plai Bang police station on Saturday to provide a statement, and stopped briefly to field a handful of questions from reporters. He said he believed the shooter was hunting, unsuccessfully, a teacher who gave him a score of zero on an assignment. Thai media, citing relatives, described him as a boy who kept to himself and spent most of his free time playing video games. Investigators say he had been searching online videos about mass shootings in the days before his attack. Wannapa did not know him. But she knew three of the dead. They were her maths and Thai teachers, and a guidance counsellor. “I feel so heavy on the inside,” she says. “I don’t know what to do.” Lifeline 13 11 14. Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636. World.title: ‘Philanthropy is not neutral’: Debate swirls at university over controversial $35m scholarship program
World.content:
NationalVictoriaUniversity ‘Philanthropy is not neutral’: Debate swirls at university over controversial $35m scholarship program Jackson Graham August 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

University of Melbourne academics have voted against a university-backed plan to use $35million from the controversial Liberal-linked Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation for student scholarships, leaving the money in limbo. The scholarships, which would fund 30 students a year to study humanities subjects, come at a time when the cost of many arts degrees has surged to more than $50,000. But the conservative Ramsay Centre’s promotion of “Western culture” has raised hackles among university staff. The university is still backing the scheme, but it is unclear what can come of the money without the support of the academic board, which has the power to vote on specifics of the scholarship such as the eligibility criteria but not the overall gift. Melbourne University has accepted funding from the Ramsay Centre but plans for it have divided the academic board. Luis Enrique Ascui



“The explicit promotion of ‘Western civilisation’ excludes and denigrates other cultures, whether intentionally or not,” said University of Melbourne history professor Zoe Laidlaw, who studies the link between philanthropy and colonialism and is one of the academics who voted against the proposal. She said if the university proceeded with the scholarship plan, “it will undermine its capacity to live up to its core values of anti-racism and truth-telling” as well as “its public commitment to addressing the harm caused by its colonial past”. “Philanthropy... is not neutral.” The vote does not mean the money is off the table. It cleared the university council’s gift procedures, and university leadership is still planning to allow students to be able to apply for the scholarships later this year.



A sub-committee of the academic board will now consider the proposal, which could result in a further vote of the full board. The board voted against the proposal despite receiving a four-page explanation of the checks and balances including that the scholarship selection panel would include only one Ramsay Centre representative and three university academics. The Ramsay Centre for Western Civilisation, which is chaired by former university chancellor Allan Myers and includes former prime minister Tony Abbott on its board, has been controversial in the higher education sector over its ‘bachelor of Western civilisation’ courses at several other universities. The university has previously said it is deeply committed to anti-racism and truth-telling. “Nothing about this announcement changes or compromises that commitment,” it said in May. David Gonzalez, National Tertiary Education Union branch president, wants transparent consultation over a controversial scholarship program. Joe Armao



The scholarship proposal split the academic board 39-37, with several academics arguing the money was much-needed and recognised the valuable contribution of humanities at a time when the price of many arts degrees has increased to more than $50,000 due to the Job-ready Graduates scheme. Sara Wills, a pro vice-chancellor at the university who voted for the proposal, said there were rigorous processes surrounding the scholarship that meant it did not compromise academic freedom. She wants students to understand the complex and multicultural histories that have influenced their area of study, including in western history. “There will be people at the Ramsay Centre who have views that are different from us, and we should accept that we live in a world where there are views that are different from us we may not agree with,” she said. “Really good scholarship looks beyond simple polarities.



“How do we, with integrity, take this gift and do good with it? And that’s really been my intention; to say, at the end of the day, we did not see or think that it had undue influence.” Still, some university staff take issue with how the money has been accepted and believe academics should have a greater say in gifts to the university. Related Article Exclusive

University ‘It’s about influence’: Melbourne Uni row breaks out over scholarships from Ramsay Centre “The initial discussions about this partnership took place behind closed doors,” said National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU) branch president at the university, David Gonzalez. “Programs that give external organisations privileged influence or access to our students deserve transparent consultation with the people who will ultimately be responsible for delivering them.”



A University of Melbourne spokesperson said the university had gratefully acknowledged the donation and the specific scholarship arrangements were now being progressed through the standard governance processes. The university plans for five annual intakes of 30 students, with five scholarships each year for under-represented groups. As well as the stipend, it offers attendance at an international summer school, an annual regional leadership program, and a community service and volunteering program. “All philanthropic donations proposed to the University of Melbourne undergo significant and rigorous assessment at the appropriate levels before proceeding,” the spokesperson said. “The university has received other gifts of similar scale previously, and these are managed in accordance with the appropriate processes.” The university says the separation of duties – with the university council and gift committee approving donations and the academic board approving the rules and conditions of the scholarship – is a common way to make sure financial and reputation risks, as well as academic standards, are “separately and robustly reviewed”.



However, Joo-Cheong Tham, Melbourne Law School professor and NTEU Victorian assistant secretary, said the academic board should have involvement in decisions over gifts, such as providing independent advice to the university council before the money is accepted. He said the current process gave the impression of a “fait accompli”. “The governance structures are not fit for purpose,” Tham said. A spokesperson for the Ramsay Centre declined to comment on the vote, saying the administration of the scholarship was a matter for the university. World.title: Liberal Andrew Hastie faces mounting pressure from One Nation as party ramps up national expansion
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation Liberal Andrew Hastie faces mounting pressure from One Nation as party ramps up national expansion Brittany Busch August 8, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation has launched its campaign against Liberal leadership hopeful Andrew Hastie, just days after the opposition frontbencher acknowledged his own “political mortality” in the face of the resurgent minor party. The party’s Western Australian leader Rod Caddies and Luke Herdegen, the state candidate for the impending Secret Harbour byelection, opened the Canning branch on Saturday afternoon. Andrew Hastie has backflipped on his staunch opposition to One Nation. Alex Ellinghausen Meanwhile in Victoria, freshly endorsed state leader Warren Pickering has de-emphasised his previous endorsement of conspiracy theories as the Victorian arm of the party also expands and garners fresh scrutiny ahead of the November election. At the Canning branch launch, One Nation did not announce a candidate or policies, but has vowed to run a strong opponent against Hastie. Party leadership has attacked the Coalition frontbencher for giving evidence in Ben Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation action against this masthead and his role as a potential witness in the accused war criminal’s upcoming trial.



Caddies said One Nation polled well in the area and would campaign hard. Related Article One Nation Hastie signals he might lose, hopes One Nation will preference him “But it won’t be because it’s [Hastie’s] seat. It’ll be because I’m planning to help target every seat in this state and join my federal colleagues in supporting them in making sure that we win as many seats as possible,” he said ahead of the launch. “You would be a fool not to be worried with the polling that’s been done and the support we’re getting on the street. One Nation’s momentum is massive. Anyone that says they’re not worried, I guess you can take that for what it is. But if I was the member... I would be concerned that there will be a change of representation.” A seat-by-seat analysis conducted by Redbridge for The Australian Financial Review in May predicated Hastie would lose his seat in a populist surge. The Liberal frontbencher this week signalled for the first time he could lose, saying he hoped for One Nation’s preferences after previously vowing never to “bend the knee” to Pauline Hanson.



The previous One Nation candidate, Fernando Bove, won 11.4 per cent of first preferences at the 2025 federal election, with a 6.8 per cent swing. Related Article Political leadership Hastie gets security upgrades as One Nation campaigns against him One Nation is mobilising in the region ahead of the Secret Harbour byelection, where long-term Labor minister Paul Papalia has retired. WA Labor Premier Roger Cook has warned voting for One Nation would bring “the chaos of the eastern states to Western Australia”. One Nation’s rapid expansion, with a goal to run candidates in every electorate around the country, has opened up fresh scrutiny for the minor party.





“With respect to conspiratorial type conversations, if you go a bit more into the context of those rallies and things I’d said previously, you will find that… it was in the build-up to a federal election, and surrounding things like a lot of these quotas under the pretense of sustainability and net zero. So the Paris Agreement and UN Refugee Convention , which are drafted and administered by UN and WEF [World Economic Forum] organisations. So, look, it’s not conspiratorial, but it’s also not related to a state election,” he told News24. Asked to explain his opposition to 15-minute cities, he said Victoria was removing community consultation processes on high-rise developments “under the pretense of sustainability”. “That’s the best way to describe it in the short term,” he said. Pickering also said it was “inevitable” that One Nation would continue banning news organisations after the minor party barred The Age, ABC and The Guardian from a press conference on Monday where it was announcing a handful of candidates for the upcoming state election. “It was a good move because within 24 hours, all three of those publications had managed to push out a bit of a hit piece on myself,” he told News24, referring to reporting on his embrace of conspiracy theories. World.title: Andrew Dillon stands by AFL chairman Drummond amid Geelong scandal
World.content:
AFL chief Andrew Dillon has refused to be drawn on whether commission chairman Craig Drummond should immediately step aside from his position while investigations into Geelong’s secret concussion waiver scandal are being conducted. Drummond, the Geelong president when the matter was dealt with by the club, has removed himself from league deliberations, apologising and conceding the Cats “went too far” in not seeking league approval before allowing premiership player Jake Kolodjashnij to sign a waiver that had him assuming responsibility for future on-field head injuries. AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui Amid the fallout from the scandal after Kolodjashnij identified himself on Friday as the player involved, Dillon has not ruled out calling in an independent party to lead the investigation. Pressure is mounting on the AFL to mete out heavy penalties. The league issued Carlton a $75,000 fine for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode during a game earlier this year, and also docked former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley $20,000 for taunting Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan with an aeroplane gesture in 2024.



“It is an issue at the moment that is at the AFL executive level,” Dillon said on 3AW on Saturday. “If it [the issue] gets put up to the commission … and as has happened so far … Craig hasn’t been involved in any deliberations or determinations and, obviously, he won’t be going forward.” Loading Pressed on whether Drummond’s position was untenable, Dillon replied: “Not on the information that’s in front of me at the moment”. Former Hawthorn president Andrew Newbold stepped aside from the commission amid the investigation into alleged racism at the Hawks, but Dillon would not be drawn on comparing the cases.



Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 These are the questions AFL boss must answer on Geelong’s concussion deal Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age “I don’t want to get into the hypotheticals ... but what we have got, at the moment, is we’re getting information from Geelong. As that information comes to light, we’ll deal with it,” he said. Dillon said he had not addressed the matter with colleague, Simon Kelleher, who was the Cats’ chief operating officer at the time before crossing to head office. In a public statement on Saturday before Dillon conducted a series of media interviews to try and shed light on the AFL’s role in the saga, Drummond apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation”. “I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024,” the AFL chairman said.



“This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board. “Jake’s welfare was central to all discussions and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days. “While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.



“Regardless of the player’s agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed.” Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract on Friday, but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age Dillon would not comment on any potential sanctions or charges the Cats could face until the league receives a response from the club over what the AFL and Geelong acknowledge to be a procedural failure. Dillon denied the league had double standards when dealing with the Cats. “What we’re looking at now is getting the information from Geelong, and then we will see what we’ve got from there, and then make a decision at that stage,” Dillon said SEN.



“I know people want answers really quickly, and we’re working on that, but we want to hear back from Geelong, give them the chance to reply to that, and then we see where that goes.” Drummond and Dillon both said the waiver didn’t remove Kolodjashnij’s protections as a player under statutory health and safety laws. “As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA [AFL Players’ Association],” Drummond said. “I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations. Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij, pictured in April, has identified himself as the player involved in the agreement. AFL Photos



“I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation.” Related Article Updated

Concussion crisis ‘My private medical information has been made public’: Cat at centre of concussion scandal speaks out Dillon said the waiver was a breach of the AFL rules and repeatedly used the word “failure” in describing the Cats’ handling of the issue. The scandal has shone the spotlight on the league’s declaration that it places player health and safety as its No.1 priority. “I don’t think the position’s weakened, but there have been failures, and they’ve been owned, and then there will be accountability,” Dillon said.



Kolodjashnij, who has a history of concussions, appeared before the AFL’s concussion panel process in 2024 and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. His twin brother Kade retired in 2020, aged 25, due to concussion issues. “There have been players who’ve gone to the panel, and the advice has been clear: you shouldn’t play. And we’ve had players retire on the back of that,” Dillon said. “We’ve had players retire as a result of concussions who haven’t gone to the panel, and they’ve come to that conclusion with their club doctor or with their independent doctor. But again, we’re very thankful for the doctors who give up their time and they serve on that panel. It’s a really important role for the game.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Deadly bird flu spreads to inland Australia, as positive cases reach 215
World.content:
The first inland case of H5N1 bird flu in Australia has been detected in western NSW at the junction of the Murray and Darling rivers on the Victorian border, in a sign the virus will spread rapidly across the continent. The NSW government announced two more cases of H5N1 bird flu on Saturday, one in Narooma on the South Coast and one near Wentworth in the far west, bringing the total number of confirmed detections across Australia to 215. The positive samples in both Narooma and Wentworth were from dead greater crested terns, that had been reported by members of the public to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline. It is the first time an Australian native bird has tested positive for H5N1 bird flu in NSW. Two deceased greater crested terns have tested positive for bird flu in NSW. Neil Bowman The highly contagious strain of avian influenza has devastated wildlife on every other continent, and arrived in Australia in June via seabirds blown off course from the sub-Antarctic flyway. As of 3pm Saturday, there had been 147 cases in South Australia, 53 in Victoria, 10 in Western Australia, four in NSW and one in Queensland, the federal Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry said.



Previous cases have been on or near the coast, whereas Wentworth is about 400 kilometres from the nearest coast in South Australia. The “doom list” put out by the federal government earlier this week found one in five native bird and mammal species was at high, very high or extreme risk. Related Article Bird flu ‘List of doom’: Bird flu puts one in five Australian bird and mammal species at risk The NSW government said surveillance work would continue at the sites to ensure early detection of any further cases. “These positive cases are not unexpected,” NSW Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said. “We have been preparing for a situation like this, and we remain well equipped to respond to manage further impacts.



“We are using the best available data and tools to target actions for our most at-risk wildlife species and important natural places.” In total, four birds in NSW have returned a positive result for H5N1 bird flu, with the first two being migratory petrel birds found near Port Stephens in early July. Jack Gough, chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said this was the first inland case, and the speed at which the bird flu was spreading to new species and new locations was alarming. “We now have it turning up for the first time in the Murray Darling Basin at Wentworth,” Gough said. “That should be ringing alarm bells for governments because it suggests it could soon be spreading among inland bird colonies ahead of spring breeding season.” Gough said birds in the Murray-Darling basin were already declining because of feral animals, insufficient water to critical wetlands and the loss of habitat.



Although there have been no detections of bird flu in commercial poultry flocks in Australia, the state Minister for Agriculture, Regional and Western NSW Tara Moriarty said the industry was prepared. “We are continuing to work with our industry partners, including key agricultural and wildlife stakeholders, ensuring the community have up-to-date information about our surveillance and response to detections of H5 bird flu,” Moriarty said. While humans can catch H5N1 from animals, there has been no recorded human-to-human transmission. The official advice for people who see sick or dead birds and other animals is: don’t touch, record their location, take photos and video if possible, and call the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Won’t back down: Petty fires broadside at chief antagonist Voss in Dees’ statement win
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Won’t back down: Petty fires broadside at chief antagonist Voss in Dees’ statement win Danny Russell August 8, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Melbourne backed born-again forward Harrison Petty for his gleeful take-down of former tormentor Patrick Voss on an afternoon that the Demons announced themselves as a serious premiership threat. Petty was a crucial key forward in the finals-like MCG clash, kicking three goals to help Melbourne down top-of-the-table Fremantle by four points – 17.11 (113) to 17.7 (109). Harrison Petty kicks three goals against Fremantle. Getty Images But it was after his first goal that he made his statement, rubbing his freshly shaved head in delight – an obvious broadside at Voss for his antagonistic treatment of Petty earlier this year. Following that round-two match at Optus Stadium, Voss was charged with misconduct and fined $1500 for mocking Petty by rubbing the then defender’s hair and simulating a crying action.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Andrew Dillon stands by AFL chairman Drummond amid Geelong scandal It prompted the AFL to instruct umpires to start paying free kicks against players who rubbed the head of an opponent. But there was no taunting Petty on Saturday. He was crucial in the Demons’ fighting win – they trailed by three points a half-time, eight points at three-quarter-time and fell 15 points in arrears during a tense final term. Teammate Bailey Laurie, who kicked three valuable goals of his own, called Petty’s actions “awesome”. “Last time, I think he got his head rubbed, so I mean, he’s probably got the laugh today. So I’m sure he’ll be pretty happy with that one,” Laurie told The Age.



Coach Steven King was also full of praise for Petty. “I think it’s just him embracing who he is, being authentic. He’s on the big stage, you know,” King said. “[There’s] nothing wrong with shaving your head. I think it looks great. It wasn’t something I was aware that was going to happen. But I think that just shows where Petts is at. “He’s enjoying his footy. He’s proud of who he is, who he plays for, and yeah, it’s a good sign for him that he’s engaged in the game, and it means something to him.”



While Voss was at the opposite end of the ground to Petty, he was making a statement of a different kind. The damaging Dockers forward kicked four straight goals for the match. His teammate Jye Amiss also booted five without registering a behind. Their accuracy was unnerving for the Demons in an opening half that both sides piled on 21 goals between them in a mouth-watering shootout. At the long break, the Dockers led 11.2 to the Demons’ 10.5. “I think Kingy said we were plus-20 something in contest, and there were periods of the game we played really well, but we knew they were kicking all these goals that were pretty good. Like, tip your hat to them,” Laurie said. “But all the stats were saying that if we kept doing what we were doing, we’d be right there at the end, which we were.”



It was a game of fluctuating fortunes. Fremantle kicked four of the first five goals, Melbourne answered with the next four, the Dockers hit back with three in succession, and then Melbourne clawed their way back with four in a row. All this before half-time. Max Gawn has a fierce battle against Fremantle’s Luke Jackson at the MCG. Getty Images Then the midfields took turns in sharing dominance. For most of the afternoon it was hard to split All-Australian ruck contenders and 2021 premiership teammates Max Gawn (16 disposals and 33 hitouts) as he did battle with Luke Jackson (17 disposals and 26 hitouts).



“They’re both unique,” King said. “You could call both of them ‘unicorns’, I guess. Max has done things we haven’t seen. I think ‘Jacko’ now, the way he plays and follows up, he’s like an extra midfielder for them. “I just think they’re both unbelievable footballers, and what a privilege it was to come here today to watch them both compete against each other.” The indefatigable Gawn played out the final term without a break as he willed his team over the line – they did not hit the front until the 21-minute mark of the final term on the back of a Bayley Fritsch snap. But the Dockers had their chances. Jordan Clark and Matthew Johnson spilled marks in the last minute, while the enigmatic Fritsch was paid a mark right on the boundary line in the dying seconds that could easily have been ruled out-on-the full, allowing the Dockers one last roll of the dice. But none of that mattered to the Melbourne-dominated crowd of 40,938 who erupted in full voice as the final siren sounded.



As they belted out the theme song, Fritsch kicked a behind, bumping the final margin to four points and bringing his total for the game to 2.5. Outside of Pickett, there were crucial bit-part players everywhere for the Demons who not only landed their biggest scalp of the season and improved their MCG record this year to 10-1, but have given themselves a chance at a top-four finish. View post on X Tom Sparrow racked up 24 disposals and two goals, Koltyn Tholstrup blanketed the dangerous Murphy Reid, Harvey Langford took a mark-of-the-year contender, while hard-running wingman Harry Sharp managed three of his own, including a 60-metre bomb on the run from the boundary and a brilliant soccer goal in the pulsating final term. “I was saying to some of the boys throughout the game, as a spectator, that would have been unbelievable game to watch,” Laurie said.



“To play my part in that was nice. It was very satisfying. We’re a special group, and anything’s possible.” King agreed, beaming with pride after winning a game at the MCG with a finals-like intensity against a team they rated as “the best team in it”. “I think for us it was a scalp we needed to take,” he said. “We needed to signify to the opposition that we’re here. We’re not just shooting to play a final. We want to make it count.”
