World.title: Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school
World.content:
WorldAsiaTragedy Barricading doors, hiding under tables: Students tell of fleeing mass shooting at their Thai school Harry Jiaravongtrakul Zach Hope and August 8, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content. Bang Kruai District, Thailand: It was school work, a short study on secondhand trade, that got 15-year-old Wannapa out of class slightly early and down the elevators – to safety. She didn’t know it then, but on the sixth floor of Debsirin Nonthaburi School’s building five, one floor below her own class, a 14-year-old boy was preparing for what in minutes would be Thailand’s worst mass killing since 2022. Wannapa outside her family’s shop on the outskirts of Bangkok. Zach Hope The boy had come to his school, on the northwestern fringes of Bangkok, fresh from murdering his grandparents at their shared home earlier on Friday morning, a fact only discovered by police when they searched the place hours later.



By 10am, the second school period was almost over, and Wannapa was among a handful of students given permission to go downstairs and submit their finished work directly to their teacher’s office. She was passing by the cafe with her friends, carrying her school work, when she heard the first pop from somewhere above. “I didn’t think that much of it – I thought maybe someone was fixing something,” she told this masthead from her family’s shop, a few hundred metres from the school. The girl, who asked that her surname not be published, spoke with her parents’ blessing. A woman lays flowers and offers prayers at Debsirin Nonthaburi School on Saturday. AP “Then I heard another four or five rounds. Students were like, ‘gunshots!’”



Wannapa and about 50 others fled into the school assembly hall, as they had been told to do in an emergency, barricading the doors with chairs and opening it only to let in students frantically knocking from the outside. “I continued to hear gunshots – two or three more rounds – then I didn’t hear anything after that, but I might have been in shock,” she said. Related Article Graphic content

Mass shooting Teen gunman watched violent videos before killing seven in shooting rampage The shopkeepers selling fried food about 15 metres from one of the school’s multistorey buildings heard the gunfire too. “I just thought they were dragging chairs or something,” one woman says. But then students started clambering out the upper floor windows and hiding on ledges by the outside air-conditioning compressors. “That room where the window is open,” the woman says, pointing. “That’s where one of the teachers got shot.”



The mass school shooting, something more associated with America than the “Land of Smiles”, is the talk of the country and the neighbourhood. In a nearby 7/11 store, young staff members are overheard discussing how some of the students left their phones and wallets in the classroom and couldn’t get taxis home. School shootings may be rare in Thailand, but gun ownership is not, and recent years have brought periodic, horrific killings, including the 2022 case of an ex-police officer who killed 36 people, including 24 kids, at a childcare centre in the nation’s north-east. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to review gun laws. The events at Debsirin Nonthaburi School on Friday may be a catalyst for change. The shooter had somehow got hold of his grandfather’s 9mm handgun, as he had done previously this year to show it off in an Instagram post.



For a time after killing his grandparents, the boy sat normally in class, investigators say, before suddenly pulling out the handgun and opening fire. CCTV footage circulating on social media – confirmed by Wannapa as showing her school – captures a student exiting a classroom while still firing shots inside. Two people emerge into the hallway from the classroom next door, presumably to see what is happening. The boy appears to shoot at least one of them, before running down the hallway and out of frame. Most of Wannapa’s classmates were still on the seventh floor. Many of them dashed down the stairway when the shooting began, and some evidently appeared in the shooter’s line of sight on the sixth floor. One was shot in the back. He was taken to hospital in a serious condition, and Wannapa says she heard that the wounded boy was going to survive. A schoolgirl walks past police standing guard after the shooting on Friday. AP On the fifth floor, below the initial volley of shots, 14-year-old Kwarchai and his classmates first thought someone was outside, shooting at birds. It soon became clear it was more serious.



“Everyone was shocked,” he says. “Some ran out of the classroom. Others hid under the tables.” Kwarchai chose the latter. Wannapa and the others hunkered down in the assembly hall for 15 minutes or half an hour – she isn’t sure – until police arrived. It’s unclear whether the gunman had shot himself by this stage. Authorities say he turned the weapon on himself inside another building after police had made a cordon around its perimeter. Left behind were five dead or dying staff members and close to 30 wounded, including students. A coffin containing the body of a victim of the school shooting is carried at a hospital in Bangkok on Saturday. AP The shooter’s motive or mental state is unclear but the prime minister, Anutin, and investigators said the boy had been pressured by his grandparents over his school performance.



One of the shooter’s classmates arrived at Plai Bang police station on Saturday to provide a statement, and stopped briefly to field a handful of questions from reporters. He said he believed the shooter was hunting, unsuccessfully, a teacher who gave him a score of zero on an assignment. Thai media, citing relatives, described him as a boy who kept to himself and spent most of his free time playing video games. Investigators say he had been searching online videos about mass shootings in the days before his attack. Wannapa did not know him. But she knew three of the dead. They were her maths and Thai teachers, and a guidance counsellor. “I feel so heavy on the inside,” she says. “I don’t know what to do.” Lifeline 13 11 14. Beyond Blue 1300 22 4636. World.title: Brian Tamaki says police have revoked his firearms licence
World.content:
Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki says police have revoked his firearms licence.

On Saturday, the church leader announced on social media that police had decided he was no longer a "fit and proper person".

He said police issued a notice revoking his firearms licence on Friday.

"I am now prohibited not only from possessing my own firearms, but from possessing or using a firearm even under the supervision of a licensed firearms holder."

Acting Executive Director of Firearms Safety Authority Bruce Bird said police were unable to comment on an individual case or licensing decisions.

"However, speaking generally, decisions about suspending or revoking a firearms licence are based on a legal standard of whether a person is 'fit and proper' to possess a firearm."

Bird said fit and proper decisions were guided by circumstances outlined in section 24A of the Arms Act.

Tamaki said he would be seeking a review of the decision.

"I now have 28 days to apply for a review ... you can be certain that I will," he wrote on social media.

Tamaki's comments about India

On Saturday, Tamaki claimed his licence had been revoked in response to statements he had made concerning Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

"I was speaking passionately. I was protesting. I was challenging what I believed needed to be challenged," he said.

"This follows the temporary suspension issued to me on 30 June and the subsequent submissions made by my lawyer opposing that suspension."

In June, police confirmed they had served a temporary firearms licence suspension notice at an Auckland property. Authorities declined to comment on the specifics.

At the time of the suspension, Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour said he was sure the police had acted within the law.

"I got zero time for Brian Tamaki," he said. "If he's got any complaints, he should take them through the proper legal channels and possibly stop being a dickhead."

Earlier that month, Tamaki accused Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi of purging Christians in the South Asian nation.

"He [Modi] is currently purging India of all Christians and burning church buildings down," Tamaki had said in a video posted on social media.

"I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let's purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. And, while we're at it, if they're burning churches down, why don't we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat."

Ethnic Communities Minister Mark Mitchell then labelled the comments as the "actions of a scared bully" and said police would assess the remarks.

World.title: Councils across country meet to finalise amalgamation proposals ahead of deadline
World.content:
Councils face deadline to propose amalgation agreements Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Councils across the country have been meeting to finalise their amalgamation proposals or face the process being dictated to them by central government.

Sunday marks the deadline for district councils to submit their proposals to amalgamate with at least one other nearby authority.

On announcing the three-month Head Start process in May, Local Government Minister, Simon Watts and Resource Management Act Reform Minister, Chris Bishop had a stark message for councils.

"Today we are giving council's a clear choice. Lead your own reform or we will do it for you," Bishop said.

This week, Hamilton District Council voted 12 to three to not participate - meaning the district would end up in a backstop process controlled by central government to ensure reforms still went ahead.

Councillor Andrew Bydder told Morning Report council didn't want to put forward a proposal and have the government think they were happy with it.

"Getting into the tent might leave us stuck in the tent which is not desirable when the tent is a brothel with a minister who wants to pimp us out," Bydder said.

Earlier in the month, Hamilton mayor Tim Macindoe told RNZ he was reluctant to cede control of the process but could not support rushing into an arrangement which did not suit his city.

Tim Macindoe. RNZ / Richard Tindiller

However this week he told councillors he received a phone call from Watts which ruled out his council's involvement in back stop decisions if they did not take the first step of submitting a proposal ahead of the deadline.

"He was also quite clear during our discussion that back-stop councils will not be at the table for that process," Macindoe said.

Down south, Christchurch City Council unanimously agreed to submit on the Head Start process.

They chose to retain the city's current city boundaries while taking on Canterbury Regional Council's functions.

But earlier in the week, councillor Melanie Coker warned the changes could cost millions to implement.

"Functions between councils that join will need to reviewed, combined, resized and this doesn't come for free. Any savings may be decades away and are not guaranteed," Coker said.

But in a Wellington City Council meeting yesterday, mayor Andrew Little said council reform was a necessary step to help address existing problems with long term infrastructure plans, economic growth and the region's ability to cope with the challenges of climate change.

Andrew Little. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"Put aside Head Start. Put aside the dodgy process. can we still address those challenges under the status quo? My view is not," Little said.

On Friday. a statement on behalf of the Wellington and Wairarapa Mayoral Forum outlined how the region could approach the merger.

Two proposals would come from councils of the region. One a region-wide proposal (supported by Wellington City Council, Hutt City Council, Porirua City Council and South Wairarapa District Council) and another proposal for Wairarapa (supported by Carterton District Council and Masterton District Council).

The statement said the proposals would convey the positions of individual councils and the forum was requesting the "door remains open" for alternative arrangements for Kapiti Coast District Council and Upper Hutt District Council.

Late last month, Taupo mayor John Funnell described a proposed Western Waikato Unitary Authority as a "hostile takeover" which would leverage his district's financial strength while ballooning ratepayer debt to nearly ten times current levels.

He said his council had decided not to engage in the Head Start process.

Funnell said he understood concerns that stepping away from the Head Start process could see a merger dictated by central government but said councils who wished to merge with Taupo should come through the front door.

"We're three months out from an election - I would say to Minister Watts 'be careful'.

"I've seen the communications from our residents of the district here and there's a fair bit at stake for everyone here.

"I think the residents are quite clear they want to have their concerns taken in consideration and they want to make sure that the investments that this council has made over many years can put them in a good position as protected - and there's many ways of doing that - but it needs time."

Watts said the government had been clear from the outset that this was a "voluntary process", giving councils the chance to put forward locally led proposals.

"Many councils and mayors have embraced that opportunity, working constructively across their regions to consider how local government can be better organised to deliver stronger services, lower costs and better value for ratepayers.

"We're undertaking the most significant reform of local government in a generation because the current system has become increasingly complex, costly and fragmented, and too often isn't delivering the outcomes that ratepayers expect."

He said no final decisions have been made regarding any backstop as any design would be informed by "the lessons from the voluntary Head Start process."

"I will have more to say once submissions have been received and we have had the opportunity to carefully consider the proposals put forward."

World.title: Am I too old to be more aggressive with my KiwiSaver? - Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

A stupid question but is 46 too old to change to aggressive for my KiwiSaver?

This isn't personalised advice but in general, I wouldn't think so. It depends on a lot of factors like your personal risk tolerance and your investing timeframe.

Aggressive funds are among the most volatile options in KiwiSaver, and have even more exposure to growth assets than growth funds. They invest in things like equities that can fluctuate in value a lot, and you need to have time to ride out any downturns which could see your fund losing up to about 30 percent in a year. But over the long term, taking more risk tends to pay off. Morningstar data shows aggressive funds have returned an average 10.3 percent a year over the past 10 years, the best of the KiwiSaver bunch.

People are usually told they shouldn't be in an aggressive fund if they don't have 10 to 15 years to stick with it.

That said, even if you were a bit older than you are now, it could work. You don't have to pull all your money out at 65, and you may want to keep some exposure to growth assets at that point to help your investment grow.

I would talk to an adviser.

I've just read your response to a question on whether an individual should put their money into a managed fund or KiwiSaver. Your comment was that it's ultimately up to them but in your response you state that "Once you reach 65, a KiwiSaver fund is much the same as any other managed fund, because there are no restrictions on access to your money".

I've recently been told by a financial adviser that this isn't correct and that if you leave your money in a KiwiSaver fund beyond the age of 65 and the government then change the eligibility age for superannuation, this money is then locked into the KiwiSaver fund until you reach that age. Is this correct?

Technically, yes. But in practice I don't think this is something you need to worry about.

At the moment, access to KiwiSaver is tied to the age of eligibility for NZ Super, which is 65.

So if the age were to be increased, at the moment the law would mean the age of access to KiwiSaver would increase, too.

There are already discussions happening, though, about whether that's appropriate. I would expect access to KiwiSaver to be addressed alongside any plans to increase the NZ Super age.

I know some people think having access to KiwiSaver earlier than NZ Super could be a way to help people who want to stop working earlier, if the pension age rises.

I would also note that even if the age was pushed up without any change to the KiwiSaver rules, it would not be something that would affect you as a recently retired person. These sorts of changes are usually signalled well in advance to take effect over a period of time, usually for future generations.

I'm a real layman in regard to financial matters, and am completely lost - perhaps you could illuminate me a little. Now retired, I contributed to a retirement fund (not KiwiSaver) and recently asked them whether PIE (like in my KiwiSaver) was automatically paid across to IRD.

Their reply as I understood it stated that they pay a base fund 28 percent to IRD - but that PIE does not apply in the instance of retirement funds. I was informed that if I withdraw funds/close my account, then I need to inform this via my IR3 and I will be taxed accordingly at my 17.5 percent rate. My quandary is, does IRD make me pay tax on the entire retirement fund amount, or just on the "growth" aspect which has occurred across the years of investing contributions into that fund, the Teachers Retirement Savings Scheme.

Also, am I better off to perhaps withdraw my retirement scheme funds and have them invested together with my other funds which I have in KiwiSaver?

Very quickly, when you're invested in KiwiSaver you're usually paying tax on the income that your investments make, not the growth in the value of the investments themselves. (There are some complexities around this for foreign investments.)

You don't pay tax on withdrawal, except where there could be a "square up" to do on the tax you would normally pay in the year. You aren't going to be charged tax on the total withdrawal amount, or the growth you've had on your investments while you've been investing, or anything like that.

As for the PIE rate, Dean Anderson at Kernel says it's possible that the fund you're in has a fixed PIE rate of 28 percent. In that case, it could be beneficial for you to move to a multi-rate PIE that could allow you you pay tax at a lower rate.

He says it could be that you can now find a fund that's a better fit for your goals, or you might want to consolidate your money into your other investments. "For someone who's now retired, if you're on a lower tax rate then looking for a multi-rate pie is probably a good option because then they tax is automatically at the correct PIR and does not involve any tax filing.

"One of the benefits at the moment of the New Zealand regime is the fact that for an investor in retirement, why PIRs are really good is there is no capital gains tax, there's no other complexity to worry about. You can get into the right risk profile and then say, 'hey I want to sell down $100 or $1000 or I want to take out some holiday money or create a regular income' and there's nothing they have to think about from a tax perspective, it's all going to get handled."

World.title: 'It's amazing': Aucklanders get first look at new City Rail Link station
World.content:
Aucklanders have been getting their first chance to see inside the new City Rail Link, with a busy turnout for the first of a series of public open day events at new railway stations - this one at Maungawhau Station.

City Rail Link (CRL) is the country's largest transport infrastructure project to date, with about three and a half kilometres of tunnels, and set to cost $5.5b. It has been long-awaited and is scheduled to open on 13 September, with promises to speed up and modernise public transport in the sprawling city.

Auckland's first CRL station opens to the public Saturday Morning Download MP3 5m

But before it opens, a series of public 'First Look' weekend events are on offer in August, with the first at the new Maungawhau Station (formerly Mount Eden Station), between Mount Eden and Eden Terrace, on Saturday.

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Auckland Transport said about 17,000 people had registered for the open day. And that translated to a steady stream of people coming in to have a look, CRL communications manager Joel Rowan said, mid-morning on Saturday.

Food and activities were set up in the surrounding streets, with busking and community performances inside the train station.

"There's a stage set up, we've got the local community really part of this. A local school kapa haka group has actually just been warming up. We've had heaps of interest in today, and everyone just seems to be just really enjoying it," Rowan said.

"I think people are relieved. Last night we had some of the locals and local businesses in here for a little preview of today's event. And they've really been hanging out - not just for today, but for the project to open.

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung, at the event at Maungawhau Station on Saturday morning. RNZ/ Lucy Xia

"This station [has] been closed since 2020 for the construction. So I know that everyone's really looking forward to I guess getting the benefits when the opening finally does arrive on the 13th of September."

Several people RNZ spoke to said they were excited about the new East-West connection and the reduction in travel times. Others say they were glad they would no longer be held up by delays at the bottleneck at the New Market station.

Catherine Hill currently takes the train at Kingsland, and transits at the Waitematā station to get to her work place in Panmure on the Eastern line - often slowed down by what she calls "the bottleneck" at Newmarket.

Now she only needs to hope on the East-West line.

"The CRL is going to be a gamechanger for me, so I only have to catch one train rather than two," she said.

Maungawhau Station (formerly Mt Eden) before its official opening, August 2026. Lucy Xia / RNZ

And for others like Swanson resident Jonathan Rankin, the difference is one of switching from driving to work to taking the train.

Rankin now has a direct route to his workplace off Karangahape Road, whereas previously, it would've taken him about an hour to take the train to Kingsland then bus into town.

West Auckland resident Harrison Fernandes-Burnard said the CRL could take about 20 minutes off his daily commute.

"The old Mount Eden Station was quite basic, rustic you could say - but yeah it's amazing ... there's now four platforms and it's really spacious." It had changed a lot, and was a good  for the city, he said.

3. AUT student Connor McGrath says the opening of the Te Waihoritiu station will reduce his walking time to university by half. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung travelled from Meadowlands in East Auckland for the First Look event. Pang hopes there will be more frequent buses to Panmure Station from where she lives.

Yueng said he was excited about taking the train during school holidays and better connections to western parts of the city.

AUT student Connor McGrath, who currently takes the train to Britomart then walks to campus, said the new station at Te Waihorotiu will cut down his walking time by half.

Disability advocate and wheelchair boxer John Fiu, pictured with his wife and brother, says he's happy with the accessibility of the station. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Disability advocate, wheelchair user and heavyweight boxer John Fiu was there on Saturday to check out accessibility. He was pleased with the lifts and said it was easy to get around at the station: "If it wasn't for the lifts we wouldn't be able to access the train station at all, and from an advocate's point of view it's pretty good. Everything is user friendly."

Fiu has a boxing match coming up in October and said he's excited to use the train to get to his match.

At Maungawhau Station on Saturday Lucy Xia / RNZ

Before the old Mt Eden Station closed, the journey downtown from Maungawhau Station to what is now Waitematā Station (formerly Britomart) took about 20 minutes, travelling through Newmarket, Auckland Transport's Joel Rowan said.

It now takes about 10 minutes, or even less for either of the two new closer central stations: just a couple of minutes to Karanga-a-Hape Station, or about seven minutes to Te Waihorotiu Station near the Sky Tower. While people going to or from the westerns suburbs will find their trips much faster using the CRL, Rowan said.

Many rehearsals and trials of the rail schedule had been carried out ahead of the full CRL opening, with big attendance expected from the first day.

Several people told RNZ they were impressed by the artworks. Water cascaded down the wall, and 53 glass triangles were set into the concrete wall to form a map of volcanoes across Auckland.

Bella Cunnington Waugh and her family - her daughter, her nieces and her brother - visiting the Manawhau station on Saturday's "First Look" event. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Aucklander Bella Cunnington Waugh said she liked a feature wall depicting Maungawhau (Mount Eden).

"It's fabulous. I really like the motifs and the imagery, and from what I understand so far of what it's about - the connections to Maungawhau the mountain, to the maunga. Yeah, it looks beautiful."

Auckland Transport's website said the new Maungawhau Station was visually striking, and "combines world-class transport infrastructure with thoughtful design inspired by the surrounding volcanic landscape and deep cultural connections to nearby maunga."

"Its dramatic architecture, natural materials and spacious platforms create a station experience unlike anything else in Auckland."

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Ongoing CRL 'First Look' events are planned for Saturday 15 August at Karanga-a-Hape Station and Saturday 22 August at Te Waihorotiu Station, with a succession of one hour tours available on each day starting from 8am.

Auckland Transport said people planning to attend should apply ahead for tickets, which are free.

World.title: Watch: National Party announces list for 2026 General Election
World.content:
Senior National MPs who might have been nervous about the party's polling have been ranked highly to give them the best shot of returning to Parliament next term.

The party released its full line-up of election candidates on Saturday afternoon, largely preserving the existing hierarchy.

Chris Bishop retained third place on National's list, a fairly safe spot, even if he lost his hold on the marginal Hutt South electorate.

Similarly, Paul Goldsmith, who's unlikely to win Epsom from ACT leader David Seymour, retained his current sixth position in caucus.

Speaker Gerry Brownlee, who's running as a list-only candidate, was boosted to the ninth spot, up from 14th in 2023.

The move stops short of the traditional third ranking sometimes given to Speakers, but makes Brownlee's return likely if National performs near its current polling.

Recent polls put National on about 31 percent, which would secure them about 39 or 40 seats. Political analysts have noted that a strong performance across electorates, however, could leave the party with very few list MPs.

But for Bishop, Goldsmith and Brownlee, the election rankings should provide a degree of protection and comfort.

Chris Bishop retained third place on National's list. RNZ / Mark Papalii

In line with the party's constitution, leader Christopher Luxon and deputy Nicola Willis took the top two positions. Willis is also reliant on her list spot to return.

The list ranked Simeon Brown fourth, Erica Stanford fifth, Louise Upston seventh and Mark Mitchell eighth. All four of them are expected to win their electorates.

Tama Potaka shot to 11th on the list, up from from 24th in 2023. In contrast, former broadcasting minister Melissa Lee dropped from 13th to 30th.

New faces who have been awarded high rankings include Dale Stephens in Christchurch Central (23), Mahesh Muralidhar in Tamaki (24), Katie Milne in West Coast-Tasman (25) and Angee Nicholas in Henderson (26).

Deputy leader Nicola Willis at National's list announcement for the 2026 election. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

The party highlighted all four candidates in its promotional material, noting Milne's history as a former Federated Farmers president and Stephens' executive experience.

Luxon: 'It's a week in politics for me'

Addressing reporters at Wellington Airport, Luxon said National was "ruthlessly focused" on maximising its party vote.

He said Brownlee's ranking reflected that he was considered a great "kaumātua" or elder in the party.

"He's been in Parliament now for 30 years. We really value Gerry. We think very highly of him."

Gerry Brownlee. Angus Dreaver / RNZ

National's list announcement comes at a difficult point for the governing party, with its support having fallen significantly from the 2023 election.

It also follows a difficult period for Luxon who began the week apologising to small businesses in Rotorua.

Luxon did win some reprieve, with the latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll predicting the coalition's return to power - and showing a significant drop in support for the current opposition parties.

Party leader Christopher Luxon speaks at National's list announcement for the 2026 election. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

He batted away questions from reporters about his performance over the past week, saying he was "moving forward" and focused on the campaign ahead.

"It's a week in politics for me," he said.

"I have some good weeks and some challenging weeks."

Luxon played down his impromptu campaign promise for an MMP referendum, saying it was his job as party leader to make decisions in the moment.

"I'm asked to form a judgement on things. I want to be as definitive and clear as I possibly can."

National president Sylvia Wood also defended Luxon's decision to make a policy decision on the fly: "I'm 100 percent fine with that."

National Party president Sylvia Wood. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Asked whether the board retained confidence in Luxon, Wood replied: "Absolutely."

World.title: New Zealand places further sanctions against Russia supporters
World.content:
New Zealand has placed another round of sanctions targeting those supporting Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The latest package targets 33 individuals and groups, with a particular focus on cyber actors, and those involved in the forced relocation, abduction and re-education of Ukrainian children.

The sanctions also target people supporting Russia's military-industrial complex, political figures, and North Koreans and Iranians providing support to Moscow.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters said New Zealand remained concerned about the treatment of Ukrainian children.

"Children should never be used as instruments of war," he said. "New Zealand remains deeply concerned by efforts to abduct and re-educate Ukrainian children through co-ercive state-directed programmes."

The package also targets malicious cyber actors and people involved in spreading anti-Ukraine propaganda aimed at legitimising Russia's invasion.

Peters said cyber activity could have real-world consequences, including helping Russia gather intelligence, evade sanctions and disrupt opponents of its war.

"New Zealand stands with our partners in calling out Moscow's use of these actors."

This is New Zealand's 36th round of sanctions against Russia, since the Russia Sanctions Act came into force in March 2022.

World.title: Beloved Nelson cafe forced to close after landlord dispute and roadworks woes
World.content:
A popular Nelson cafe and gallery has announced its closure, after a dispute with the landlord and ongoing roadworks made it untenable to continue.

Red Art Gallery & Café owners Ant and Suzi Stevens say after nine years in business, its closure was forced after the landlord chose not to renew the lease, a devastating blow after months of roadworks on the two adjacent streets had seriously impacted revenue.

The work, part of the $78 million Bridge to Better project, has seen water pipes and other infrastructure along the the length of Bridge Street replaced, causing disruption to a number of businesses since it first began last year.

The couple said the decision to close in September was not the outcome they wanted, especially on the back of a tough few years,

"It's just heartbreaking, I just feel like I'm losing a child to be honest, it's just been my baby for so long," Suzi said.

The business had survived a global pandemic, a recession and roadworks which effectively left them an island, with the cafe and gallery entrance hidden behind fences, trucks and diggers.

Bridge Street and Haven Road either side of the business have been closed for months while the roads are ripped up and pipes replaced, with customers having to walk down narrow, uneven gravel paths between temporary fences to reach the business.

The gallery represented about 60 artists, most of them from Nelson and Tasman, and they had taken on more after the Suter Art Gallery made the decision to stop stocking the work of around 40 local artists, after getting advice from external retail specialists.

Roadworks in Nelson are taking a toll on local businesses. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Since announcing the closure on social media, the couple had received hundreds of comments in support.

The cafe was full on Friday morning when RNZ visited. Within an hour, it had made as much money as it had over the previous two days combined.

"We knew there would be strong support, but not the way it's been with the messages, with the people coming in," Ant said.

"Love and compassion and heart will beat greed any day."

He said the council told the couple they would be the "most impacted business" given their proximity to the roadworks, but there had been "zero talk of compensation or help in any way", except to be asked whether they had two hard years in them until the upgrade was complete.

"It'll be wonderful for someone else, but it won't be us," Ant said.

Council agrees to defer rates if landlords come to the party

Nelson mayor Nick Smith previously said he had met with a number of "very distressed" business owners who were feeling the pressure of the ongoing roadworks.

Staff had gone to "tremendous effort" to try and minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses, he said.

Smith acknowledged the work was "incredibly disruptive" but said it was essential to renew and upgrade infrastructure that, in some places, was over 100 years old.

Once complete, Bridge Street was tipped to be a "people-focused corridor" with utility services capable of supporting inner city development.

At a council meeting on Thursday, elected members agreed to allow affected businesses to defer rates from the current year, with repayments split over the next three years, if landlords agreed to provide the equivalent financial relief to the tenant.

Nelson's mayor says council staff are trying to minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Nelson Tasman Chamber of Commerce chair Venus Guy said it was disappointing to see the closure of long-standing local businesses.

"Red Gallery has been part of our city centre, and our thoughts are with the owners and everyone affected by this decision."

She said while the Bridge to Better project was an important investment in Nelson's future, the major infrastructure work placed very real pressures on businesses during construction.

"It is essential that we continue working together to minimise disruption, support affected businesses and remind our community that our city centre remains open for business.

Central city businesses feeling the hurt

Longstanding cafe and food store Prego Mediterranean Foods & Comida Cafe shut its doors in June, and the owners said at the time that the [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/625679/road-closures-and-rising-costs-force-closure-of-nelson-businessongoing ongoing roadworks were one of the factors in its closure].

Further down Bridge Street, Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten said he thought more could be done to support businesses affected by the infrastructure works.

At lunchtime on Friday, his restaurant was empty and the noise of roadworks outside made it hard to be heard when speaking.

He had organised a meeting with about 30 Bridge Street business owners that were also struggling around two months ago.

He said the rates deferral scheme made little difference. It gave relief of about $80 per month, but would have to be paid back in the years to come.

Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten sits in front of his restaurant and behind a fence while work is done on Bridge Street. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Corten, who had owned and operated hospitality businesses in Nelson for more than a decade, said he bought Pizzeria Bella a year ago. He started out with nine employees, but was now down to three. Only he and his son were working full-time, with debt that kept rising.

Pizzeria Bella's revenue was down 80 percent since the roadworks began. On Tuesday, Corten made $300 between the lunch and dinner services. His accountant had told him he needed turnover of $2000 a day to survive.

"Every day I am more negative, more negative."

Corten said two businesses had closed and it was possible that more would follow.

World.title: Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off'
World.content:
The catchcry of the Tour de France Femmes by its lead sponsor, Zwift, is pretty simple: Watch the Femmes.

By and large, the viewership data shows that people are doing exactly that.

And why wouldn't they?

After a riveting seven days of racing so far, capped by Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney's masterful ascent of the legendary Mont Ventoux, the top three riders in this year's race are separated by just 39 seconds.

Six different riders have claimed stage victories so far, with the overall race lead changing hands three times since the opening stage.

The 2024 champion, Niewiadoma-Phinney, holds a 15-second advantage over Demi Vollering, the woman she beat two years ago by a measly four seconds.

This is a race that has had it all.

The three-way battle between Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney has captivated fans this year. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

But fans, as yet, cannot watch the race in its entirety, with just three of the nine stages of this year's race televised from start to finish.

The lack of comprehensive live coverage is a growing pain that the women's edition of the Tour de France is hoping to overcome as the fifth edition of its most recent iteration comes to a close in Nice this weekend.

It is something that women's riders' union, The Cyclists' Alliance (TCA) — whose president is Australian former world and Olympic champion Grace Brown — has criticised throughout the race.

"For the biggest race in women's cycling, partial coverage is no longer enough," TCA wrote in a social media post.

The 'accursed' mountain that stands apart this Tour de France The ascent to hell on the punishing slopes of Mont Ventoux is one of the Tour de France's most formidable and iconic theatres.

"Fans will still miss the attacks, the tactics, and the moments that could define the race."

Broadcaster Orla Chennaoui, who hosts the coverage for TNT Sports in the UK, was less diplomatic.

"I'm getting really annoyed now. I'm getting really, really pissed off," she said on an Instagram reel that she titled: Women's sport done a disservice Editions #4957.

"What the heck? There is so much excitement and interest in the Tour de France Femmes.

"The riders, the race have proven over and over again how dynamic and dramatic this sport is.

"I have never seen my [social media] algorithm so flooded with excitement, with joy, with celebration for this race.

Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney won her first Tour de France Femmes stage on the slopes of Mont Ventoux. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's everywhere, on Instagram, podcasts popping up all over the place, YouTube videos, more written articles that I would ever have imagined when I started covering women's cycling 10 years ago.

"And we still, despite this, despite how proven the interest is, we cannot get live TV coverage.

"ASO [Amaury Sport Organisation], what are you doing? Why can we not get to watch all stages live?"

The astonishing story behind the women's Tour The Tour de France Femmes produced one of the closest finishes in cycling stage race history last year. But when the women's Tour was first revived, it was called "ugly".

Chennaoui said there was a "huge will" from broadcasters to show the race in its entirety every day in that post, which she acknowledged she may get in trouble for and be asked to delete.

All 21 stages of the men's Tour de France were broadcast live in their entirety.

On the same day that the third stage of the women's Tour de France Femme was half-shown, stage one of the men's Tour de Pologne World Tour race was shown in full, all five hours, four minutes and 11 seconds of what was a flat, 234.2-kilometre race.

The duration of the Tour de France Femmes broadcast has increased to 27 hours and 40 minutes for this year's race, up five hours and 20 minutes from what was shown live in 2024.

However, TCA noted that France Télévisions data showed a 40 per cent increase in viewership from 18.3 million in 2024 to 25.7 million in 2025.

"The demand is undeniable," TCA said.

"We are asking for the coverage to catch up."

One of the pre-race favourites, Demi Vollering crashed early in the stage. (Getty Images: Alex Broadway)

That post was put up in the hours before stage three took place, a stage won by Norway's Sigrid Haugset with an 88km breakaway attack.

However, the move that saw the Norwegian break away from the peloton was completely missed, as the TV cameras had not started rolling.

Additionally, one of the pre-race favourites, Vollering crashed early in the stage, an incident that was, again, missed by the cameras, and could have huge repercussions for the rest of the race.

"That was disappointing," former world champion on the track and the road Lizzie Deignan told the For The Love Of Cycling podcast.

"There's no substitute for footage. You can't get a feel of the race, of the tension, of the atmosphere."

According to organisers, this year's Tour de France Femmes is being broadcast in 190 countries, including by SBS in Australia.

France Télévisions keeps the supporters of women's cycling in the shade with their coverage. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Romain Doucelin)

However, SBS and the Tour's other broadcast partners around the world can only show the footage they are provided with.

France Télévisions handles production and distribution of the broadcast on behalf of the Amaury Sport Organisation [ASO].

The ASO is also responsible for the men's Tour de France, as well as other major cycling events, including two of cycling's monument one day races, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix.

The organisation was heavily criticised for its coverage of the women's edition of Paris-Roubaix earlier this year, with less than 90 minutes of the three-and-a-half hour race shown.

"Paris-Roubaix this year, regardless of what they are going to say about TV numbers, was a step backwards," Chennaoui said in her Instagram reel.

"They're still doing a disservice to women's racing."

Tour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse says things are moving in the right direction. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

As for the Tour de France Femmes, Deignan, who won the 2020 edition of La Course by Le Tour de France, a one-day precursor to the current women's multi-stage Tour, said the lack of coverage was a return to the "old days" of following professional cycling.

"It was very hard to follow from home," Deignan said of stage three of this year's Tour.

"It was like being back in the old days, refreshing news feeds, trying to figure out what's going on."

Cycling Weekly spoke to race director Marion Rousse about the criticism, and she said the race was moving towards full broadcast coverage.

"We're giving serious consideration to broadcasting all the stages in full in the future because the women deserve it," Rousse told Cycling Weekly.

"It works well in terms of audience figures.

"We're currently giving it real consideration, which is a step forward. Things are moving in the right direction."

World.title: AFL chair apologises for his part in Cats concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond has apologised for his part in Geelong's controversial concussion contract with defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

Drummond was Geelong president two years ago when premiership defender Kolodjashnij signed a contract in which he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

It is understood Kolodjashnij's agent was not aware of the contract, and neither the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) or AFL were informed at the time.

It is also understood that while Kolodjashnij passed an independent medical test, he was still considered at risk of future complications from head injuries.

Jake's twin brother, Kade, was forced to retire from the game in 2020 due to ongoing concussion problems.

"I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024," Drummond said.

"This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board.

"Jake's welfare was central to all discussions, and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days.

Cats face 'please explain' Geelong is finally issued a 'please explain' over its controversial concussion contract with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

"While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.

"Regardless of the player's agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed."

Drummond said it was an error to keep the process quiet, and clarified that he would not be involved in AFL discussions about the matter.

"As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA," Drummond said.

"I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations.

"I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation."

Speaking to ABC Sport ahead of the Saturday games, AFL boss Andrew Dillon reiterated that it was a complex situation.

"This is an issue that is really complex and in this one in particular it's complex and unique," Dillon said.

"But concussion and the effects that has on players or participants in contact sports ... is an issue that's confronting contact sports worldwide.

"What we have here is a player that has suffered multiple concussions, went before an AFL concussion panel, ultimately over a period of months was cleared as fit to play.

"Through that period, over a number of months, Jake's worked with the club doctors, independent medical experts, the club, and the club board and management to make sure that he understood their were risks to continue playing, not withstanding that you've been cleared medically fit to play.

"That was the intent behind what was going on."

Dillon said the please explain was around why the concussion agreement sat alongside his playing contract.

"We've gone to Geelong under the rules and asked them why it wasn't lodged with us," Dillon said.

"So we're waiting to hear back from Geelong on that."

The Cats are expected to be fined over the contract saga after initially being cleared of wrongdoing.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
